editorial.feelRationale: Devin Desktop is the rebranded Windsurf editor, a VS Code/Electron-derived shell rather than a GPU-native renderer; the desktop changelog logs concrete UI-speed fixes ('Faster startup, bounded memory for background transcripts and streamed file writes, and cheaper loading spinners' and 'Significantly improved performance for switching between Agent and Editor mode') and a customer quote calls the local app 'snappier' than the cloud version, evidencing rough edges that were actively found and fixed rather than a pristine native feel.

tools.name: Diri
tools.tagline: Run coding agents side by side
tools.valueProp: Diri keeps native GPUI agent sessions alive through app and Engine restarts while agents spawn helpers into managed worktrees. Notes, schedules, voice replies, and an in-app review panel bring planning and integration into the same workspace.

pricing.notes: Diri is free under AGPL-3.0 and uses coding-agent CLIs and accounts installed by the user; agent vendor charges remain separate.

featureNotes.platforms.windows: As of October 2026, ROADMAP.md listed Windows as in progress; no Windows release is offered.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: As of October 2026, the install guide labelled Linux beta; Ubuntu x86_64/arm64 packages are not included with every release and lack some macOS features.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: As of October 2026, the signed iPhone companion was in beta, paired over Tailscale; there is no App Store release.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Connects by SSH to machines the user controls; optional per-user diri-node adds account and migration features.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: Optional diri-node runs on a user-controlled VPS; ordinary remote sessions need only SSH and no vendor relay.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: A user-written JSON manifest can add a terminal agent or replace a built-in agent definition; it must describe launch and status rules.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: The Worktrees guide documents dirijor worktree create/remove, fresh worktrees for recipes and schedules, and agent MCP worktree creation. Diri manages the checkout and branch rather than merely accepting an existing worktree.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: The Review panel follows existing pull requests and links to GitHub for merge; the docs do not describe creating a PR in Diri.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: An agent can use integrate to merge, squash, or cherry-pick a helper branch into its local checkout; conflicts abort and report paths.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Notes contain to-dos that can launch agents and track their progress, but the docs show no dedicated Kanban or general task queue.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Version 0.10.0 adds spoken completion summaries and voice replies on macOS.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Optional diri-node adds per-machine account logins, but the docs do not establish a shared multi-person workspace.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: The phone companion accesses the owner’s Mac sessions; the docs do not establish simultaneous multi-person control.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The app and Engine run on the user’s machine; remote sessions use the user’s SSH host without a Diri relay. Optional diagnostic uploads can be disabled.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Privacy.md documents a sharing switch and DIRI_TELEMETRY=off, which disables recording; uploads are enabled unless the user turns sharing off.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial: docs/agents describes JSON manifests that add or replace agent launch/status definitions, and docs/cli documents external commands that drive Diri sessions and layouts. No documented loader adds third-party code to Diri panels or core; Cursor’s plugin directory and agent MCP/skills in docs/mcp are agent-side.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: The built-in MCP server and dirijor CLI can create and control sessions, worktrees, notes, schedules and layouts.

github.description: The best way to work with coding agents. Run fifty in parallel, let them spawn each other, review everything in one place.

activity.changelogCadence: frequent: 39 Diri v-tags in 90 days; v0.10.0 on October 18 followed v0.9.7 on October 12

editorial.reachRationale: The product has 16 GitHub contributors, 453 stars and 1,237 asset downloads across its five most recent versioned releases as of October 19. These show early use; stars measure attention rather than active users, and asset downloads can include repeat installs.
editorial.polishRationale: Signed/notarized macOS builds, a self-updater, detailed install/security/recovery docs, and an in-app review flow support a finished experience; Linux and iPhone were beta as of October 2026.
editorial.depthRationale: Managed worktrees, agent spawning and coordination, branch integration, diff review, notes with agent-linked to-dos, schedules, remote SSH hosts, and session recovery extend well beyond a terminal wrapper.
editorial.feelRationale: The native Rust/GPUI client and per-session Holder processes avoid a browser or Electron layer. The project’s performance audit documents first-frame session switching, a binary terminal input path, and measured latency fixtures; no independent hands-on responsiveness check was possible here.

tools.name: Emdash
tools.tagline: Open-source agentic development environment
tools.valueProp: The widest agent registry in the set: 35 CLI providers detected automatically, plus a provision script contract that gives each task its own machine on your AWS, Hetzner or Docker. Desktop-only and single-user; managed cloud is contact-sales.

maker.name: General Action, Inc.
maker.funding: YC W26; San Francisco

pricing.notes: The desktop app is free and Apache-2.0 (terms page: 'a free, open-source desktop application'). Agents run through their own CLIs on your own logins or keys; Emdash does not proxy or resell model usage. 'Emdash Cloud' (ephemeral vendor-run workspaces) and 'Emdash Enterprise' (managed dev environments, centralized configuration, admin controls) are contact-sales forms with no published pricing. Remote Tasks docs also say 'Contact us to get started: founders@emdash.com'.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Electron app; Apple Silicon and Intel DMGs, or `brew install --cask emdash` (homebrew-core cask).
featureNotes.platforms.windows: x64 installer, MSI and portable EXE. tmux session persistence is not available for local Windows projects.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: AppImage, DEB and RPM for x64 and (since v1.2.x) native ARM64.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: No user-facing CLI. The only command-line binary is `emdash-workspace-server` (start/stop/status of the remote daemon), not a way to start or steer agents.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Remote Projects: the UI stays local while worktrees, Git, terminals, lifecycle scripts and agent CLIs run on an SSH host (agent, key or password auth; ProxyJump/ForwardAgent supported). Since v1.2.0 the desktop installs an Emdash Workspace Server daemon on the host and talks to it over SSH stream-local forwarding; optional tmux keeps sessions alive across reconnects.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: 'Emdash Cloud' (ephemeral, isolated vendor infrastructure per task) exists only as a contact-sales page; nothing self-serve is documented.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The Apache-2.0 `@emdash/workspace-server` daemon runs on your own remote host, exposes no TCP port (Unix socket reached over SSH) and needs no vendor service.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Auto-approve, resume and lifecycle hooks; MCP configs synced into ~/.claude.json.
featureNotes.agents.codex: Auto-approve, resume, hooks; ACP chat with Default/Plan modes and a model selector (GPT-6 Astra listed).
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Not in the 35-provider registry as of 2026-09-18 (Google is represented by Antigravity and Jules).
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Listed as 'GitHub Copilot' (`copilot`): auto-approve, resume, hooks.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: `cursor-agent`: auto-approve and resume; no lifecycle hooks.
featureNotes.agents.amp: Auto-approve, resume, hooks; prompt is passed over stdin.
featureNotes.agents.pi: `pi`: resume and hooks; Oh My Pi (`omp`) is a separate provider.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Providers come from a fixed in-app registry ('Provider behavior is based on the Emdash app registry'); an unlisted CLI cannot be pointed at. Missing agents are requested via GitHub issue or added by PR to the registry.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Emdash runs agents only through their official CLIs; it ships no agent or model routing of its own.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Default per task, under ~/emdash/worktrees locally or <project>/.emdash/worktrees on SSH hosts; can be disabled per task to work on the checked-out branch, with a warning.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Remote Tasks: a per-project provision script you write (VM, Kubernetes pod, Docker container or internal dev platform) prints SSH details as JSON and Emdash runs the task inside it, then calls your terminate script. Emdash supplies no sandbox itself, and the docs gate the feature ('when the workspace provider feature is enabled in your Emdash build'; 'Contact us to get started').
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Each task gets its own branch and worktree from a chosen base; names auto-generated, or Linear's branch name for Linear issues.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Changed/Staged/Pull Requests panel with unified or split diffs, stage/unstage/discard, inline editing of unstaged diffs, and PR files, commits, checks and comments.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: 'Commit & Create PR' or 'Push & Create PR' through a connected GitHub account (Emdash account, gh CLI import or device flow). GitHub only.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: PRs can be merged from the Pull Requests section via the GitHub API and the panel shows merge state; no conflict-resolution helper is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Only session resume (terminal state saved, agents resume on relaunch) and 2-second autosave of unsaved editor buffers; no snapshot or rollback of files or agent state.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: A per-project task list (sortable by last used or creation time) fed by 'From Issue' creation from Linear, Asana, Monday.com, Trello, GitHub, Jira, GitLab, Plane, Forgejo, Featurebase, Plain and Notion. No kanban columns or queue; automations have their own run history list.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Cron-scheduled, project-scoped automations that spin up a workspace (new worktree, existing workspace, repo root or sandbox) and start an agent with a saved prompt and provider; 'run now', enable/pause, full run history, and any run can be converted into a regular task. No event triggers documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Lifecycle hooks (installed into each agent's user config, marker-tagged) report working / awaiting input / done and drive notifications for 20 of the 35 providers; the other providers only show terminal state.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: An optional Emdash account (created in the browser via GitHub) exists only to attach GitHub accounts; the app itself is single-user with local SQLite state. Teams share project defaults by committing .emdash.json. Org accounts and admin controls are promised only on the contact-sales Cloud/Enterprise pages.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: No published team plan. The Cloud page ('for business and team setups, including managed remote environments, centralized configuration, and admin controls') and the Enterprise page are contact forms with a company-size picker and no pricing.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Local-first SQLite state, no sign-in required (an optional Emdash account is one of three ways to connect GitHub). The only vendor endpoints are PostHog telemetry (off-able) and the contact-sales Cloud.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: README: 'Bring the CLI agents you already use'; each agent CLI authenticates with its own provider and 'may send code, prompts, and context to their own providers'. Emdash bills nothing.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Anonymous PostHog telemetry on by default in production builds, allowlisted events only; disable in Settings > General > Privacy & Telemetry or with TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false. Signed-in users may have github_username/account_id attached.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Nothing for third parties: `packages/plugins/package.json` (`@emdash/plugins`, "Plugin interfaces and helpers for agent providers") is an internal, compile-time TypeScript workspace package with exports like `./agents` and `./integrations/github` resolving to build output under `./dist`, consumed by Emdash's own build, not a runtime loader third-party code can hook into. No extensions folder, manifest or SDK is documented anywhere in emdash.com/docs. The Library's skills and MCP servers (emdash.com/docs/library) extend the agents Emdash runs, not Emdash's own panels or commands.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: No API, CLI or MCP server for driving Emdash from outside. The MCP Library (54-server catalog, custom stdio/http servers) writes configs into each agent's native config file for the agents' use.

github.description: Emdash is the Open-Source Agentic Development Environment (🧡 YC W26). Run multiple coding agents in parallel. Use any provider.

top.title: Show HN: Emdash – Open-source agentic development environment

editorial.reachRationale: 133,270 release-asset downloads, 131 contributors, and a strong 206-point Show HN (71 comments) support an established user base; the Discord (630 members) is modest and X follower count could not be measured, so this stops short of 'major'.
editorial.polishRationale: A v1 stable across macOS, Windows and Linux (x64 and ARM64) with a homebrew-core cask, a 25-page docs site refreshed shortly before the September 2026 research pass, a weekly stable release train (five in the two weeks after v1.2.0) with a canary channel, 131 contributors and the homepage's 'Over 1M downloads' claim. Held back because the marketing pages are thinner than the docs (FAQ accordions, Cloud and Enterprise are one-screen contact forms), Remote Tasks are gated behind 'contact us', and 100 open issues on a 2,600-commits-per-quarter repo signal churn.
editorial.depthRationale: Well past a tmux wrapper with worktree-per-task, a diff/PR/CI panel that merges from inside the app, twelve issue-tracker integrations, cron automations with run history, an in-app browser with profiles, a Library that syncs prompts, skills and MCP configs into every agent's config, and a script contract for provisioning ephemeral per-task remote workspaces. Held back because there is no orchestrator agent, no agents-spawn-agents flow, no kanban, no API/CLI/MCP control surface and no collaboration beyond a shared .emdash.json.
editorial.feelRationale: Electron desktop app (telemetry schema logs `electron_version`; in-app browser docs mention opening 'Electron DevTools'), a typical Electron stack with no Rust/Swift/Go in the repo's language breakdown. No maker performance claims and no user reports of lag or notable speed turned up in docs, changelog, or web search.

tools.name: Factory
tools.tagline: The foundation for your software factory
tools.valueProp: Factory routes work across any model, Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, open-weight, instead of shipping one house agent, and can run entirely inside a customer's network via hybrid or airgapped deployment. Missions add a structured Orchestrator/Worker/Validator layer that Devin, Codex and Cursor don't have.

maker.name: Factory AI
maker.funding: $150M Series C from Khosla Ventures, Sequoia Capital, Blackstone, Insight Partners, Evantic Capital, 20VC, NEA and Mantis VC at a $1.5B valuation (factory.com/news/series-c).

pricing.notes: Individuals: Pro $20/mo (Factory App, Droid CLI, Droid SDK, cloud and local background agents), Plus $100/mo (~5x Pro usage, Managed Droid Computers for remote runs), Max $200/mo (~10x Pro usage, early feature access). No free tier; usage governed by rolling 5-hour/7-day/30-day Rate Limits plus prepaid Extra Usage credits and a free Droid Core open-weight model pool. Organizations: Teams $60/mo + $40/seat (up to 10 seats), Business custom (up to 150 seats, SSO/SAML/SCIM, ZDR, audit logging), Enterprise custom (unlimited seats, dedicated compute, on-prem/airgapped, data residency). BYOK is free up to an allowance on Individual plans, then billed per plan.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Factory App ships separate Apple Silicon and Intel .dmg downloads (factory-app/quickstart).
featureNotes.platforms.windows: Factory App ships Windows x64 and ARM64 installers, plus an MSIX path for managed device deployment (enterprise/windows-msix-deployment).
featureNotes.platforms.linux: No Factory App desktop build for Linux, the quickstart's download step only lists Mac and Windows. The `droid` CLI is a cross-platform npm package (installed via `curl -fsSL https://app.factory.ai/cli | sh` or npm) and runs on Linux, so CLI-only usage is covered.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: No native iOS app or App Store listing found. The quickstart says 'Factory sessions carry the same project context across desktop, web, and mobile surfaces,' and a screenshot references a 'mobile composer keyboard' bug, implying a mobile-responsive web session view rather than a dedicated app.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Same as iOS: no native app or Play Store listing; only a mobile-responsive web surface is evidenced.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: `droid` CLI (npm), full command/flag reference at droid-cli/cli-reference including `--worktree`, `--mission`, `--worker-model`, `--validator-model`, and autonomy-level flags.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: The CLI is an interactive terminal chat with a Mission Control overlay (`Ctrl+T`) that shows live worker/validator status for the active mission, but this multiplexes workers within one mission, not independent droid CLI sessions like a tmux-style multiplexer.
featureNotes.execution.local: Factory App and CLI connect directly to your local machine and working directory (factory-app/quickstart: 'The Factory App connects directly to your local machine').
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Droid Computers BYOM: `droid computer register` turns your own machine into a persistent remote target you fully control (droid-computers/overview).
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Droid Computers Managed: Factory-provisioned cloud VMs (4 CPU / 8GB RAM / 6GB swap) with auto-pause/resume, selectable as a Mission's execution target.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: Enterprise-only, contract-gated: the Hybrid deployment pattern runs Droid entirely inside customer infrastructure with LLM/OTEL traffic staying internal, and a Fully Airgapped pattern isolates the network completely with on-prem models (enterprise/network-and-deployment). Not available on self-serve Individual/Teams plans.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Droid is Factory's own agent; model choice is decoupled via BYOK/model routing (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Kimi, DeepSeek, Mistral, Qwen, Llama, or a custom endpoint) rather than by embedding third-party CLI agents inside Factory's own interface.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Factory App: dedicated Settings → Worktrees feature with ephemeral/persistent lifecycle, setup profiles (`.factory/worktree-setups/*.yaml`), `.worktreeinclude`, default location `~/.factory/worktrees`, default ephemeral limit 15. CLI: `-w, --worktree [name]` flag. This is the mechanism for running multiple isolated Droid sessions on the same repo in parallel.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Quickstart's core workflow is 'Droid analyzes your codebase, proposes changes, and shows what will be modified before applying anything'; IDE integrations add IDE-native diff views for VS Code/Cursor/Windsurf.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Software Factory's 'Ticket to Code' and Code Review use cases and the GitHub/GitLab connectors describe Droid implementing tickets and reviewing every PR, which presumes Droid opens PRs as part of that flow; the CLI reference documents PR-oriented autonomy levels.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Two complementary mechanisms: Worktrees let one person run several isolated Droid CLI/App sessions on the same repo at once, and Missions/Mission Control run a single Orchestrator plus multiple Worker agents (and a Validator) on different features/milestones simultaneously, monitored via the Factory App dashboard or the CLI's `Ctrl+T` overlay.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Mission Control's main view tracks features and milestones with a live per-worker progress log in the sidebar (missions/running-app), functioning as a task board over the mission's plan.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Custom Droids (`.factory/droids/*.md`) are Task-tool-invoked subagents with their own model/tools/autonomy, runnable in the foreground or backgrounded (`run_in_background: true`) and resumable; built-in `worker` and `explorer` droids ship by default (harness/subagents).
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Software Factory / Automations: scheduled or triggered engineering workflows (triage, code review, QA, incident response, docs) wired to GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear, Slack, Sentry, PagerDuty and other connectors.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Within a Mission, the Orchestrator directs and can be paused/redirected to re-instruct Worker and Validator agents ('pause the orchestrator ... instruct it to re-assess or re-plan'); this is orchestration-hierarchy messaging, not a general agent-to-agent inbox.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Business (up to 150 seats, SSO/SAML/SCIM) and Enterprise (unlimited seats, centralized org config) tiers on top of Teams (up to 10 seats).
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Teams $60/mo + $40/seat, Business and Enterprise custom seat-based contracts (pricing/organizations).
featureNotes.openness.openSource: Closed source. The public `Factory-AI/factory` GitHub org/repo is a README-only landing page ('Copyright © 2025-2026 Factory AI. All rights reserved.'), not the product's source, so no repo is listed.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Partial: the Hybrid and Fully Airgapped enterprise deployment patterns let Droid run entirely within customer infrastructure, including on-prem/in-network models with no outbound connectivity, but this is an Enterprise-tier contracted deployment, not a self-serve download-and-run option.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Model Independence / BYOK: `customModels[]` in `~/.factory/settings.json` supports Anthropic, OpenAI and generic chat-completion-API providers plus AWS Bedrock routing and an `apiKeyHelper` for dynamic credentials; free up to an allowance on Individual plans.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Partial: message-content export is off by default and can be forced off by an org-managed `telemetry.logMessageContent: false` (never sent to Factory's own collector in any configuration), but usage metrics always fan out to Factory's collector except in a Fully Airgapped enterprise deployment, there is no self-serve switch to stop metrics entirely (enterprise/telemetry/privacy).
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: False: Factory's Plugins (`droid plugin install`, `.factory-plugin/` manifests, `droid plugin marketplace add`) and Internal Plugin Marketplaces (enterprise governance over the same system) exclusively package skills, commands, custom droids (subagents), output styles, hooks and `mcp.json`, i.e., they extend what the agent can do, not Factory App's or CLI's own interface, panels, or session lifecycle. Hooks (`~/.factory/hooks.json`) are lifecycle callbacks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, etc.), which don't count either. No mechanism for third-party code to add a panel, view, command, provider, or runtime to Factory's own core was found (harness/plugins, harness/hooks, enterprise/internal-plugin-marketplaces).
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: MCP is a first-class integration path (harness/mcp; connected via Step 4 of the quickstart) alongside direct connectors (Linear, Slack, GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Notion, Sentry, PagerDuty, Asana, Microsoft Teams, Codecov, Google Cloud/Drive, Azure, Docker, DX, CircleCI) and a documented REST surface for automations.

top.title: Factory AI Code Droid Achieves SOTA on SWE-Bench

activity.changelogCadence: near-daily: 8 dated releases from 2026-09-17 to 2026-09-24 (v0.222.0 to v0.226.1) on docs.factory.ai/changelog/release-notes

editorial.reachRationale: Factory is the company’s only product: a $1.5B Series C with named enterprise customers (RBC, T-Mobile, Blackstone, DoorDash) and about 45k monthly npm downloads of the droid CLI put it past emerging, though its 1.6k-member Discord and small Show HN footprint keep it short of major.
editorial.polishRationale: My call, judged from docs rather than hands-on: documentation is extensive and dated (226 changelog releases at a weekly-ish cadence, MSIX enterprise deployment guides, telemetry docs with granular OTEL semantics). Gaps: no Linux desktop build, mobile is a responsive web surface rather than a native app, and several core orchestration fields (containers, checkpoints, notifications, voice, shared sessions) have no first-party documentation either way.
editorial.depthRationale: Beyond a single-session assistant, Factory stacks Worktrees (parallel isolated sessions on one repo), Missions (Orchestrator/Worker/Validator multi-agent orchestration with a visual Mission Control dashboard or CLI overlay), Droid Computers (BYOM and managed persistent remote compute), Custom Droids/subagents, model-independent BYOK routing across many providers, and enterprise hybrid/airgapped self-hosting. Short of platform depth: Missions' own docs list open questions ('Is parallelization necessary?') and recommend a sweet spot of up to 500 features, so the orchestration layer was still being tuned as of September 2026, and the shared Remote Delegations flow for Slack/Linear is explicitly Private Preview.
editorial.feelRationale: No implementation language, rendering stack, or performance claim was found for the Factory App: the public Factory-AI/factory repo is a README-only landing page with no source, and the docs never name an engine, so the client's stack cannot be determined.

tools.name: GitHub Agent HQ
tools.tagline: AI agents that do more than write code
tools.valueProp: GitHub’s Agents view assigns Copilot, Claude, Codex and partner agent apps from the same repository and PR workflow. Sessions can start on GitHub or mobile, then continue in the Copilot CLI or app.

maker.name: GitHub
maker.funding: Microsoft subsidiary

pricing.notes: Cloud agent is in paid Copilot plans: Pro $10, Pro+ $39, Max $100 per user/month, plus Business/Enterprise. Tasks consume GitHub Actions minutes and AI credits; third-party agents are included subject to plan and policy.

featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Copilot CLI sessions can run on a user-controlled, online machine and be steered from GitHub.com or Mobile; this is remote control of that session, not a GitHub-provisioned host.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: The first-party Copilot app offers New working tree for each local session; GitHub cloud agent instead creates a branch in a GitHub Actions environment.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: GitHub web/mobile can surface and answer CLI permission requests and questions when remote control is enabled; general push notification coverage for all agents is not documented.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: The Copilot app allows a bring-your-own API key for local sessions, but GitHub cloud agents and partner agents use paid Copilot plans and AI credits.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, preview extension: partner-built GitHub Agent Apps install code-backed agents into the Agents UI selector and issue/PR entry points, but the documented Agent Apps mechanism was public preview as of September 2026 and does not add arbitrary panels or commands. See About agent apps; MCP, skills and custom prompts alone are agent-side.

top.title: Agent HQ: Any agent, any way you work

activity.changelogCadence: weekly: 4 Copilot weekly release roundups in 4 September weeks

editorial.reachRationale: My call: few people use the Agents view itself. It ships with paid Copilot plans and has a documented web, mobile, CLI and app route, and the Copilot CLI package recorded 8.8 million monthly downloads. Those numbers measure Copilot, not Agent HQ, so they do not carry over.
editorial.polishRationale: The Agents page, repository tab, app, mobile and CLI have first-party instructions and weekly releases, but third-party agents, Agent Apps and the agent tasks API remain public preview.
editorial.depthRationale: Parallel cloud sessions, local app worktrees, session sharing, live logs, PR review and merge, automations, custom agents, agent apps, mobile monitoring, remote CLI control and enterprise policy extend beyond session switching.
editorial.feelRationale: GitHub’s September 2026 engineering write-up describes a virtualized diff renderer, batched measurement and cached recent diffs in the Copilot app to keep very large PRs responsive. The main Agents view is browser-based and no measured session-switch latency is established, so the neutral web middle score is more defensible than a native-speed claim.

tools.name: Golutra
tools.tagline: Beyond the IDE. Multi-Agent Era.
tools.valueProp: A solo-built Tauri desktop app that turns Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and OpenClaw into “squad members” who message each other and a human Commander in one chat feed. One indie maintainer, BSL source, and an enterprise waitlist rather than a company.

pricing.notes: Desktop app and Web Server builds were free downloads as of September 2026. Homepage has a 'Golutra Enterprise' waitlist ('intelligence of a thousand engineers') collected by email only, no live paid tier, seats or pricing page exists.

featureNotes.agents.builtIn: v0.3.3 release notes (2026-09-24) list '新增 Golutra Agent', a built-in 'Golutra Agent' added alongside the wrapped third-party CLIs; scope beyond that name is undocumented.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: v0.3.1 release notes add a '派发队列展示' (dispatch-queue view) on the session page showing pending/dispatched status; this is a queue indicator inside the chat view, not a separate kanban board.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: README markets 'custom workflows' with one-click import/export of workflow templates for long-running automation (novel writing, video pipelines, etc.), but no scheduled or event-trigger mechanism is described.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: v0.3.1 added member-level Feishu (Lark) connectors so individual agent 'members' can be wired to a Feishu account; this reads as a chat/notification bridge rather than a documented desktop 'agent needs you' alert.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Homepage collects emails for a 'Golutra Enterprise' waitlist; no team plan, seats or billing existed as of September 2026.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: README calls BSL 1.1 an '开源' (open source) licence, but Business Source License 1.1 is not OSI-approved, so per this dataset's stricter definition it counts as source-available, not open source.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No working plugin system. The repo has a Plugin Marketplace view (src/features/PluginMarketplace.vue) but it is scaffolding: an empty `plugins` array with a TODO, and install/remove only persist a numeric id locally, no code is loaded. golutra-mcp connects external tools to the agents (agent-side) and workflow templates are config. No plugin mechanism appears in the README.

github.description: Multi-agent AI orchestration platform for automation, workflows, and developer tools. Golutra transforms Codex, Claude Code, and OpenClaw into a unified agent system with parallel execution, task orchestration, long-running workflows, and AI productivity workspace.

top.title: Demo of an indie AI collaboration app – beyond Codex and Claude Code desktop

activity.changelogCadence: roughly every 3-6 weeks (v0.2.8 May 31, v0.2.9 Jun 16, v0.3.0 Jun 29, v0.3.1 Jul 21, v0.3.2 Aug 6, v0.3.3 Sep 24)

editorial.reachRationale: Every product-specific signal is tiny: a 3-member Discord, one HN submission with 1 point and 1 comment, a single GitHub contributor (the solo author), and no registry/download data. 3.8K GitHub stars are discounted, a viral README/marketing push on a one-person project created in February 2026, not evidence of a used product; this is the niche tier (like Tortie: one maintainer, a handful of users).
editorial.polishRationale: The public site undercuts polish: as of September 2026 the homepage still banners 'v0.2.0 Now Live' while GitHub is on v0.3.3, and the 'Learn more' links under each feature card go nowhere (href="#").
editorial.depthRationale: Goes beyond a tmux wrapper with reusable workflow templates, a per-session dispatch queue, an external memory layer (EverOS) and an MCP connector.
editorial.feelRationale: Tauri (Rust) + Vue 3 desktop shell, lighter than Electron by construction, but v0.2.8's release notes added dedicated 'hang diagnostics... to identify freezes, unresponsive states', the maker's own words indicate freezing/unresponsiveness was a real enough problem to need a diagnostic feature.

tools.name: Google Antigravity
tools.tagline: Google Antigravity is our agentic development platform, allowing anyone to build in the agent-first era.
tools.valueProp: Google's own agent harness is the only door in, the Terms of Service ban logging into third-party CLIs like Claude Code or Codex with an Antigravity account, but that harness is free, routes across Gemini, Claude and GPT-OSS models, and reaches you through a desktop command center, a terminal-first CLI, five IDE extensions, a browser-based Remote Control, and an SDK, sandboxed with OS-native primitives instead of Docker.

pricing.notes: Individual $0/month: Gemini 3.8/3.7/3.6 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet & Opus 4.6 and gpt-oss-120b as the agent model, unlimited Tab completions and Command requests, basic weekly-refreshing rate limits, all product features (Scheduled Tasks, CLI). Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra (bundled Google-wide subscriptions, not Antigravity-specific plans) raise the quota to a 5-hour-refresh pool with higher weekly ceilings, Ultra adds access to third-party (Claude/GPT-OSS) models, and both can burn purchased AI credits for overage once the baseline is exhausted. Organization plan (new, via Google Cloud/Gemini Enterprise Standard or Plus license, or direct Cloud-project consumption billing): SSO, BYOID/Workforce Identity Federation, VPC Service Controls, regional (US/EU/global) data residency, centralized admin. Docs state explicitly there is no bring-your-own-key/endpoint support and no organizational tier via contract outside Gemini Enterprise.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Native .dmg (Apple Silicon and Intel), macOS 12 Monterey or later; Antigravity 2.0, the standalone Antigravity IDE and the CLI all ship macOS builds.
featureNotes.platforms.windows: Native .exe (x64 and ARM64), Windows 10 64-bit or later; Windows-specific file/network sandboxing landed in 2.15.1 and a WSL-connect option in 2.16.0.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: tar.gz for x64/ARM64, glibc >= 2.28 (Ubuntu 20+, Debian 10+, Fedora 36+, RHEL 8+).
featureNotes.platforms.ios: No App Store or TestFlight app found; the Remote Control 'push notification on mobile' example is a browser/PWA notification to antigravity.google.com, not a native iOS app.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Same as iOS: Remote Control is reachable from any mobile browser but there is no Play Store app or APK.
featureNotes.platforms.web: Remote Control (antigravity.google.com) is a browser-based window into a running Antigravity session on one of your machines, with full file, credential and environment access and its own push notifications; it is not a hosted execution environment.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: Antigravity CLI installs via curl (macOS/Linux) or PowerShell/cmd (Windows) from antigravity.google/cli/install.*, described as 'the lightweight, fast, terminal-first surface' with shell execution and background subagent management.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: Marketed as 'terminal-first' and keyboard-driven, but no page read described a full-screen multi-pane terminal UI the way Claude Code's or Gemini CLI's TUI is documented, so this is unconfirmed rather than denied.
featureNotes.execution.local: Antigravity 2.0, the standalone IDE, the CLI and the IDE extensions all run the agent loop and tool calls on the machine they're installed on.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Remote Control (docs/remote-control) lets you 'connect and drive your Antigravity sessions running across your different machines (laptops, servers, desktops)' from a browser, keeping full access to files, build tools, credentials and env vars on that machine, explicitly a machine you own, not a vendor sandbox.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: No Cursor-style vendor-provisioned execution VM was found: Gemini Enterprise integration provisions model inference under your own Google Cloud project (data residency, VPC-SC) rather than an agent execution sandbox, and Scheduled Tasks/subagents run as background processes on your own machine.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: No self-hostable relay or server component is documented; Remote Control and Gemini Enterprise both route through Google-operated infrastructure.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Not a runnable third-party harness inside Antigravity, Claude Sonnet/Opus 4.6 appears only as a selectable model under Antigravity's own agent loop, and the Terms of Service prohibit using third-party agent software (including Claude Code) with an Antigravity account.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Antigravity's own agent harness (subagents via invoke_subagent, custom Markdown+YAML agents, Hooks, Scheduled Tasks) with model routing across Gemini 3.x, Claude Sonnet/Opus 4.6 and gpt-oss-120b; the SDK ('Antigravity's harness with minimal code') is built on the same loop.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Antigravity 2.0 has native Git worktree support: pick 'New Worktree' when starting a conversation and it provisions and later cleans up the worktree; when a main agent delegates to subagents needing isolation it creates and tears down their worktrees automatically.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: File and network sandboxing use OS-native primitives (Terminal Sandbox via Linux namespaces and macOS Seatbelt, with Windows sandboxing added in 2.15.1) through a Deny/Ask/Allow permission engine, not Docker or microVMs per task.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Worktree creation is per-conversation/per-task and a worktree implies its own branch; no separate documentation of a branch-naming scheme independent of worktrees was found.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: The right-side VCS panel (Aug 24, 2026 update) shows Agent Edits, Uncommitted and Branch diff views with split/unified toggles and inline comments, alongside an embedded terminal.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: The same VCS panel only documents Stage, Unstage, Commit and Push actions; no pull-request-creation action from inside the product was found.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Conversations can be rewound to a snapshot (a Sep 22, 2026 fix corrected rewind picking a stale snapshot); a Reddit thread ('Antigravity deleting files when reverting checkpoints?') suggests the restore path has had reliability complaints.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Antigravity 2.0 is pitched as 'your command center to manage multiple local agents in parallel,' with conversations groupable into Projects and sortable by project, status or recency.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: The left sidebar groups and sorts conversations (by project/status/recency) but this is a list, not a kanban board or drag-to-queue; Scheduled Tasks and subagent runs surface as sidebar items rather than a queue.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Subagents are modular/specialized/blank-slate agents the main agent spawns via invoke_subagent, inheriting scoped tool and permission access; they can run synchronously or as polled background tasks, and appear as live, followable/stoppable cards since 2.16.0.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Scheduled Tasks run cron-style prompts against a project without manual invocation (e.g. daily PR digests); as of the 2026 I/O launch these agents are fixed to Gemini 3.5 Flash.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Remote Control ships 'proactive push notifications' so you're alerted on any device when an agent finishes a turn and needs input, even away from the workstation.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Live voice transcription using Gemini Audio models is available on all tiers via a mic icon next to text inputs, converting rambling speech into clean prompt text before you send it.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Gemini Enterprise / Google Cloud Organization accounts support SSO (including BYOID/Workforce Identity Federation), per-user license assignment and centralized admin controls across Antigravity 2.0, the CLI and all IDE extensions.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: A 'Share' action was added to the conversation right-click menu in the 2.14.0 release, alongside 'Move to Group'; no detail was read on what a recipient can do with a shared conversation.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Organization plan via Google Cloud: Gemini Enterprise Standard/Plus licenses with included quota and managed overages, or direct Google Cloud project consumption-based billing.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: docs/plans states plainly, as of September 2026: 'There is currently no support for: Bring-your-own-key or bring-your-own-endpoint for additional rate limits', usage is metered by Google's own plan tiers and AI credits, not a Claude/OpenAI login.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: False, agent-side only, none of it touches Antigravity's own interface. The documented plugin directory format (`plugin.json` manifest plus `skills/` SKILL.md, `agents/` subagent markdown, `rules/` behavioral markdown, `mcp_config.json` MCP server registration, `hooks.json` shell commands run before/after tool calls) installs via `.agents/plugins/` or the CLI's `agy plugin` commands, but every one of the four supported components (skills, agents, MCP config, hooks) is agent-side, so it doesn't count. There is no documented way to add a panel, view, command-palette command, provider/runtime or theme to Antigravity's own IDE surface. Documented at https://antigravity.google/docs/plugins/.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: MCP client support with a first-party store of 50+ servers, plus the Python `google-antigravity` SDK (497k downloads/month on PyPI) for scripting the same agent harness outside the apps.

top.title: Google Antigravity

activity.changelogCadence: near-daily (Antigravity 2.0 shipped 2.14.0 through 2.17.0 between Sep 15 and Sep 22, 2026)

editorial.reachRationale: Product-specific signals put this past hobby scale fast: the official `google-antigravity` SDK alone sees ~498k PyPI downloads/month, the launch HN thread hit 1,088 points/1,085 comments (131 stories total for the product query), and Google is shipping near-daily releases plus Gemini Enterprise distribution to whole orgs. Discounted the 189k-follower @antigravity X handle only partially (it's product-specific, not @google) and did not credit Google's company-wide accounts or stars (closed source, none exist); held back from dominant because it launched in November 2025 with no independent Discord/community signal and no public usage numbers for the flagship desktop app itself.
editorial.polishRationale: The product ships fast and broad (3 desktop platforms, 5 IDE extensions, CLI, SDK, web) but each Antigravity 2.0 release in the read window (2.14.0-2.17.0, Sep 15-22, 2026) fixed 10-18 user-visible bugs including crashes, data-loss-adjacent issues (stale file restores on rewind, settings overwritten on failed state read) and accessibility gaps, suggesting the surface was settling rather than mature.
editorial.depthRationale: Parallel local agents grouped into Projects, native worktrees with autonomous subagent isolation, a VCS side panel with commit/push, OS-native (not container) sandboxing, Hooks, cron-style Scheduled Tasks, voice input, an MCP store, a Remote Control web surface, and a Python SDK for scripting the same harness. It falls short of Cursor mainly on PR/merge tooling and vendor-managed cloud execution, both apparently absent.
editorial.feelRationale: Multiple independent, non-first-party reports describe real sluggishness: a Reddit r/GoogleAntigravityIDE thread titled 'Antigravity has become extremely laggy,' a Google AI Developers forum thread 'Antigravity Slow' ('It take 5 or more than 5 min to complete the simple task'), another forum thread on v1.18.3 being 'glitchy and slow,' an X report of high battery drain on macOS even when idle, and a Facebook vibe-coding group calling it 'laggy as hell'; Antigravity 2.0's own changelog repeatedly ships main-thread freeze fixes (e.g. 'Large files and diffs no longer freeze the app,' 2.17.0), consistent with an Electron-class app under real load rather than isolated complaints.

tools.name: Grok Build
tools.tagline: Bring Grok to your computer.
tools.valueProp: A single-agent TUI that grew its own multiplexer: a dashboard groups every Grok session by needs-input, working and done, and dispatches new agents into worktrees. It only ever runs Grok, and stays local with no PR flow or cloud sandbox.

maker.name: xAI (SpaceXAI)
maker.funding: corporate; the site, docs and repo brand the maker as SpaceXAI

pricing.notes: Homepage says 'Available to try for Free'. Grok Build is included in the consumer Grok plans: Free, SuperGrok Lite (price not shown), SuperGrok $30/mo, SuperGrok Plus $100/mo (higher usage across Chat, Imagine, Voice & Build), SuperGrok Heavy (price not shown), plus X Premium Plus per the launch post. Alternatively sign in with an xAI API key and pay per token. Business and Enterprise tiers add seat management, consolidated billing, RBAC, SSO, SCIM and custom data retention (contact sales).

featureNotes.platforms.windows: Prebuilt binary via PowerShell installer; README says Windows builds from source are best-effort and untested. Windows on ARM64 builds are mentioned in the changelog.
featureNotes.platforms.web: `/share` produces a session URL via code.grok.com, but no browser client for running or steering sessions is documented. The 'Web, iOS, Android apps' row on the pricing page is the Grok chat app, not Grok Build.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Enterprise network table lists code.grok.com for 'Remote session sync, sharing, WebSocket relay' and device-code login exists for SSH hosts, but no page documents attaching a local client to a session on another machine you own.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Grok Build runs where you install it. xAI's separate Grok Bot product runs on a vendor cloud computer; the `devbox` sandbox profile targets cloud devbox environments you supply.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: No server component. Session sharing and sync go through xAI's code.grok.com relay; blocking it leaves sessions local-only.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Does not run Claude Code, but reads Claude Code's CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules, plugins, skills, MCP config, hooks and MDM managed-settings.json for compatibility, and ships `/import-claude`.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Does not run Cursor's agent; reads Cursor hooks, rules, skills and mcp.json for compatibility.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Ships its own Rust agent runtime on grok-4.6 by default; `[model.<name>]` config lets you point it at any custom model endpoint with a base_url and API key.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: `grok -w`, `/fork --worktree`, Ctrl+W in the dashboard; subagents can request their own worktrees. Managed under ~/.grok/worktrees with `grok worktree list|show|rm|gc`.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: OS-level sandbox (Landlock on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS) with workspace/devbox/read-only/strict profiles, off by default. Not a container or VM; child-network limits are Linux-only.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: A worktree is a detached checkout at its base commit; no branch is created or named.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Every file edit shows an inline diff in the permission prompt, and approved plan changes render as diffs. No whole-branch review pane documented.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Homepage lists git integration (stage, commit, push, branches) and line-by-line code review 'before opening a PR', but no PR command exists in the CLI or slash-command reference.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Worktree docs: 'land changes with ordinary git'.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: `/rewind` (or Esc Esc) restores all files and truncates the conversation to a chosen prompt; per-prompt file snapshots are saved automatically.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Agent Dashboard (`grok dashboard`, `/dashboard`, Ctrl+\) lists every session grouped by Needs input / Working / Idle / Inactive / Completed / Failed, with peek, inline reply, attach, pin, rename, stop and Ctrl+[ / Ctrl+] to cycle sessions.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Dashboard rows are sessions, not tasks; the prompt queue and todo list are per-session. No cross-session task queue.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: general-purpose, explore and plan child types with their own context windows, user-defined types under .grok/agents/, and Rhai workflows (`/create-workflow`) that fan out to subagents in the background.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: `/loop <interval> <prompt>` schedules recurring prompts (60s minimum, expire after 7 days, 50 max) and monitors turn script output into events, but all of it runs inside a live session process; there is no server-side scheduler.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: The dashboard's Needs-input group and `Notification` / `Stop` hook events (shell command or HTTP POST) let you wire your own alerts; no built-in desktop or push notification is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Parent sessions can message subagents, including finished ones, and the dashboard lets you reply to any session; peer-to-peer messaging between sessions is not documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Changelog v1.0.25 mentions voice dictation inserting text at the cursor; the feature is not described in the docs.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Team logins: `force_login_team_uuid`, enterprise OIDC (Entra, Okta, Auth0), team-level ZDR; pricing page lists team seat management and RBAC for Business/Enterprise.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: `/share` shares the current session via URL through code.grok.com; docs do not say whether a viewer can steer it.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Business and Enterprise tiers on x.ai/pricing: seat management, consolidated billing, RBAC, SSO, SCIM, audit controls.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: Apache-2.0 on the full CLI/TUI/agent-runtime source, synced periodically from the SpaceXAI monorepo (1 GitHub contributor). External contributions are not accepted.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The client is self-contained and can target a custom model endpoint, but default auth and inference go through x.ai and session sharing through code.grok.com.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Custom models via `[model.<name>] base_url` + `env_key` (BYOK to any endpoint); Grok itself is billed through SuperGrok plans or an xAI API key. No Claude or OpenAI subscription login.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Enterprise page says `/etc/grok/requirements.toml` can pin telemetry off and `/privacy` toggles data-retention status; the exact setting key is not in the public settings reference.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system for the Grok Build app itself. Its “plugins” bundle skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers for the agent, installed from git marketplaces, with hooks as shell commands or HTTP endpoints; that extends what the agent can do, not the multiplexer’s own panels, commands or providers. Documented at docs.x.ai/build/features/skills-plugins-marketplaces.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: `grok agent stdio` runs it as an Agent Client Protocol agent over JSON-RPC; `grok -p --output-format json|streaming-json` for headless control; MCP client for stdio and HTTP servers (no MCP server of its own).

github.description: SpaceXAI's coding agent harness and TUI. Fullscreen, mouse interactive, extensible.

top.title: Grok Build is open source

editorial.reachRationale: Backed by xAI/SpaceXAI with a well-received 590-point Show HN on its open-sourcing, but xAI's 11.2M X followers belong to the company, not this product, so that number was discounted entirely; with only 816 brew installs/30d, 11 commits/30d and a single-contributor repo (real development is closed and just mirrored here), the concrete usage signals support established rather than major or dominant.
editorial.polishRationale: A 1.0.x product with near-daily changelog entries, an installer for all three desktops plus a homebrew-core cask, a full docs site with keyboard-shortcut, settings and enterprise MDM pages, and a launch that went to all SuperGrok subscribers.
editorial.depthRationale: Beyond a plain agent loop it has a real multi-session dashboard, managed worktrees, subagents, Rhai workflows, scheduled loops, rewind and an OS sandbox, but it stops short of a task board, PR or merge flow, cloud execution, or hosting any agent other than its own.
editorial.feelRationale: GitHub's languages API shows the xai-org/grok-build repo is ~72MB Rust (plus a small Swift/Kotlin companion), matching the README's description of a 'full-screen TUI'; the homepage markets it as 'Minimal & terminal-native... keyboard-first, no excess chrome.' A targeted search found an HN commentator calling it 'impressive... And fast' with no jank or slowness complaints surfacing in docs or search results.

tools.name: HAPI
tools.tagline: Vibe Coding Anytime, Anywhere.
tools.valueProp: A single AGPL binary bundling CLI, hub, web app and SQLite, built as a self-hosted alternative to Happy’s cloud relay. The only tool here where one live Codex session can be driven from the terminal and the web client at the same time.

pricing.notes: Open source (AGPL-3.0) CLI/hub, free to self-host; the optional public relay (relay.hapi.run) and push relay (push.hapi.run) are free vendor-run infrastructure with no paid tier documented.

featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system for hapi itself: nothing in the README or hapi.run docs (installation, how-it-works, agents, native-apps, FAQ) describes a way to load third-party code that adds panels, commands or providers to hapi; the only configurable surface is namespace/session settings. Checked https://hapi.run/docs/guide and github.com/tiann/hapi README, 2026-09-26.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: Native SwiftUI/UIKit app lives in-repo (ios/); no App Store or TestFlight listing found. Requires Xcode build and your own signing (device builds require a developer account).
featureNotes.platforms.android: Native Kotlin Compose app lives in-repo (android/); no Play Store listing found. Ships as a self-built/signed debug APK or a maintainer-signed release APK/AAB from CI, not a store download.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: The CLI wraps and streams the underlying agent's own terminal session (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) directly; no distinct full-screen TUI of HAPI's own for session/task management is documented.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Google sunset the consumer Gemini CLI (2026-06-18); `hapi gemini` is kept only as a tombstone command that errors, and old Gemini sessions are viewable but not resumable.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: The agent picker is a fixed, named integration list (see support matrix in docs/guide/agents.md); no generic arbitrary-command adapter is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Only Cursor's own `--worktree` flag is forwarded through HAPI (`~/.cursor/worktrees/<repo>/<name>`); Codex's `--worktree` launch flag is explicitly rejected by HAPI's shared-session wrapper. Not a HAPI-managed worktree feature across agents.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Web app offers session fork/rewind/export, and Grok sessions get ACP-based fork and rewind when the CLI build advertises the extension methods; Codex explicitly disables native in-place rewind and Web Rewind for concurrent (shared) sessions, requiring 'Fork at message' instead.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Cursor's own `/multitask` subagents surface as read-only CursorTask notification cards when the agent emits them; HAPI does not provide its own fleet pane to spawn or steer subagents through the tool.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Web app supports scheduled message sends to a session; native iOS/Android apps can view existing scheduled messages but have no UI to create one.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: MCP peer tools (`list_peers`, `inspect_peer`, `ping_peer`) let an agent inside one HAPI session discover and message other sessions/machines sharing the same hub and namespace.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Namespaces give lightweight multi-account isolation on one shared hub (each user appends `:namespace` to the base token); sessions, machines and users are not visible across namespaces, so it isolates accounts rather than providing shared team visibility. Single-user by default.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Privacy Policy: the apps and hub contain 'no advertising or tracking SDKs and no product analytics'; only the optional push relay processes device/operational metadata needed to deliver encrypted notifications.

github.description: App for Codex / Claude Code / Pi / OpenCode / Kimi Code / Grok Build, vibe coding anytime, anywhere

editorial.reachRationale: Modest product-specific usage signal (3,690 npm downloads/month for the CLI, an order of magnitude below established remote-control tools like Happy's ~30k/month); no dedicated Discord, no product X account, and an HN search for the name and variants returned zero stories. No App Store or Play Store listing either, native apps must be self-built and signed, which caps how many people can actually install it versus store-distributed peers. Discounted the 5,129 GitHub stars; noted but did not weight heavily 107 contributors and a fast weekly release cadence on a repo created 2025-12-24, which show real but early momentum rather than an established user base.
editorial.polishRationale: Extensively documented (10+ guide pages, a full privacy policy, a client protocol contract) and shipping weekly, but several rough edges are self-documented, no App Store/Play Store distribution (build and sign it yourself), asymmetric native features (Android exposes Rename/Delete/Reopen that iOS lacks), and an openly listed set of 'current limitations' (Cursor's multitask fleet view not replicated, DSH sessions can't resume, Web Rewind disabled for concurrent Codex sessions).
editorial.depthRationale: Goes beyond a plain terminal wrapper with in-app diff/git review, a voice assistant, cross-session MCP messaging between agents, and web-only scheduled message sends, but there is no task board/kanban, no PR creation or merge assistance, no HAPI-managed worktrees or containers, and subagent activity is only surfaced as notifications rather than spawned/steered through the tool.
editorial.feelRationale: CLI and hub are TypeScript running on Bun, streaming the wrapped agent's own PTY directly in local mode (Bun POSIX PTY on macOS/Linux, Bun ConPTY on Windows) rather than reimplementing a terminal renderer; native iOS (Swift) and Android (Kotlin) clients are genuinely native, not a hybrid/Electron shell. No first-party latency figures are published for the hub→client SSE path or the WireGuard/TLS relay, and a targeted search turned up no independent reports calling HAPI especially fast or slow.

tools.name: Happy
tools.tagline: Leave your desk. Keep your agents moving.
tools.valueProp: Wraps the vendor `claude`/`codex` CLI process directly rather than reimplementing it, so every agent feature works unchanged on the phone, behind a documented zero-knowledge relay you can self-host. Its companion Happy Desktop app layers its own multi-provider harness, Claude, Codex and Grok in one session, with live subagent delegation and native multiplayer, on top of that wrapper.

maker.name: Slopus
maker.funding: No VC funding; docs describe a small, self-funded team ('No VC funding... Can't rugpull you').

pricing.notes: The app, CLI, desktop app and relay server are free and open source (MIT) with no usage or seat limits, using your own Claude Code/Codex/Grok logins. The built-in voice agent is free for 3 trial uses and then requires a paid subscription (Dec 22 2025 release notes); the known-issues page separately estimates voice cost at about $8/hour.

featureNotes.platforms.tui: The CLI wraps and streams the vendor agent's own terminal session (`happy claude` / `happy codex`); no distinct full-screen terminal UI of Happy's own is documented.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Release notes: ACP support announced Dec 22 2025 ('Gemini support coming via ACP') and 'Latest Gemini models in the picker' Apr 8 2026; not named as a first-class harness the way Claude Code, Codex and Grok CLI are.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Happy's own alternatives-comparison table checks 'Use any coding agent' for itself, but the documented integrations are a curated, growing list of named agents (Claude Code, Codex, Grok CLI, Gemini, Antigravity, OpenClaw) added one release at a time, not a generic arbitrary-command adapter.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Happy Desktop ships its own 'Chief of Staff' onboarding/orchestration agent and a multi-provider harness ('Happy Harness') that runs Claude, Codex and Grok in one session, on top of wrapping the vendor CLIs.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Desktop 'Auto' session mode: reads and workspace edits are unrestricted, 'everything else is sandboxed' and cross-boundary actions are reviewed automatically; the sandboxing mechanism itself (containers vs. something else) is not documented.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Session fork and rewind: 'branch off any session or roll back to any message' (May 7 2026 release notes); FAQ also lists rollback to checkpoints.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Happy Desktop markets 'delegate to subagents' across providers, and the July 11 2026 release notes say Claude/Codex subagents 'render live in chat'; not confirmed whether this is Happy's own orchestration versus surfacing the underlying provider's native subagent feature.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The happy-server relay (TypeScript, ~1,293 lines per the docs) is fully self-hostable via Docker, Compose or Kubernetes with a documented guide; the mobile and desktop apps themselves still ship from app stores and GitHub releases.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: FAQ: 'limited, pseudonymous product analytics' that exclude code/message content, with a documented toggle in app settings.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system: agent-side only, and even that is undocumented. The single mention of 'plugins' across https://happy.engineering/docs is a table row naming `~/Happy/Plugins` as a folder plugins write to; there is no manifest format, loader, API reference or marketplace for extending Happy's own UI or core.

github.description: Orchestrate Claude, Codex and Grok in one app. Open-source (MIT), reuses the subscriptions you already pay for.

top.title: Show HN: Happy Coder – End-to-End Encrypted Mobile Client for Claude Code

editorial.reachRationale: App Store rating 4.9 from 970+ ratings and Google Play 4.8–5.0 from roughly 3,000 reviews are strong product-specific usage signals, rarer in this dataset than star counts; ~30k npm downloads/month for the CLI and 23.9k GitHub stars (discounted) point the same direction. Discounted the modest 669-member Discord, the absence of any dedicated product X account (only the two co-founders' personal accounts turned up), and a soft 30-point Show HN launch, together these place it at established rather than major.
editorial.polishRationale: 4.9/4.8/5.0 App Store and Play Store ratings across thousands of reviews, six platforms (macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android, web) plus a CLI, and a steady cadence of UI passes (a full 'liquid glass' mobile redesign in July 2026, a desktop sidebar/editor/zen-mode refresh in May 2026) show real investment; release notes list basic-reliability fixes (blank screen on launch, settings randomly resetting, stuck sessions) into Q2 2026, showing rough edges persisting as late as that point.
editorial.depthRationale: Beyond parallel sessions it has managed worktrees with auto-cleanup, an in-app diff viewer, session fork/rewind checkpoints, MCP permission prompts, a voice agent, a plugin folder and, on Desktop, a multi-provider harness with subagent delegation and native multiplayer; it stops short of documented automations/scheduling, a task board, or PR/merge-conflict flows, keeping it below the deepest tools in the set.
editorial.feelRationale: Cross-platform TypeScript stack: happy-desktop's languages are TS/CSS/JS (Electron-style, no Rust/Swift/GPUI core) and the mobile/web app is Expo/React Native, with state synced through a relay (FAQ cites a ~300ms typical phone-to-desktop round trip). Release notes repeatedly patch responsiveness, 'no more freezing on sessions with thousands of messages' via parallel decryption (May 13 2026), 'the view stays put while the agent streams' (May 15 2026), 'session launch and resume are more reliable' (as late as July 24 2026), consistent with a typical cross-platform app that was still maturing as of September 2026 rather than a native fast one. A targeted search turned up no independent user reports calling it especially slow or fast.

tools.name: Herdr
tools.tagline: the runtime your coding agents live on.
tools.valueProp: A tmux-style runtime rather than an app: a background server owns the agents’ terminals, so any client can quit or crash without stopping them, and agents drive each other through the same CLI. Diff review, PR flow and task boards are left to its plugin marketplace.

maker.name: Herdr (Can Ogulcan Celik)
maker.funding: Y Combinator F26 (announced 2026-08-06); solo sponsor-backed project before that. Licence moved from AGPL to Apache-2.0 at the same time.

pricing.notes: The runtime is free and Apache-2.0; nothing was sold as of September 2026. 'Herdr Cloud' (a connection layer for your own machines without SSH setup, not hosted compute) is waitlist-only with no announced price. Enterprise/partnership contact is an email address.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Single Rust binary (Intel and Apple silicon) that runs inside whatever terminal you already use; no GUI app. Homebrew-core formula `herdr`, mise, Nix flake, curl installer.
featureNotes.platforms.windows: Native Windows build (ConPTY) is generally available with a documented limitations table; direct terminal attach is not available on native Windows and plugins are 'preview' there. ARM64 runs the x86_64 build under emulation.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: x86_64 and aarch64 binaries; the same binary is the server and the client.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: No first-party app. Docs point phone users at any SSH client (the TUI adapts to narrow screens). Third-party native iOS clients exist in the marketplace (ZingerLittleBee/Heeler, arronKler/pairfob) and a community iOS app is mentioned in the YC post.
featureNotes.platforms.android: No first- or third-party native Android app found; third-party mobile web apps (AltanS/collie PWA, 0cv/herdr-mobile-relay) count as web, not Android.
featureNotes.platforms.web: No first-party web UI; docs say Herdr 'works on your phone without a mobile app or web dashboard'. Third-party web clients exist in the marketplace (AltanS/collie, powerfooI/roamgate, 0cv/herdr-mobile-relay).
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The full control surface: `herdr workspace/tab/pane/agent/worktree/machine/plugin/session ...` with JSON output; `--machine <label>` forwards commands to saved SSH machines.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: Mouse-native full-screen TUI with tmux-style `ctrl+b` prefix keys, sidebar of workspaces and agent states, right-click menus.
featureNotes.execution.local: A background `herdr` server holds the PTYs; the client attaches and detaches. Multiple clients can view different tabs on the same server.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: `herdr --remote <ssh-host>` attaches a local UI to a server on any SSH-reachable box (it installs the matching binary there if needed); `herdr machine add` keeps Local and several SSH machines in one sidebar with independent reconnects. Plain `ssh host; herdr` also works.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: As of September 2026, 'Herdr Cloud' was waitlist-only and not yet released; the blog states it only connects machines you bring and 'doesn't host the agents for you'.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The runtime is the server; there is no vendor component in the path. The only outbound calls documented are the release check and the remote agent-detection manifest fetch.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Auto-detected via screen manifest; `herdr integration install claude` adds a SessionStart hook so Herdr can `claude --resume <id>` after a server restart.
featureNotes.agents.codex: Auto-detected; integration writes a Codex hook for native session resume (`codex resume <id>`).
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Docs list Gemini CLI (and Cline) as 'detected but less thoroughly tested'; no integration and no native session restore. `--kind gemini` is accepted by `agent start`.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Auto-detected; integration hook enables `copilot --resume=<id>` restore.
featureNotes.agents.opencode: Lifecycle-authority integration (OpenCode plugin reports idle/working/blocked and session id); supports OpenCode V1 and V2.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Cursor Agent CLI auto-detected; integration enables `cursor-agent --resume <id>` restore.
featureNotes.agents.amp: Screen-manifest detection only; the docs table lists integration role 'none', so no native session restore.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Lifecycle-authority integration (Pi extension reports state and session); the founder's own agent of choice per the docs examples.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Herdr does not wrap agents at all: any process runs in a pane. Unrecognised agents 'still run normally' but only get rich state if they report it through `herdr pane report-agent` or the socket API (custom integration guide); adding a new auto-detected agent needs a Herdr release.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Docs and blog are explicit that Herdr ships no agent of its own ('Let my agent integrate with your product, don't offer me another agent').
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: `herdr worktree create/open/remove` and the sidebar's 'New worktree' create Git worktree checkouts under a configurable directory, open each as a workspace grouped under the parent repo, and run `git worktree remove` on delete.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Herdr provisions no sandboxes. Docs describe running an agent inside a wrapper such as fence or nono with `HERDR_AGENT=<agent>` so detection still works.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: `worktree create --branch NAME [--base REF]` checks out or creates a branch, but you name it; there is no automatic branch naming per task.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Nothing first-party. The compare page says Herdr 'pairs with' a worktree and diff-review flow rather than providing one; third-party marketplace plugins cover it (persiyanov/herdr-reviewr, alexarthurs/herdr-sidebar, smarzban/herdr-file-viewer).
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: No first-party PR command; not in the CLI reference or socket API.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Not documented. `worktree remove` explicitly never deletes the branch.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Session snapshot restore (layout, cwd) and native agent session resume after a server restart are persistence, not a user-triggered checkpoint or rollback of files or conversation state.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: The core workflow: many agents in panes across workspaces, each marked working/blocked/done/idle in the sidebar, with state rolled up to tab and workspace. Homepage counter says '22 agent CLIs detected'.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: No first-party board or queue. Third-party marketplace plugins add one (nelsonPires5/herdr-board kanban, smarzban/tsk).
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: `herdr agent start --kind codex`, `agent prompt --wait`, `agent wait --until blocked` and the agent-skill file let an agent in one pane start, prompt, read and wait on another; the homepage calls this 'agent-native'.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Plugin manifests declare `[[events]]` hooks that run a command on Herdr events (e.g. `worktree.created`) and `[[startup]]` hooks; scripts can drive agents through the CLI. No scheduler or cron is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Fires when 'a background agent finishes or needs input'; delivery is `herdr` toast, `terminal` (works over SSH), `system` (OS notification; macOS via terminal-notifier or osascript) or `off`, plus optional MP3 sounds. Phone push only via third-party companions.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Agents prompt each other by name or pane id via `agent prompt`; the session-state page also references pane-to-pane messages.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Not documented anywhere in docs, README or changelog.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: No accounts of any kind; auth is your OpenSSH setup.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Multiple clients can attach to the same server (tmux-style, anyone with a shell on that box) and view different tabs independently; no roles, presence or invitations.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Nothing is billed; enterprise contact is an email address.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: Apache-2.0 on the whole product (switched from AGPL in August 2026 per the YC post).
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Server and every client are the same binary on your machines; SSH is the only transport. Third-party phone relays are the exception, not part of the product.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Herdr never touches model vendors; it owns the terminal your existing `claude`, `codex`, etc. login runs in.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: No telemetry statement in docs, README or CHANGELOG and no analytics crates in Cargo.toml. Documented outbound calls are the in-app release check and a background fetch of agent-detection manifests from herdr.dev, which `[update] manifest_check = false` disables.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Extends Herdr itself: a plugin is a directory with a `herdr-plugin.toml` manifest that can register actions, event hooks, panes (UI panels) and link handlers, written in any language and installed via `herdr plugin install owner/repo`. Documented at https://herdr.dev/docs/plugins; the marketplace at https://herdr.dev/plugins listed 1,208 plugins across 1,186 repos (checked 2026-09-18).
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Local Unix socket / Windows named pipe JSON API with a printable JSON Schema (`herdr api schema`), event subscriptions, and CLI wrappers for every method. No MCP server is documented.

github.description: the runtime your coding agents live on

top.title: Herdr: A tmux-like terminal multiplexer for AI coding agents

tools.authorNote: The terminal king. If you prefer the CLI, there still isn’t really a better solution out there than this. Super powerful, flexible, well-made and fast.

editorial.reachRationale: Homebrew formula installs (13,224/30d) and release-asset downloads (178,153) are among the strongest install signals in the set, and its own X account has 26,747 followers; discounted this toward established rather than major because there is no Discord at all, the one Show HN scored only 5 points, and the repo was created in March 2026, so as of September 2026 it was not yet a name most practitioners would recognize.
editorial.polishRationale: The docs are unusually precise about edge cases (what survives a restart, which client owns input, exact error codes), there are stable and preview channels, a homebrew-core formula, GA Windows support with a limitations table, and the homepage counts 39k stars and 900k installs; held back because it is TUI-only, live handoff was marked experimental as of September 2026, and Windows plugins were 'preview' at that point. Judged from docs and release notes, not hands-on use.
editorial.depthRationale: Well beyond a tmux wrapper on the runtime side (semantic agent state, prompt/wait API, agent-to-agent control, managed worktrees, multi-machine sidebar, a plugin host with a 1,200-entry marketplace), but review flows, PRs, task boards and scheduling are deliberately left out of the core and delegated to third-party plugins, so it scores in the middle on product depth. Judged from docs and release notes, not hands-on use.
editorial.feelRationale: One Rust binary with no Electron, and its pane runtime is Ghostty's native, SIMD-optimized libghostty-vt terminal engine (the changelog documents replacing a legacy vt100 backend with it and then repeatedly tuning key-encoding and redraw paths for responsiveness), a direct match for the rubric's libghostty criterion. The site owner separately reports it feels exceptionally fast, and no current jank reports turned up.

tools.name: HumanLayer
tools.tagline: The Multiplayer Coding Agent Workspace
tools.valueProp: The methodology product: every task runs a gated research, design, plan, implement workflow whose artifacts teammates comment on, and a CLI runs sessions inside CI. Closed source, Apple-silicon-only app, everything synced through their cloud.

maker.name: HumanLayer (QueryTale, Inc. d/b/a HumanLayer)
maker.funding: YC F24; homepage lists Y Combinator, Massive, Pioneer Fund, Batch, Multimodal and Preface as investors

pricing.notes: Starter: free, up to 3 team members and 200 sessions/month, otherwise everything in Pro. Pro: $100/user/month with BYOK for Claude Code, Codex and others, unlimited tasks and sessions, multi-repo workspaces and worktrees, artifact collaboration, remote daemons, Advanced Metrics. Enterprise: custom, adds SSO/SAML, audit logs, volume pricing, on-prem and private VPC, ZDR and DPA. No per-token bill: you bring your own model subscriptions or API keys (Anthropic API, Bedrock, Codex, Azure AI Foundry, OpenAI Responses).

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Desktop app is Apple silicon only (download is darwin-arm64; Homebrew cask humanlayer/humanlayer/humanlayer).
featureNotes.platforms.windows: No desktop app. The docs' Linux/Windows path is the npm CLI running a remote daemon on that machine, driven from the browser app; the browser app lacks workspace management, embedded terminal and directory auto-complete.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: No desktop app. Same daemon-plus-browser path as Windows; a systemd user service recipe is documented.
