featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Pay-as-you-go billing is managed by Model API team admins; the flat subscriptions are per Meta Account through Accounts Center and 'for use with Muse Code only'.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: The `muse` binary is proprietary (curl installer, no source). Only the TypeScript/Python SDK and protocol schema (meta-models/muse-code-sdk) are MIT.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Everything runs locally except the model, which is only available from Meta's API.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: You authenticate with a Meta Model API key or Meta Account subscription; Meta bills the tokens. No documented way to point it at Anthropic/OpenAI/local models.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: The settings file is said to hold 'telemetry options' but no page documents what is collected or how to turn it off; the Model API ToS defines Usage Data (tool call sequences, logs, telemetry) that Meta may use.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial: Muse Code's marketed 'Plugins' are agent-side bundles of Skills + Hooks + MCP servers (explicitly compatible with/importable from Claude Code and Codex plugins) that shape the agent's behaviour, not Muse Code's own panels/commands, so these do not count and the prior `true` was wrong. However, Muse Code separately documents the Muse Session Protocol (MSP) and a `@muse-code/sdk` TypeScript SDK, a JSON-RPC-style wire protocol (`session/start`, `turn/start`, `approval/decide`, `view/subscribe`, etc.) explicitly built so third-party code can drive a Muse Code session from outside the app, which matches the 'control protocol that can drive the app from outside' bar for partial. Documented at https://meta-models.github.io/muse-code-sdk (MSP reference) and https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/extending (Skills/Hooks/MCP, agent-side).
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: `muse serve` speaks the Muse Session Protocol (JSON-RPC-style over stdio) with an MIT TypeScript SDK (@muse-code/sdk) and Python SDK in developer preview; it is an MCP client (stdio and streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1 login), not an MCP server.

top.title: Meta debuts first AI coding agent to take on Anthropic and OpenAI

editorial.reachRationale: Meta's own AI account (@AIatMeta, 852k followers) was discounted heavily since Muse Code is not Meta's flagship product; concrete product signals are thin, only 8,740 monthly downloads for the SDK (no CLI registry), no Discord, no product-specific X, and the top HN story for a supposed 229-story query drew just 8 points, consistent with a tool that had only come out of beta on August 31, 2026.
editorial.polishRationale: Docs are thorough and consistent, the changelog is long and security-annotated, and it left beta on 2026-08-31 with paid plans, but the flagship workflow feature is missing from the public Apple silicon build and behind rollout gates, Windows lacks voice and messaging, the homepage contradicts the docs on Linux, and the SDK is a pre-1.0 developer preview. Judged from docs and release notes, not hands-on.
editorial.depthRationale: Far more than a session switcher inside one process: an eight-to-64 agent tree with a /workflows control room (pause, skip, restart children, save the orchestration as JavaScript), four background observer agents, goals that hold the agent to completion, cron loops, session-to-session messaging, hooks, MCP, a stdio session protocol with SDKs, and an OS sandbox with stage-by-stage shell approval. It stops short of platform depth because it has no diff review, PR flow, task board, or any way to see two top-level sessions together. Judged from docs and release notes, not hands-on.
editorial.feelRationale: The changelog reports deliberate responsiveness work rather than complaints: the '--resume' picker 'stays responsive while sessions are still being discovered on a cold start' and the task/subagent tree 'stays responsive as the number of tasks grows.' A Reddit thread calling recent Muse Spark 'slow' ties it to free-tier removal and rate limits (model/agent speed, not interface lag, which Feel leaves out), and no TUI jank or freeze reports turned up in docs or search.

tools.name: Nebula
tools.tagline: The multiplayer AI workspace
tools.valueProp: A Slack-like team chat workspace, not a coding tool: channels hold text, voice and video where an always-on orchestrator agent (Nebula) assembles and runs a team of specialists, mixing Claude Code, Codex and other coding CLIs on your own plan with Nebula's own credit-billed models, thousands of app connections, scheduled jobs and monitors, and AI-built mini-apps. There is no git worktree, diff-review or self-hosting story here, coding agents are just one agent type among many, and every device (yours or Nebula's cloud) routes through Nebula's own backend.

pricing.notes: $25 per seat / mo, 7-day free trial, no separate free tier found. Includes unlimited messaging/calls, orchestration and a cloud device with no usage charge. Two ways to run agents: bring your own Claude/ChatGPT (etc.) subscription at no extra cost, or use Nebula's own built-in models paid per task with Nebula Credits (auto-topup available). GitHub, Gmail, Slack, Notion, Linear, Stripe, Google Workspace, Discord, Telegram, PostgreSQL and 'thousands' of other app connections are included.

featureNotes.platforms.web: Changelog v1.0.175 (Aug 10, 2026): 'Nebula mobile, now in your browser', a browser client exists, framed primarily as the mobile-web path rather than a full desktop-parity web app.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: `nebula-ai` CLI, run via `npx nebula-ai` (no install) or `brew install agent-labs-dev/nebula/nebula-ai` (own tap, not homebrew-core). Full command surface: chat, channels, agents, calls, models, local-device, plus `--json` one-shot output and `acp` mode for editor integration.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: Running `nebula-ai` with no subcommand opens a full-screen terminal app with vim-like modal keybindings ('Nebula CLI' docs page).
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: `nebula-ai local-device enable` registers the current machine as a device; docs explicitly frame this as 'the right tool for a server or a dev box you reach over SSH' ('Devices' and 'Computer use from the CLI' docs pages).
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Cloud devices are vendor-provisioned ('the agent works in the cloud sandbox rather than on your machine'), billed in Nebula Credits, and cleaned up after 60 days idle if the workspace is unsubscribed ('Devices' docs page).
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: No self-hosted relay/server option is documented anywhere; both local and cloud devices authenticate to and route through Nebula's own backend, there is no vendor-server-free deployment path.
featureNotes.agents.amp: Amp is not named anywhere in the docs' coding-agent list (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, opencode, Aider, Goose, or Custom CLI) or the changelog.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Pi is not named anywhere in the docs or changelog; only usable, if at all, via the generic 'Custom CLI' option.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: 'Custom CLI' is one of the listed coding-agent options alongside the named ones ('Coding agents' docs page), a generic adapter for an arbitrary command.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Nebula Flash (default, fast) and Nebula Ultra (deeper, slower) are Nebula's own models with a 'Built-in' badge, distinct from 'coding agents' which run under the user's own plan/API key ('Models' docs page). Chat and calls always run on Nebula's own model regardless of task-model settings.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Cloud devices run as isolated vendor-managed sandboxes, but sandboxing is per-device, not spun up per task/branch the way a coding-focused tool would use containers; there is no per-task container or microVM lifecycle documented.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: No git worktree concept anywhere in the docs; Nebula is not git-native. Work is tracked by task state (Queued/Running/Paused/Needs your attention) inside a channel, not by branches.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: No branch-management feature documented; git only ever appears as something a connected coding-agent CLI or GitHub connection might do on its own.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: No in-app diff viewer is documented anywhere in the docs or changelog.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: GitHub is one of many app connections agents can use as a generic tool action (create issues, open PRs, etc. via the connected account), but there is no dedicated PR/review UI built into Nebula itself.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Not documented; no merge or conflict-resolution feature anywhere in the docs.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Not documented; no snapshot/rollback mechanism for agent work or files is described anywhere in the docs.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Per-channel 'Tasks' box plus a workspace-wide 'Tasks' feed (left rail) list every task with a state (Queued/Running/Paused/Needs your attention), grouped by day, a queue/list view, not a drag-and-drop kanban board ('Tasks, scheduled tasks and monitors' docs page).
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Nebula (the orchestrator) creates the specialist agents a channel's goal needs without being asked, and is always on the team itself ('Agents and your channel's team' docs page).
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Scheduled tasks (cron-like schedule) and monitors (short one-shot watches of a public page/search) run via the 'Jobs' box, plus GitHub/webhook/app-event and presence triggers (changelog v1.0.175).
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Calls (voice/video) with the team and with Nebula are a first-class surface, including a CLI 'call' command set and a `--headless` audio-only mode for servers/containers ('Calls with your team and Nebula', 'Calls from the terminal' docs pages).
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Per-seat pricing ($25/seat/mo), a workspace-level Nebula Credits balance/auto-topup (`user billing`), and admin-only controls over the model catalog/default imply org-level billing, though no dedicated 'Team plan' or admin-billing doc page beyond the pricing page and CLI reference was found.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Every device (local or cloud) still authenticates to and is billed through Nebula's own servers; there is no path to run the product without Nebula's backend.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Pricing page: 'Bring in your Claude or ChatGPT subscription' (coding agents run on your own plan/API key, no extra cost) as an alternative to 'Nebula agents' paid via Nebula Credits, both models coexist rather than the vendor exclusively reselling tokens.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: CLI reference: `user config set telemetry false` turns off product analytics, and the `DO_NOT_TRACK` env var does the same without touching config. The website privacy policy only covers generic marketing-site analytics (Google Analytics/Ads, ConvertKit) and does not separately address in-app telemetry.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system for Nebula itself. The only extension point is pointing agents at a custom OpenAI-compatible model endpoint (Settings → Workspace → Models), which is model configuration, not an extension of the app; Skills, Apps and MCP servers are agent-side. Documented at docs.nebula.gg/docs/workspace/models.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: `nebula-ai` supports `--json` output on one-shot commands for scripting, agents can add tools 'from any MCP server' (changelog v0.5.46), and `nebula-ai acp` exposes Nebula to ACP-compatible editors, no separate public REST API was found.

activity.changelogCadence: very frequent: 84 dated entries logged June 2026 - August 13, 2026, the page's own count, often several per day

editorial.reachRationale: A product-specific X account (NebulaAI, 4,917 followers, posting almost daily) and modest npm downloads (4,717/month) show real, growing use, but there's no Discord, no GitHub presence to gauge contributors, and zero HN stories, so this reads as early rather than an established quantity.
editorial.polishRationale: Judged from docs/marketing/CLI reference rather than hands-on use: the docs site is unusually thorough (own llms-full.txt, per-page .mdx, in-page 'Ask AI'), the changelog ships close to daily, and the brand mark was refined (Aug 12, 2026 'orbit' to 'loop' logo update), but no independent reviews or hands-on reports were found to confirm real-world polish.
editorial.depthRationale: Far beyond a session switcher: channels with text/voice/video, an always-on orchestrator that builds its own specialist team, tasks/scheduled jobs/monitors, AI-built channel mini-apps, local and vendor-cloud devices, 4,000+ app connections, a model catalog spanning built-in/catalog/custom-endpoint/local-via-Ollama, skills as slash commands, notifications with write-approval rules, a full CLI/TUI with ACP editor integration, and computer-use from the CLI. Judged from docs/marketing/CLI reference rather than hands-on use.
editorial.feelRationale: No implementation-language or rendering-stack claims were found (closed source, no repo); the desktop apps ship as standard macOS/Windows/Linux downloads with no native/GPU-rendering claims, consistent with a typical Electron-or-web-tech cross-platform app. A web search for 'Nebula agent labs workspace slow OR fast OR laggy' returned no reviews of this product at all (only unrelated same-named tools: Slack's Nebula overlay network and ThreatDown/Malwarebytes' Nebula endpoint console), so there is no direct performance evidence either way.

tools.name: Nimbalyst
tools.tagline: Open-source visual workspace for building with Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and other coding agents.
tools.valueProp: A visual workspace that pairs WYSIWYG editors (markdown, mockups, Mermaid, Excalidraw, data models) with parallel Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode/Copilot sessions in worktrees, a kanban-style tracker, and a native iOS companion for triaging agents remotely. Free and MIT-licensed solo (successor to the archived Crystal); real-time team collaboration and a self-hosted sync server require a paid Teams or Enterprise contract.

maker.name: Nimbalyst Inc.
maker.funding: Not disclosed; founders previously built and sold Evergage to Salesforce in 2020 (grew to $250M+ ARR by 2023).

pricing.notes: Individual is free forever, no account or credit card required, with the full feature set (visual editors, all supported agents, tracker, worktrees, mobile app, MCP support). Teams is $20/user/month or $200/user/year (free during Beta) and adds real-time multiplayer editing and shared trackers. Enterprise is custom: a collaboration server in your own Cloudflare account or Nimbalyst-managed, source-available (not open) collaboration code for that company's use only, data residency, and an embedded engineer. AI access is bring-your-own: a Claude/Codex subscription, an API key, or local models via LM Studio.

featureNotes.platforms.web: console.nimbalyst.com lets an invited teammate open, edit and comment on a team's shared documents in a browser with no install, but it only reaches content promoted into Nimbalyst Teams (docs: team-collaboration/overview, 'Teammates without the app').
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The `nim` npm CLI (`@nimbalyst/cli`) is a full read/write client for Trackers (list, create, update, comment, import from GitHub issues, `--json`/`--csv` output) but does not start or steer AI sessions; it talks to the running app or reads the local tracker DB directly.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: v0.78.0 (2026-09-14) changelog: 'Run remote sessions in your own Cloudflare sandbox with attachments, Actions, and saved account preferences,' plus 'Removing a Cloudflare sandbox also removes its container application.' No dedicated docs page was found for this as of 2026-09-25, so treated as new/unconfirmed-in-docs.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: No evidence Nimbalyst provisions or manages agent-execution compute itself; the only cloud infrastructure documented is the Cloudflare sync/collaboration service for Teams data, and the new remote-sessions feature runs in the user's own Cloudflare account, not a Nimbalyst-managed one.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The core desktop/iOS app needs no vendor server for solo local use. A self-run collaboration server is offered only on Enterprise (custom pricing): 'Collaboration server in your own Cloudflare account, or managed by us' with 'Collaboration code source available for your company only use' (pricing page), source-available under contract, not part of the open MIT repo.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Listed as 'Gemini through Antigravity (Alpha)': it uses the language server bundled with Google's Antigravity desktop app (Antigravity must be installed and signed in once), not the standalone Gemini CLI directly.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: 'GitHub Copilot (Alpha)' via ACP server mode, using your existing `copilot` CLI login (`npm install -g @github/copilot`, then `/login`).
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: 'Cursor Agent (Alpha)' runs the Cursor CLI headlessly against the project, using your existing `cursor-agent login`.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Providers come from a fixed, named list (Claude Agent, Codex, Claude Code CLI, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, Cursor Agent, Gemini/Antigravity); no generic 'point it at an arbitrary command' adapter is documented.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: 'Claude Agent is Nimbalyst's integrated Claude coding agent' (docs), a first-party agent loop distinct from the opt-in, separately toggled Claude Code CLI provider.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Local isolation is via git worktrees, not containers/sandboxes. The only container-like isolation is the new (2026-09-14) BYO Cloudflare sandbox for remote sessions, which the changelog says has 'its own container application.'
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Docs (developer-features/worktrees): a worktree 'gives an AI session its own branch and its own working directory, isolated from your main checkout,' created automatically from the New Worktree action, a Tracker item, or 'Open in Worktree' on a pull request.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Pull Request mode (via the `gh` CLI) reviews, comments on, approves and merges existing GitHub pull requests, including choosing squash/merge-commit/rebase; no in-app 'open a new PR' action is documented in Working with Git or Pull Request Reviews, so opening the PR itself is left to `gh`/GitHub.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: 'Merge to master' from the worktree panel, rebase with automatic stashing of uncommitted changes, and in Pull Request mode, approve/merge with a choice of GitHub's squash, merge-commit or rebase strategies (limited to what the repo allows, always confirmed).
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: File History and Restore: automatic snapshots of every edited document with built-in version history and restore, independent of git (docs.nimbalyst.com/file-management/file-history-and-restore). This covers file content, not a broader agent-state/session rollback.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Agent Teams (Experimental, toggle in Claude Agent settings): a session can spawn parallel teammate agents for independent subtasks, each with its own progress indicator, contained output, at the cost of more tokens; a Super Loop instead re-runs one agent iteratively in a dedicated worktree until a task completes.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: v0.77.5 changelog: 'Coordinating agents read sibling reports during long-running work without replaying them as extra turns,' and Agent Teams coordinates teammate agents within one session, real but narrow evidence, short of a general cross-session messaging feature.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Nimbalyst Teams gives real-time multiplayer editing of shared documents, mockups, diagrams and trackers, but each teammate runs their own local agent against those shared files ('Each teammate's local Claude Code and Codex agents edit the same shared documents, not separate copies'), no evidence two people can see or steer the same live agent session together.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The local desktop/iOS app needs no vendor server for solo use, but Nimbalyst Teams data always flows through Nimbalyst's own Cloudflare sync service (hosted keys, 'encrypted but not zero-knowledge'), and personal device (mobile) sync is relayed, E2E-encrypted, through Nimbalyst's own sync servers. A self-run collaboration server is Enterprise-only and source-available under contract, not part of the open repo.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: Extensions (Settings → Extensions → Marketplace, or install-from-GitHub-URL with a `manifest.json`) are third-party code that adds custom editors, sidebar/fullscreen/floating panels, settings pages and themes to Nimbalyst's own app, integrating through the same EditorHost contract as first-party editors, a genuine app-level extension point, not just agent tools. Built with the bundled Extension Dev Kit and Extension SDK. Documented at docs.nimbalyst.com/extensions/extension-system-and-marketplace.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Nimbalyst is an MCP client (connect GitHub, Linear, Slack, etc.) and ships its own MCP tools for agents to drive the editor (AskUserQuestion, PromptForUserInput, screenshot/display tools), plus the separate `nim` CLI/npm package for external, scriptable control of Trackers specifically. No evidence Nimbalyst exposes its own MCP server or API for outside control of sessions/the app as a whole.

github.description: Nimbalyst - The open-source visual workspace for Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. Run multiple coding agents in parallel, edit their work visually in markdown, mockups, and diagrams, and track tasks. Free, MIT-licensed desktop app for macOS, Windows, Linux, with mobile companion for iOS and Android.

top.title: Show HN: Nimbalyst open-source visual workspace for ClaudeCode, Codex, OpenCode

editorial.reachRationale: 906 Discord members (ahead of Emdash's 630, an established tool), 48 contributors and 50,153 release-asset downloads across the last 5 releases show a real, active user base past the early-adopter stage, reinforced by inheriting Crystal's prior audience as its announced, first-party successor. The 8-point/4-comment Show HN launch and 1,776 stars (well below Emdash's 5,768) are discounted as weak attention signals rather than usage.
editorial.polishRationale: Broad platform coverage (macOS arm64/x64, Windows, Linux .deb+AppImage, a Homebrew cask, and a real iOS App Store app rather than TestFlight-only), SOC 2 Type 2 certification, and a large GitBook docs site (dozens of pages, most updated within 14 days) show a serious production effort. Set against that: pre-1.0 as of September 2026 (v0.78.5), 678 open GitHub issues against 1,776 stars (a much heavier backlog ratio than comparable tools), and the changelog shows the same categories of stutter and freeze bugs (autosave, diff-mode versioning, tool-call hangs, editor screenshots) recurring and being re-fixed release after release.
editorial.depthRationale: Goes further than a worktree-and-diff-review tool: parallel worktree-isolated sessions, an agent-spawn-agent Agent Teams mode plus iterative Super Loops, a built-in kanban/list task tracker with its own scriptable CLI (`nim`) and GitHub-issue importers, in-app PR review/approve/merge via `gh`, real-time multiplayer Teams collaboration on documents/mockups/diagrams/trackers, a full extension SDK and marketplace, MCP client support plus Nimbalyst's own MCP tools for agents, voice mode on desktop and mobile, and a native iOS companion with push notifications and offline queuing.
editorial.feelRationale: Electron/React/Jotai desktop stack (TypeScript dominates the repo's language breakdown at 46.5MB; Swift, 1.8MB, is only the separate native iOS app), not a native-perf framework. Changelog entries across several consecutive releases describe and fix stutter/freeze issues: markdown autosave stutter in a workspace with a large tracker (v0.76.3), an autosave/freeze bug that could revert agent edits already open in diff mode (v0.76.2), a stuck tool call that could hang an agent indefinitely with nothing in the logs (v0.77.0), and editor-screenshot freezes (v0.78.0). A Reddit user separately asked 'is the chat speed as fast as if I was using Claude code natively? It seems to lag a bit,' and the maker replied a fix shipped in v0.57 (https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeAI/comments/1pfu3hs/). The recurring pattern of distinct perf bugs across many releases, even though each is patched quickly, points to real ongoing jank rather than a snappy interface.

tools.name: Omnara
tools.tagline: The open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents.
tools.valueProp: Relaunched in September 2026 from a Claude Code phone remote into durable-agent infrastructure: an agent’s config is immutable and its state commits atomically to Postgres, so it survives crashes and disconnects. Runs its own tool loop on pluggable sandboxes rather than wrapping Claude Code or Codex.

maker.name: Omnara (Ishaan Sehgal & Kartik Sarangmath)
maker.funding: Y Combinator S25; no priced round disclosed

pricing.notes: Self-serve platform fee is $0: you pay model-provider token rates plus, if you use Omnara-managed sandboxes/storage, $0.0414/GiB-hr machine runtime and $0.20016/GiB per 30 days retention. BYO models and BYO machines are free with no credit card. Self-hosting the whole platform is free under Apache-2.0. Enterprise tier (BYO cloud, on-prem, SSO, custom SLAs) is quote-based.

featureNotes.platforms.ios: A native iOS app ('Omnara: Claude & Codex Mobile', App Store id6748426727) remained listed as of September 2026, but its last update was 2026-04-07, before the September 2026 relaunch; it describes the retired Claude-Code/Codex remote-control product and was not referenced from the homepage, README or docs at that time, so treated as legacy/unsupported rather than part of the relaunched platform.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Same legacy app situation as iOS: the Play Store listing predates the September 2026 relaunch and was not linked from any first-party page as of September 2026.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Pre-relaunch Omnara (through mid-2026) was literally a CLI wrapper that parsed ~/.claude/projects session files to mirror the Claude Code terminal. The platform relaunched in September 2026 to run its own configurable tool-calling loop instead of invoking the claude or codex binaries; the only relationship to those tools since the relaunch is the reverse direction, connecting Claude Code or Codex as MCP *clients* to the Omnara API (docs.omnara.com/changelog, Sept 14 2026).
featureNotes.agents.codex: See agents.claudeCode note - same reverse-direction MCP relationship, not process wrapping.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: 'Machines': ephemeral sandboxes from Blaxel, Daytona, Modal or Unikraft Cloud, created per machine pool (README Features; docs.omnara.com/machines overview referenced from /concepts).
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Durable execution commits agent state atomically to Postgres and resumes after crashes/restarts/disconnects; the event_webhook config also exposes a discrete 'context_checkpoint' event type (docs.omnara.com/agents/configuration).
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Dashboard organizes agents under organizations -> projects -> agents; no kanban-style board is described anywhere in docs.omnara.com/concepts or the changelog.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: No dedicated notification center; the ability to interact with an agent from Slack via the 'first-party Slack connector' (README, 'Who it is for -> Teams') functions as a notification/interaction channel, but no push/email notification feature is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Voice control was a feature of the pre-relaunch mobile app ('Omnara: Claude & Codex Mobile', YC launch post Jan 2026) and was not present in docs.omnara.com pages or the README feature list as of September 2026.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: README 'Who it is for -> Teams': 'Interact with agents directly through Omnara's dashboard or first-party Slack connector', implying multiple team members can view/interact with the same agent's conversation; not spelled out as a named feature beyond that line.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Sept 18 2026 changelog: 'New usage pages for your organization, projects, profiles, and agents show model API usage, and the model catalog now lists pricing per million input and output tokens' - usage/cost tracked at the organization scope.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: No telemetry policy or opt-out control found in the README, docs.omnara.com, or SECURITY.md; not stated either way.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system for the Omnara dashboard itself. Custom model providers (base URL, auth headers) are model configuration; Skills are instruction bundles the agent loads and MCP servers add tools to the agent, all agent-side. Nothing adds or changes a panel, view or command in Omnara. Documented at docs.omnara.com/organization/model-providers and docs.omnara.com/tools/skills.

github.description: The open-source managed agent platform. A self-hostable alternative to Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API.

top.title: Show HN: Omnara – Run Claude Code from anywhere

activity.changelogCadence: weekly since the September 2026 relaunch (Sept 2, 9, 14, 18 entries)

editorial.reachRationale: Product-specific signals are modest and mostly predate the relaunched product: ~2,870 stars / 15 contributors, a 508-member Discord (66 online), and 2,620 weekly npm downloads for the `omnara` CLI. The single biggest traction signal - a 310-point, 173-story-query HN presence - is almost entirely the old 'Run Claude Code from anywhere' mobile-remote-control product (Aug 2025), which was retired at the September 2, 2026 relaunch; it should not be read as validation of the durable-agent-API platform that replaced it. YC S25 backing is a company-legitimacy signal, not a usage signal. This sits below established multiplexers like cmux or herdr (established reach) and roughly level with humanlayer (emerging reach): real but early, a product-specific community rather than a dominant or major one.
editorial.polishRationale: The API, CLI, SDK and dashboard are all documented and shipping, but the platform relaunched on Sept 2, 2026 after retiring its prior product entirely, so the surface had about three weeks of field mileage when it was researched in September 2026; the changelog shows active near-weekly iteration (subagents, deferred tools, usage pages all shipped in September alone) consistent with a product that was still settling as of September 2026.
editorial.depthRationale: Durable Postgres-backed execution, four pluggable sandbox providers plus BYO machines, subagents with configurable fan-out/depth, RBAC, MCP client and server support, and an event-webhook system go well beyond a CLI wrapper - but it is agent infrastructure rather than a coding-specific tool, so it has zero git-native review features (no worktrees, diff review, PR creation, merge assist).
editorial.feelRationale: No first-party performance claims or architecture deep-dive were found for the relaunched platform, and a targeted search for 'Omnara slow OR fast OR laggy' surfaced no user reports of jank or speed either way (only App Store/GitHub/LinkedIn/Reddit listings). The backend is Go (per go.mod) with a Postgres durability layer and a Next.js-style web dashboard; built-in tool results over 50 KiB are automatically spilled to files to keep the model's context (and by extension the UI) responsive (Sept 18 2026 changelog). Scored in the middle: professionally engineered, but the rewrite was only weeks old when researched in September 2026, too early for real user sentiment.

tools.name: Omnigent
tools.tagline: A common layer over Claude Code, Codex, Pi, and the agents you write yourself: swap or combine harnesses without rewriting, keep them in check with policies and sandboxing, and collaborate in real time on the same live session, from any device.
tools.valueProp: The governance layer: spend caps, risk scores and a kernel-enforced sandbox with placeholder credentials sit under every session, whichever of its 17 harnesses runs it. Databricks-backed and open on every platform, but self-described alpha as of September 2026.

maker.name: Databricks, Inc.
maker.funding: Databricks-funded open-source project (launched by Databricks on 2026-06-12; pyproject author is Databricks, Inc.; a managed 'Omnigent on Databricks' beta runs inside Databricks workspaces)

pricing.notes: Free and Apache-2.0; nothing is sold on omnigent.ai. Models come from your own Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, a Claude Pro/Max or ChatGPT plan through the official claude/codex CLIs, any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible gateway (OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Ollama, vLLM, Azure), AWS Bedrock/Vertex, or a Databricks workspace. Cloud sandboxes bill through your own Modal/Daytona/E2B/etc. account. The only vendor-run option is 'Omnigent on Databricks' (Beta), covered by the customer's Databricks contract or Free Edition terms; no Omnigent-specific price is published.

featureNotes.platforms.windows: Desktop app ships as a Windows .exe. The CLI runs natively 'in a degraded mode': server, web UI and SDK harnesses work, but the tmux-based `omnigent claude/codex/cursor` terminal wrappers and the bwrap/seatbelt sandbox and egress proxy are unavailable (use WSL).
featureNotes.platforms.linux: Desktop app ships as .deb and .AppImage; CLI sandboxing on Linux requires bubblewrap.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: Native App Store app (id6783102694); a thin shell over the server-served web UI that requires an https:// server URL, so a bare local server is rejected. Notifications only while the app is in the foreground.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Native Google Play app (ai.omnigent.android); same thin-shell model, with EMM/MDM managed server presets.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: The terminal mode is a streaming chat REPL that needs tmux, plus the vendor's own TUI (claude-native, codex-native, etc.) mirrored in a pane; there is no multi-session full-screen TUI of Omnigent's own.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Any machine you run `omni host <server-url>` on becomes a host the server can dispatch sessions to; the server itself deploys via docker compose on a VPS, or over Tailscale/Cloudflare tunnel from a laptop.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Server-provisioned 'managed hosts' need your own account with Modal, Daytona, Blaxel, Islo, E2B, Gensee, CoreWeave, Kubernetes, OpenShell, Boxlite or microsandbox. The only vendor-operated option is 'Omnigent on Databricks' (Beta) inside a Databricks workspace.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Two paths: `claude-sdk` (direct, Omnigent drives the model/tools) and `claude-native` (Claude Code's own TUI mirrored into the UI). Both 'Fully supported'.
featureNotes.agents.codex: `codex` (direct) and `codex-native`; both 'Fully supported'. Approval presets and reasoning effort are set from the composer.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Gemini CLI is not in the harness table. Google's Antigravity CLI (`agy`, Gemini-backed) is supported as a community harness instead.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Listed as harness `copilot` ('Maintained', direct execution only, installed via the `copilot` SDK extra); the docs do not say whether it wraps the Copilot CLI binary or the SDK.
featureNotes.agents.opencode: `opencode-native` only (vendor TUI in a pane); no direct-execution mode. 'Maintained'.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: `cursor` and `cursor-native` (cursor-agent CLI), 'Maintained'; supports Plan/Smart Auto/yolo execution modes from the composer.
featureNotes.agents.pi: `pi` (headless, any gateway model) and `pi-native`; Pi is the default review/explore worker in Polly.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: No arbitrary-command adapter. A custom agent must speak the Agent Client Protocol (declared as an `acp:` agent; Goose, Grok Build, Devin, Jcode and OpenClaw come this way) or be packaged as a community harness plugin.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Ships its own agent runtime: YAML agents on `claude-sdk` / `openai-agents` harnesses, plus bundled agents Polly (multi-agent coding supervisor), Debby (Claude-vs-GPT debate) and Deep Research.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Name a branch in the new-chat composer to run the session in its own git worktree; 'Always use a random worktree' (global or per-project) makes every new session get one. Polly workers each get a worktree.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Two layers: Omnibox, a kernel-enforced OS sandbox (bubblewrap+seccomp on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS) with filesystem grants, default-deny egress proxy and placeholder-credential injection; and per-session cloud sandbox hosts on Modal/Daytona/E2B/Kubernetes/etc. Neither is on by default for a plain local session.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Automatic only when 'Always use a random worktree' is on (off by default) or a project sets Random worktree; otherwise you type the branch name.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Changes tab with syntax-highlighted diffs, an 'Attach to agent' button for a selected line range, inline comments on agent output, and a GitHub tab with the PR's stacked diff and CI checks.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: No create-PR control of its own. PRs are opened by the agent (`gh` or GitHub MCP), auto-discovered and tracked in the GitHub tab; in managed sandboxes 'GitHub Connect' vends a per-user token so pushes and PRs run as you. Polly's workers each open their own PR.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Nothing documented for merging or conflicts; Polly's docs say 'Polly never merges. The human decides.'
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: No file or agent-state rollback. Sessions can be forked (conversation history copied to a new session, optionally onto a different harness or a fresh sandbox), which is not a restore.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Sidebar of sessions grouped into Projects, desktop multi-window, Canvas board (gated), a dock badge of sessions waiting on you, and Polly's /fanout running workers in parallel worktrees.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Canvas is a per-project board of draggable live session cards (status, worktree branch, PR link) but is off by default behind OMNIGENT_FEATURES=canvas, and there is no queue of tasks feeding agents; the workspace rail has a Todos tab.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: YAML agents declare sub-agents a supervisor delegates to; Polly plans, spawns coding workers on different harnesses and routes diffs to a different-vendor reviewer; 'agents can build agents' from chat. Sub-agent terminals are visible in the Agents panel.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Scheduled tasks: a saved prompt + RFC 5545 RRULE (hourly at most) fired on a connected host, created from the web UI dialog or by agents via built-in sys_scheduled_task_* tools. Missed fires are not replayed; no event triggers.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Desktop app: OS notifications (with sound) and a dock badge when an agent finishes, asks for input or a runner disconnects, combined across servers. iOS: foreground-only notifications. Web: none documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Any agent can read the history of other sessions you have access to, and supervisor agents message their sub-agents; no direct session-to-session messaging is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: A 'Toggle voice dictation' shortcut (Cmd+Alt+V) exists in the web UI and the iOS app requests microphone access; dictation only, no documented voice command mode.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Built-in invite-only accounts (OMNIGENT_AUTH_ENABLED=1, default on in Docker), OIDC SSO (Google, GitHub, Okta, Microsoft) or header auth behind a proxy; admins get Members, server-wide Policies and Sharing settings.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Share a session link with Read (watch stream) or Edit (co-drive; teammate's messages execute on the host machine) access; `omni attach` from the terminal; messages are labelled per account for the model.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Org admin exists (members roster, SSO, server-wide policies, macOS MDM and Android managed configuration) but there is nothing to bill; the paid path is Databricks' managed service under Databricks terms.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Server (Docker, Fly, Railway, Render, Kubernetes, Databricks Apps), runner and all clients talk only to your server. Telemetry fetches a remote config from Omnigent at startup unless disabled.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Claude Pro/Max and ChatGPT plans are used through the official `claude`/`codex` CLIs; API keys, gateways and Databricks profiles are the other credential kinds. Omnigent resells no tokens.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Anonymous telemetry is on by default since v0.6.0; off via OMNIGENT_ANALYTICS=0, DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or telemetry: false in ~/.omnigent/config.yaml.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: harness plugins are Python packages that declare an `omnigent.community.harness` entry point and export get_contribution(); once installed they show up in agent YAML, --harness, and the web UI's harness picker exactly like a built-in harness, without touching the core omnigent package. Same entry-point pattern extends sandbox providers (Modal/Daytona/etc.) for the deploy layer. This is third-party code adding real runtime/provider surfaces to Omnigent itself, not agent-side skills/MCP. Documented at omnigent.ai/docs/build/harnesses/community and omnigent.ai/docs/deploy/cloud-sandbox-host.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: REST API (openapi.json in repo, machine tokens via client_credentials) and a Python SDK (omnigent-client). An MCP server for Omnigent itself is on the launch-blog roadmap, not shipped; agents consume MCP servers as tools.

github.description: Omnigent is an open-source AI agent framework and meta-harness: orchestrate Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, and custom agents — swap harnesses without rewriting, enforce policies and sandboxing, and collaborate in real time from any device.

top.title: Omnigent: A Meta-Harness to Combine, Control and Share Your Agents

editorial.reachRationale: 259 contributors and a weekly release cadence back a genuinely large open-source community; discounted the flaky, mostly-null PyPI download numbers and the 10k stars, and noted Databricks' backing (a Databricks-funded project, not Databricks' flagship, so the company's scale doesn't transfer); the 1,583-member Discord and steady commit activity support established rather than major.
editorial.polishRationale: The FAQ says 'Is it ready for production? No. It is alpha.'; 1,373 open issues three months after launch; the v0.14.0 changelog is dominated by bug fixes (approvals lost across restarts, sessions reappearing after archive); the Windows CLI is documented as 'degraded'; Canvas is behind a feature flag; and the docs, while thorough and consistent, sprawl across quickstart/docs/reference with duplicated sections. Against that, it ships on every surface at once (three desktop OSes, App Store, Google Play, web, CLI) with a weekly release and a curated release-notes page. Judged from docs and release notes, not hands-on use.
editorial.depthRationale: Far past a session switcher. A supervisor agent (Polly) plans, fans work out to Claude Code/Codex/Cursor/OpenCode/Hermes/Antigravity workers in parallel worktrees and routes each diff to a different vendor's reviewer; sessions can be co-driven, forked onto another harness or onto a fresh sandbox; the workspace rail has a diff viewer, inline comments that become agent instructions, a GitHub PR panel with checks; stateful policies (cost budgets, risk scores, PII holds, model routing) stack at server/agent/session level; Omnibox gives a kernel sandbox with a default-deny egress proxy that swaps placeholder tokens for real ones; scheduled tasks, a REST API and Python SDK, twelve cloud sandbox providers, SSO, MDM presets. Judged from docs and release notes, not hands-on use.
editorial.feelRationale: The web UI is a browser-based PWA (Monaco editor plus an xterm terminal) relayed through a server to local or cloud sandbox runners, with desktop/mobile as thin native wrappers around it, so it isn't GPU-native; but the v0.13.0 release notes make a direct performance claim about the app's own responsiveness - 'Sessions now feel instant... long transcripts virtualize so switching between them stays fast even when history is deep' - addressing session switching and scrollback specifically.

tools.name: OpenChamber
tools.tagline: An agentic development environment.
tools.valueProp: Wraps one backend, not many: every "agent" is a named model-and-prompt preset running inside the bundled OpenCode server, so switching agents means switching models, not switching CLIs the way multi-harness tools do. Session Goals hands an independent auditor model the job of deciding after each turn whether to keep going, stop, or flag you, so a session can work unattended toward a stated outcome instead of one reply at a time.

maker.name: Bohdan Triapitsyn
maker.funding: bootstrapped; optional Patreon support (patreon.com/openchamber)

pricing.notes: Homepage FAQ: "What does it cost? Nothing. OpenChamber itself is free. You pay only your model provider, on your own keys." MIT-licensed, no OpenChamber account or subscription exists; sign-in/accounts are listed on /activate as "almost here" but were not open as of September 2026. An optional Patreon (patreon.com/openchamber) supports the project.

featureNotes.platforms.ios: TestFlight beta only (testflight.apple.com/join/5ek6GU1E); not on the App Store. The PWA also installs via Safari "Add to Home Screen" as an alternative.
featureNotes.platforms.android: APK distributed from the GitHub releases page, not the Play Store. The PWA also installs via Chrome "Add to Home Screen".
featureNotes.platforms.tui: The app has an in-panel terminal (built on a browser adapter for libghostty-vt) and a CLI, but no full-screen terminal-UI mode of its own.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Desktop app connects to a machine you own over SSH (managed: OpenChamber installs and starts itself; or external: connect to one already running). Web/VS Code connect to a remote OpenCode server via OPENCODE_HOST/OPENCODE_SKIP_START env vars.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: No vendor-provisioned sandbox exists; every instance runs on a machine (local or remote) that the user controls. The optional Private Relay only routes encrypted traffic between your own devices, it does not run agents.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The whole stack (OpenChamber server + OpenCode) is self-hosted by design; a reverse-proxy guide covers running it behind your own HTTPS server. The optional Private Relay is vendor infrastructure but is E2E-encrypted, opt-in, and not required (LAN, tunnel or direct connection work without it).
featureNotes.agents.opencode: OpenChamber is a visual workspace built on top of the OpenCode CLI/SDK (a prerequisite install); OpenChamber's own "agents" (Settings > Agents) are named model+prompt+tool-rule presets inside that one OpenCode backend, not separate CLI harnesses.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Claude, Codex/ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub Copilot and others appear only as connectable model providers (Settings > Providers, Usage & Quotas) behind OpenCode, not as alternate agent CLIs OpenChamber launches.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: No generic "point it at any command" agent adapter; the only supported agent runtime is the bundled/attached OpenCode server.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: OpenChamber does not ship its own agent loop; OpenCode (a separate required install) provides it.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: No session/file snapshot-and-restore feature found across the docs (install, worktrees, git, troubleshooting); git history, stash and the worktree/branch model are the only rollback paths.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: The sidebar lists sessions by status (working/waiting/finished/failed) grouped by project or a chronological Timeline view; there is no kanban board or queue. A third-party extension could add one (Extension pages can offer a full-screen board), but none ships built-in.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: The built-in "Agent Control Tool" (openchamber tool, on by default with the managed OpenCode server) lets an agent inside a session create, follow up on, and fork other OpenChamber sessions, including isolated worktree sessions, and manage scheduled tasks, from chat.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: No inbox or channel between sessions beyond one agent using the Agent Control Tool to create/check other sessions; sessions do not message each other directly.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Voice Mode: browser, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible or macOS `say` for text-to-speech; browser, an OpenAI-compatible server, or an on-device model for dictation.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: The /activate page states "Accounts are almost here. Sign-in is not open yet." Device pairing (QR code, Private Relay) is for one person's own devices, not separate user accounts.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Fully self-hostable end to end (own server, own reverse proxy); the only vendor-run component is the optional, opt-in Private Relay (relay.openchamber.dev), which is end-to-end encrypted and not required for LAN/tunnel/direct use.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Homepage FAQ/Privacy section: "OpenChamber collects nothing about your work and sends nothing anywhere... does not collect project names, paths, prompts, code, diffs, or session content." No telemetry environment variable or setting was found because none is needed to opt out of.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: Settings > Extensions installs third-party code (from a local folder, zip, or git URL) that registers real UI surfaces, custom panels, inside Openchamber itself, gated by a declared, user-approved permission list; the @openchamber/sdk is the build kit for that panel/permission contract. This is an app-level extension point (adds to Openchamber's own interface), separate from OpenCode's own plugin system and from agent-side Skills. Documented at docs.openchamber.dev/extensions.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Add local or remote MCP servers per project or personally (Settings > MCP) to give agents extra tools; the extension SDK (`@openchamber/sdk`, `connectHost`) is a separate programmatic-control surface for third-party panels.

github.description: Agentic Development Environment based on OpenCode AI agent

top.title: Open Camera is a FOSS camera app for Android

editorial.reachRationale: Strong product-specific signals past early-adopter scale: 609,684 GitHub release-asset downloads over the last five releases, 229 contributors, an active Discord (1,028 members, 213 online) and a 190-point/93-comment Show HN launch. Discounted the 10.6k GitHub stars as attention rather than use, and discounted the modest 1,371 X followers/3 HN stories since the product is young (created Sept. 2025) and its dedicated X account only exists because the founder split it off from his personal one.
editorial.polishRationale: A professional, 11-language-localised site and docs, structured near-daily release notes (New/Improvements/Fixes/SDK sections), clients across desktop (Win/Mac/Linux), web/PWA, VS Code Marketplace, Android APK and iOS TestFlight, and user testimonials calling the app "phenomenal" with "unreal" polish. Held back: iOS is TestFlight-only, accounts/sign-in are explicitly "not open yet," and the changelog itself is full of UI-jank fixes (scroll twitching, stuck cards, session-list stalls) each release.
editorial.depthRationale: Well past a tmux wrapper: Session Goals runs an independent auditor loop to completion, Multi-run/Fusion compares up to five models per task, Changes Walkthrough narrates diffs, GitHub/Linear issues and PRs (with CI failures and review comments) round-trip through sessions, scheduled tasks/loops, MCP servers, skills, an agent control tool that can spawn/steer other sessions, and an extension SDK. Held back by having no task board/kanban and no cross-session messaging, and running only one backend (OpenCode) rather than aggregating agents.
editorial.feelRationale: Electron app (packages/electron; a maker tweet confirms "Desktop builds are now on Electron") with a browser-based terminal (README credits a libghostty-vt browser adapter), so not a native-rendered instant-feeling app. Evidence is genuinely mixed: homepage testimonials call it "smooth and silky" and praise its "streaming feature," while a Reddit thread is titled "Openchamber laggy and slow" and another lists blocking issues; the changelog carries recurring performance fixes release after release (far less CPU on streaming code blocks, scrollbar twitching fixed, faster session-list open/scroll, faster app startup in v2.0.0).

tools.name: OpenHands
tools.tagline: The self-hosted developer control center for coding agents and automations.
tools.valueProp: Agent Canvas is a self-hosted MIT control center that runs OpenHands’ own agent out of the box, or Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI over the Agent Client Protocol, switching between local, Docker, Kubernetes and cloud backends from one browser UI. A paired automation server runs scheduled and webhook-triggered workflows with no chat open.

maker.name: All Hands AI
maker.funding: VC-backed startup trading as OpenHands; a $18.8M raise is cited in a third-party tweet the company itself features as a homepage testimonial (openhands.dev), not a first-party funding announcement. npm package maintainer emails use both @openhands.dev and @all-hands.dev domains, and the SaaS product lives at app.all-hands.dev, confirming All Hands AI as the legal maker behind the OpenHands brand.

pricing.notes: Open Source tier: free, self-hosted, single user (this repo). Individual (SaaS, app.all-hands.dev): free, BYOK or pay-at-cost for the hosted OpenHands LLM provider, includes mobile access via tunneling and Slack/Jira/GitHub integrations. Enterprise: custom pricing, SaaS or self-hosted/VPC, adds SAML/SSO, multi-user RBAC, unlimited concurrent conversations, centralized team billing, a "Large Codebase" SDK tier, and priority support (openhands.dev/pricing).

featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: README: "Run OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or any ACP-compatible agent across local, remote, and cloud backends." The acp-agents doc lists exact launch commands (e.g. npx wrappers) and an authentication table per agent.
featureNotes.agents.opencode: Not named in the README's agent list or the acp-agents supported-providers table found; only OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI are named explicitly, alongside a generic "any custom stdio ACP server" option.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Agent Canvas is built on the Agent-Client Protocol (ACP): any agent that speaks ACP over stdio can be registered as a custom agent, not just the four named integrations.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Not documented; conversations get a workspace (host path, Docker container, VM, or cloud sandbox) but no first-party doc describes automatic git-worktree-per-conversation isolation.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: No first-party doc describes an automatic branch-per-task naming convention. "Fork a Conversation" (Conversations doc) branches the conversation's history/config/workspace context, which is a conversation-level fork, not a confirmed git-branch mechanism.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: No dedicated "open a PR" button is documented in Agent Canvas itself, the closest first-party features are PR *review* automations (GitHub PR Review Assistant, PR Review SDK guide). The agent can create PRs via its general shell/git or GitHub-MCP tool access when asked, and the Daily Workflow guide explicitly gates this behind confirmation policy ("its ability to push code, update GitHub... depends on the permissions granted to the MCP servers and the confirmation policy you use") rather than presenting it as a dedicated app feature.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: No dedicated commit/merge/discard review-UI controls are documented; git operations happen through the agent's own tool calls (terminal, GitHub MCP) rather than a Canvas-native review action.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Not documented; the Conversations doc covers branching, a judge-verified /goal loop, transcript export and archiving, but no checkpoint/restore mechanism.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: The Daily Workflow guide documents dispatching "a separate agent" for independent work, viewable afterward from the conversation list, but this is a manually-started parallel conversation, not a lead-agent-coordinated subagent tool like some competitors document.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Automations post digests and comments to Slack and GitHub (e.g. a weekday standup digest, PR-triage summaries), which is an external-notification mechanism; no dedicated in-app/browser notification system is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: No agent-to-agent messaging protocol is documented; parallel agents run as independent conversations you coordinate manually.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: No voice or dictation feature is documented in any Agent Canvas usage page found.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: The Open Source and Individual tiers are explicitly single-user (pricing page: "self-hosted, single user"); "Multi-user RBAC" is listed as an Enterprise-only feature.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: README: "you can share an Agent Server with your team for agents doing code review and dependency updates, then have your personal agents running on your laptop", a shared backend multiple teammates' Canvas instances can connect to; Enterprise adds formal RBAC on top of this.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: The Agent Canvas frontend (OpenHands/OpenHands, MIT, this repo), the Agent Server SDK (OpenHands/software-agent-sdk), the TypeScript client, and the Automation Server (OpenHands/automation) are all public repos under the OpenHands GitHub org. OpenHands Cloud and OpenHands Enterprise, the managed hosting/infrastructure products sold on top, are closed commercial services, hence partial rather than fully open.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: 'Apps' (Beta) are third-party JS bundles with a `canvas-extension.json` manifest and an `activate(host)` entrypoint that calls `host.registerPage()` to add real custom pages/panels to the Agent Canvas sidebar itself, app-level UI code, installed from a git repo or local path with a trust/install gate. Explicitly distinct from Skills (agent instructions) and Plugins (agent capability/config bundles), which are agent-side and don't count. Only available on local backends, not OpenHands Cloud. Documented at docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/canvas-extensions.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Not confirmed in the pages read; no telemetry settings page was found in the docs.

github.description: 🙌 OpenHands: AI-Driven Development

top.title: Agent Canvas

activity.changelogCadence: near-continuous (38 tagged releases in the trailing 90 days, roughly every 2-3 days)

editorial.reachRationale: Weighted toward the underlying OpenHands project's real usage rather than the newer Agent Canvas UI alone: the classic `openhands-ai` PyPI package pulled ~191k downloads/month as of September 2026, the repo has 565 contributors and 11,741 forks (community engagement, not just star-gazing), and the homepage names enterprise adopters (TikTok, VMware, Roche, Amazon, C3.ai). Discounted the specific Agent Canvas rebrand's thin social signal (11.6k X followers, only 1 low-engagement HN story since its May 2026 npm debut) and the unverified $18.8M-raise figure, which comes from a reposted third-party tweet rather than a funding announcement; net, a well-known name among practitioners but not a default choice as of September 2026 the way Claude Code or Cursor are.
editorial.polishRationale: Extensive, well-organized docs (35+ Agent Canvas pages, per-backend setup guides, troubleshooting) and a mature core project, but the Agent Canvas UI itself was labeled beta (status badge in the README) as of September 2026, a pivot from the older Docker-based OpenHands GUI that happened only months earlier, with a young npm package (first published May 2026).
editorial.depthRationale: Runs its own agent or four categories of third-party ACP agents across five backend types (host process, Docker, Kubernetes, VM, managed cloud/enterprise), a separate Automation Server for scheduled/webhook-triggered work with Slack/GitHub/Linear integrations, conversation branching and a judge-verified /goal loop, and MCP-based extensibility. It lacks dedicated PR-creation, checkpoint/restore, or task-board features that some competitors document explicitly.
editorial.feelRationale: Agent Canvas is a React/Vite single-page app (React Router 7, TanStack Query, Tailwind v4, Monaco editor, xterm.js per package.json) served locally or self-hosted, a typical modern web app rather than a native or GPU-rendered client. A targeted search ("OpenHands Agent Canvas slow OR fast OR laggy") returned only product/doc/marketing pages, with no user reports of sluggishness or claims of exceptional speed, so scored as unremarkable rather than notably fast or slow.

tools.name: Orca
tools.tagline: Ship 100x with the agent IDE
tools.valueProp: The maximalist: an MIT-licensed IDE with an embedded browser, a scriptable CLI, and agents that spawn agents across local, SSH and self-hosted runtimes. Several of those surfaces were marked experimental as of September 2026.

maker.name: Stably AI (Lovecast Inc.)
maker.funding: YC W22 (Stably AI); 'Backed by Y Combinator' on homepage

pricing.notes: Free and open source (MIT); no pricing page (onorca.dev/pricing is a 404). You bring your own Claude Code / Codex / other CLI-agent subscriptions. Enterprise page offers rollout help via email, no published tiers.

featureNotes.platforms.android: Sideloaded APK from GitHub releases (mobile-android-v0.0.48) with an install guide; not on the Play Store.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: Orca IDE on the App Store (id6766130217); TestFlight also offered.
featureNotes.platforms.web: A browser client can pair to a Remote Orca Server / `orca serve` host (pairing emits a webClientUrl); there is no standalone hosted web app and the web client lacks some desktop actions such as SSH folder download.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The `orca` CLI ships with the desktop app and drives a running Orca (worktrees, terminals, browser, automations); it is not a standalone way to run agents without the app.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Two paths: SSH targets (laptop Orca drives agents on any SSH host) and Remote Orca Servers (Orca desktop or headless `orca serve` on a machine you own, paired over Tailscale/LAN).
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Docs state Orca 'does not sell managed VPS hosting'. Per-workspace Cloud VM recipes (Vercel Sandbox, Fly, Modal) use your own provider account and are marked Experimental.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: `orca serve` runs the Orca runtime headless on Linux/VPS; desktop, web and mobile clients pair to it with revocable per-client tokens.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Listed on the homepage ('Gemini' preconfigured) and as a telemetry agent kind; not in the README agent grid.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: README: 'if it runs in a terminal, it runs in Orca'; Settings → Agents lists detected CLIs to enable/disable.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Per-workspace environment recipes (orca.yaml) can boot a local Docker container or a cloud sandbox per worktree; feature is under Settings → Experimental.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: In-app PR merge and GitHub auto-merge / merge-queue controls, remote-conflict check before push, and PR stack view; homepage claims 'resolve conflicts' in-app but docs do not describe an interactive conflict resolver.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: 'Worktree checkpoints' in the docs are free-text status comments, not snapshots. Structured chat offers session rewind of conversation turns (v1.4.199); no file-level snapshot/restore documented.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Diff against start-from ref plus Annotate AI Diff: line-anchored comments batched and sent back to the agent.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Task sources are external drawers (GitHub issues/PRs/Projects, Linear, Jira, GitLab) that open worktrees, plus per-worktree status chips and an experimental Agent Dashboard kanban (Needs You / Working / Done). No native task queue that auto-dispatches agents outside the CLI orchestration layer.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: CLI orchestration layer: a coordinator agent runs `orca orchestration worker-start` to spawn supervised workers in child worktrees, waits on worker_done, and can retry/release them.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: `orca orchestration send` with inbox delivery and group addresses (@all, @idle, @claude, @codex, @worktree:<id>).
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: `orca automations` and a desktop Automations page: cron/RRULE/preset schedules that run a prompt with a chosen agent against a repo or worktree, with prechecks and run history.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: System notification, sound, Dock badge and header bell when an agent goes idle or blocks on a question; mirrored as push notifications to the mobile companion.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Mobile companion has microphone dictation into replies/terminal; no desktop voice control documented.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Orca has no account system for the app itself; a Remote Orca Server can be shared by several paired clients with individually revocable tokens, and the sidebar can hide other clients' workspaces. An Orca sign-in exists only for Relay pairing and artifact sharing.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Clients paired to the same Remote Orca Server see and drive the same worktrees, terminals and agents; documented as one person's devices rather than named collaborators.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: No plans or billing; Enterprise page is a contact email offering rollout guidance and org-level defaults.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Desktop, `orca serve` and LAN/Tailscale mobile pairing need no vendor server. Orca Relay (mobile over the internet) source is in-repo under MIT but requires sign-in and its API/auth services live in a private repo; mobile push banners go through Orca's hosted push gateway.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Anonymous PostHog events; off via Settings → Privacy, DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or ORCA_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: Settings → Plugins (Experimental, opt-in and off by default) installs third-party code from git marketplaces whose workers 'always run on this computer' and can add panels, commands, language packs and VM recipes to Orca's own app, a code-level, app-facing extension point, not config. Docs mark the plugin API as experimental/subject to change and warn to treat third-party plugins as untrusted software. Agent skills (installed via `npx skills add`) are a separate, agent-side mechanism that doesn't count. Documented at onorca.dev/docs/settings.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Programmatic control is via the `orca` CLI with a `--json` contract (status, worktrees, terminals, browser, orchestration). MCP support means registering MCP servers for agents under Settings → Integrations; Orca does not expose itself as an MCP server.

github.description: Orca is the place for working with a fleet of agents (e.g. Grok Bot, Claude Code). Run any coding agent with your own subscription. Available on desktop, mobile and remote runtime.

top.title: Orca – Agent Development Environment (ADE) for shipping with coding agents

tools.authorNote:
If you live in the CLI but still want something to package up those CLI experiences, Orca is great. It does very little to abstract away the native CLI experience offered by Claude Code, etc. while still giving you the stuff you can’t get in a terminal like a browser pane, automatic worktree management, etc.

Very clean UX and a good mobile app, and multi-platform support is one of its main advantages. Slower to feel than Zeron or Herdr, but it does a lot more.

editorial.reachRationale: Github numbers here are extreme (376 contributors, 6.9M release-asset downloads, 71k stars) for a project whose repo was created in March 2026, out of proportion with its comparatively modest, product-specific community signals (4,448-member Discord, 16k X followers, no real HN reception, the top hit is an unrelated namesake); treated the download/star figures with real skepticism as likely inflated by auto-update pings rather than unique installs, and weighted the community-size signals more heavily, landing at established alongside similarly-evidenced peers rather than major.
editorial.polishRationale: App Store iOS app, signed Windows builds, Homebrew/AUR packages, a docs site with per-feature pages and a changelog that ships every one to two days with structured release notes; held back because core surfaces (Chat UI, Cloud VM, plugins, Agent Dashboard) sit behind Experimental toggles, Android is sideload-only, and the repo carries ~5.9k open issues.
editorial.depthRationale: Beyond worktree-per-agent it has a CLI orchestration DAG (runs, tasks, dispatches, messages, decision gates), scheduled automations, line-anchored diff annotation sent back to agents, GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/Linear/Jira drawers, an embedded Chromium with Design Mode and CLI browser automation, computer use, and iOS/Android emulator control.
editorial.feelRationale: Electron (the packaged binary is 'orca-ide' and headless Linux setup requires the Electron runtime plus Xvfb), but the maker ships dedicated performance work, v1.4.198's release notes headline 'Faster workspace, renderer, editor, terminal, Git, and remote operations' and a separate PR fixed the editor re-rendering every code block on each keystroke. A 'safe-graphics' fallback marker in the changelog points to occasional GPU-path issues as a remaining rough edge, and the tool's own authorNote calls it 'slower to feel than Zeron or Herdr.'

tools.name: Pane
tools.tagline: the terminal-first agent manager for every coding CLI, every OS.
tools.valueProp: Pane gives any CLI agent an isolated worktree, port range, and terminal on Windows, macOS, or Linux. Its self-hosted remote daemon lets you control those panes from desktop or a phone browser.

pricing.notes: Desktop app and self-hosted Remote Pane are free; users pay their chosen agent/model provider. Managed cloud worktrees and team services are stated as future plans.

featureNotes.platforms.ios: Native companion is available through TestFlight and labelled early access; browser UI is separate (docs/remote-control).
featureNotes.agents.opencode: OpenCode is explicitly supported through a terminal or saved custom command, rather than a dedicated agent tab (docs/quick-starts/opencode; docs/custom-agents).
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: GitHub Copilot CLI is explicitly supported as a saved custom command; dedicated resume and token tracking are not documented (docs/custom-agents).
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Custom commands launch any terminal CLI, but dedicated resume and token tracking are limited to named agents (docs/custom-agents).
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Creating a pane runs git worktree add; deleting it runs git worktree remove (docs/panes-and-worktrees).
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Creating a pane creates an isolated branch, with a selectable base branch (docs/panes-and-worktrees).
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Git toolbar squashes the pane branch into main after rebase; no conflict editor documented (docs/git).
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: External cron or shell scripts can drive the documented runpane CLI; no built-in scheduler is documented (docs/agent-loops).
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Agents can read another panel output and send follow-up input through runpane CLI; no peer message bus documented (docs/agent-loops).
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Config and external control only: saved custom CLI commands add terminal tools, and the documented runpane CLI/MCP contract can create panes and control panels. README says “no plugins, no SDK”; no documented third-party code loader adds Pane panels, views, or app commands (README; docs/custom-agents; docs/runpane-cli).
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: The local runpane CLI and Pane MCP server operate app panes and panels; the website OpenAPI only serves public product information (docs/runpane-cli; docs/api).
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Settings > Privacy > Disable analytics opts out of PostHog product analytics (privacy page); wrapper telemetry can be disabled with RUNPANE_TELEMETRY_DISABLED (docs/RUNPANE_CLI_CONTRACT.md).

github.description: Terminal-first, open-source AI agent manager for any CLI agent (agent agnostic), any OS (mac, windows, linux). The Open-Source Agentic Development Environment for running multiple coding agents in parallel. Run locally or self-host Remote Pane to manage agents from desktop or phone. Simplify multi-agent orchestration with the runpane CLI.

top.title: Is anyone else drowning in terminal tabs running AI coding agents?

activity.changelogCadence: near-daily: multiple releases on September 27 and 28; GitHub shows at least 100 releases in 90 days

editorial.reachRationale: Pane reports 1.4k active users in 30 days; its wrappers logged 8,274 npm and 6,553 PyPI monthly downloads, with 140 Discord members and 601 downloads of the last five release assets. These are early product-specific signals; 494 GitHub stars measure attention, not active use.
editorial.polishRationale: Install paths across three desktop OSes, remote browser access, detailed docs, persistent panes and many themes; direct binaries were unsigned on macOS and Windows as of September 2026.
editorial.depthRationale: Managed worktrees and branches, diff review, git actions, remote daemon, agent-operable CLI, Pane Chat orchestration, status cues, and resource monitoring extend well beyond terminal tabs.
editorial.feelRationale: Pane's GitHub repo is tagged electron and its README names xterm.js, the same engine as VS Code's terminal, with 50,000 lines of scrollback; its changelog logs a run of scrollback stutter and duplication fixes plus dedicated terminal rendering patches, the well-optimised-Electron-with-known-scrollback-rough-edges case.

tools.name: Paperclip
tools.tagline: A team of agents for every person.
tools.valueProp: Not a session switcher: agents are employees on an org chart with titles, reporting lines and budgets, and work arrives as tickets they claim on scheduled heartbeats, not sessions you steer live. Governance, cost caps and goal ancestry are enforced platform-wide, across an unlimited number of isolated companies.

maker.name: Paperclip Labs, Inc.
maker.funding: not disclosed; MIT license notice credits "Paperclip Labs, Inc" as of 2026. A third-party writeup (Contabo blog) says the project was launched March 2, 2026 by a pseudonymous developer known as @dotta; unverified against any first-party source.

pricing.notes: Paperclip itself is free and open source (MIT), self-hosted with an embedded or your own Postgres, no Paperclip account required. You supply your own model/agent credentials (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, etc.) for the agents it orchestrates. The homepage also offers a "Join the waitlist" hosted option alongside "install the local version"; no pricing for that hosted tier had shipped as of September 2026.

featureNotes.platforms.web: No native desktop app (Roadmap lists "Desktop App" as not-yet-started, ⚪). The React dashboard is served locally and can be proxied to phones/tablets via `pnpm dev:mobile` or Tailscale, responsive web, not a native iOS/Android app.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: README, "What's Under the Hood": Workspaces & Runtime provides "isolated execution workspaces (git worktrees, operator branches)" so agents "work in the right directory with the right context every time." This is server-side, per-execution-workspace isolation driven by the Paperclip server, not a per-session worktree picker like the desktop multiplexers in this dataset.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Roadmap: "✅ Cloud / Sandbox agents (e2b, Cloudflare, Daytona, Modal, Novita, self-hosted Kubernetes)", sandboxed/containerized execution backends are supported as environment drivers, pluggable via the plugin system.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: README pairs "git worktrees" with "operator branches" under execution-workspace isolation; docs confirm every execution workspace is scoped to a project, but do not spell out a strict one-branch-per-issue guarantee.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: README, "What Paperclip is not": "Not a code review tool. Paperclip orchestrates work, not pull requests. Bring your own review process."
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Same first-party statement as diffReview, PR creation and code review are left to the underlying coding agent/adapter, not Paperclip itself.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Same first-party statement as diffReview, Paperclip is explicitly not positioned as a merge/PR tool.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Agents delegate to one another through the org chart ("Task routing flows through the org chart... Cross-team requests are routed automatically", per Contabo writeup corroborating README's org-chart/CEO-hires-team framing); a CEO agent can effectively steer subordinate agents inside the same Paperclip company.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: The dashboard's "Pending Approvals" card and activity feed surface blocked/awaiting-input states in-app; docs read did not confirm whether alerts also reach email, Slack, or mobile push.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Not a payment/billing product, "teamBilling" here means the built-in Budget & Cost Control system: token/cost tracking and scoped budget policies by company, agent, project, goal, issue, provider, and model, with warning thresholds and hard stops.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: an instance-wide plugin system runs third-party plugins as out-of-process workers with capability-gated host services (UI contributions, job scheduling, tool exposure), code that extends Paperclip's own app surface, not just the agent. README: "Extend Paperclip without forking it." Built against a dedicated `@paperclipai/plugin-sdk` (PluginContext gives UI/job/environment-driver clients); the SDK is flagged "in alpha" and shipped breaking changes between releases as recently as September 2026. Documented at docs.paperclip.ing/reference/plugins/sdk.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: "Bring Your Own Agent" is a headline feature, any agent, any provider, any runtime; you supply the model credentials (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, etc.).

supportedAgents: Hermes Agent (hermes-paperclip-adapter, maintained by Nous Research)

github.description: The open-source app everyone uses to manage agents at work
