activity.changelogCadence: Very frequent, versioned dated releases (paperclip.ing/changelog): roughly weekly to twice-weekly since launch, with several tagged "Breaking" (v2026.916.0, v2026.831.0, v2026.824.0, v2026.817.0), most recently v2026.916.1 on Sep 21, 2026.

editorial.reachRationale: 85k GitHub stars and 15k forks are real but discounted, the project's own third-party coverage (Contabo) brags about star velocity, which is a hype signal, not usage. Weighed more heavily: a genuinely active product-specific Discord (8,019 members, 1,042 online at fetch time), 93k lifetime npm downloads of the `paperclipai` CLI, 219 GitHub contributors and 664 commits/30d (real outside contribution, not just the founder). Against that: no dedicated HN discussion turned up under several query variants, and the project was created March 2, 2026. That's a real, engaged community past the early-adopter stage but not a name most practitioners know, established, not major.
editorial.polishRationale: A dedicated, versioned design system (paperclip.ing/brand) with shared design tokens between marketing and product, an official logo/lockup kit, screenshot-documented guides for every dashboard surface, and frequent dated releases (several marked "Breaking" and called out explicitly) suggest a product treated as finished software, not a demo. It is held back only because the plugin runtime is explicitly flagged "in alpha" in its own docs.
editorial.depthRationale: This is the deepest tool in the dataset by this page's measure of depth: org charts with roles/budgets/reporting lines, goal ancestry, atomic task checkout, approval/governance workflows with rollback, scheduled heartbeats and event triggers, a skills system, multi-company data isolation, and a plugin SDK, none of which reduce to a tmux wrapper.
editorial.feelRationale: Implementation is a standard Node.js API server plus a React 19 + Tailwind + shadcn/Radix dashboard (docs.paperclip.ing, paperclip.ing/brand) backed by Postgres, not a native or GPU-rendered UI, so it does not qualify for the top tier. No first-party performance claims or user complaints about sluggishness were found (a third-party Reddit thread referenced in search results returned a blocked/unsupported-site error and could not be read). Work itself is asynchronous (heartbeat-driven, not a live terminal), so the relevant 'feel' is dashboard/ticket-UI responsiveness, which reads as a typical, unremarkable React SPA.

tools.name: Paseo
tools.tagline: The control plane for coding agents.
tools.valueProp: Phone-first and fully self-hostable: native iOS and Android apps steer agents on machines you own through a relay you can run yourself. It brings no cloud compute and no agent of its own.

maker.name: Mohamed Boudra (Mo)
maker.funding: self-funded, full-time solo maintainer; GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Buy Me a Coffee

pricing.notes: Free and open source with no seat limits; you install agent CLIs with your own credentials. The optional Paseo Hub (GitHub/Slack/Discord triggers) is free to self-host or €15 per seat/month hosted, with a free trial.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Electron app; macOS 13 or newer since v0.8.0. Homebrew cask `paseo`.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: App Store listing 'Paseo: Pocket Engineer' (id6758887924). Store builds lag desktop; no TestFlight beta channel.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Play Store (sh.paseo) plus APK on GitHub releases. The F-Droid-style source build documented in docs/android.md drops push notifications and QR pairing.
featureNotes.platforms.web: Hosted web app at app.paseo.sh, or the daemon serves the same UI itself (docs/web-ui, Docker image).
featureNotes.platforms.cli: `paseo run/ls/attach/send/logs/wait/schedule/permit`; docs say anything the app can do the CLI can do.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: The CLI streams output (`paseo attach`, `paseo logs -f`) but no full-screen terminal UI is documented.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Daemon on a VPS, homelab, Mac mini or Docker; clients attach via SSH (desktop/CLI), the E2E-encrypted relay, or Tailscale/direct TCP.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Paseo provisions no compute. Hosted Hub is a trigger service; agents still run on daemons you operate. 'Provisioning daemons for your team' is listed as planned, not built.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: Daemon, bundled web UI, relay (getpaseo/paseo-relay, Elixir) and Hub (getpaseo/hub) are all self-hostable.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Via the ACP catalog (one-click install), not a native harness.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Via the ACP catalog, not a native harness.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Via the ACP catalog, not a native harness.
featureNotes.agents.amp: Via the ACP catalog through a community amp-acp adapter (tao12345666333/amp-acp), not a native harness.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Custom providers in ~/.paseo/config.json accept custom binaries and any ACP agent; only Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Pi get the structured native harness.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Docs: 'Paseo manages other agents, it doesn't ship one.'
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Workspace isolation mode `worktree`: Paseo creates the worktree, runs paseo.json setup hooks, assigns per-worktree service ports and proxy URLs, and removes it on archive.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Isolation modes are only Local and Worktree. The official Docker image containerises the daemon, not individual tasks.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Each worktree workspace gets a slug and branch (branch-off from a base, checkout-branch, or checkout-pr).
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Diff viewer pane against the base branch on desktop, web and mobile; changelog covers diff performance and context-menu work.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Requires the GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed and authenticated; docs list it as a prerequisite for PR-aware worktrees.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: First-party comparison pages say the app handles commit, push, PR, checks, reviews and merging; no conflict-resolution help is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Only a provider-native rewind is referenced (changelog: 'Fixed Codex rewind failing'); no Paseo-level checkpoint or snapshot feature is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Sidebar groups workspaces by state (Ready to review / Working / Done) in the homepage mockup; no kanban board or task queue feeding agents is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: With 'Enable Paseo tools' on (off by default) agents get MCP tools create_agent, send_agent_prompt, kill_agent etc.; workers appear in a Subagents track. Also works via the CLI without tool injection.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Cron schedules start fresh agents; heartbeats re-prompt an existing agent; Hub triggers start agents from GitHub, Slack and Discord mentions.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Server-side attention policy pushes on 'finished' and 'permission' reasons when no client is focused on the agent; mobile push goes through Expo's push API (exp.host), a third-party server.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Agents send prompts to other agents by ID (send_agent_prompt MCP tool, `paseo send`).
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Dictation and voice mode; STT/TTS run locally by default (Parakeet/Kokoro ONNX) or optionally via OpenAI endpoints.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: The daemon has a single shared password, no user accounts. Hub adds members and invitations ('seats') and a shared activity record; more team features are listed as planned.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Any paired client sees and controls the same workspaces on a daemon; sharing the pairing link grants full control (docs: treat it like a password). No per-person presence or roles.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Only for Hosted Hub (€15 per seat/month). The core product has no plans or billing.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Relay and Hub are optional and open source; the only vendor server in the default path is Expo's push API for mobile push notifications.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Runs the provider CLIs you installed with your own OAuth/API credentials; docs say Paseo never stores or transmits provider keys.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: README: no telemetry, tracking or forced log-ins; the configuration reference has no telemetry setting to opt out of.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True (the clearest example here): a plugin is a TypeScript project with a `paseo-plugin.json` manifest plus separate client (`index.client.tsx`) and server (`index.server.ts`) entries; a `contribute` function calls client.addSurface/addSidebarItem/addWorkspacePanel/addCommandCenterItem and server.handle(rpcContract) to add real surfaces, panels, commands and themes to Paseo's own app, and can connect a coding agent as a provider. Plugins are trusted, unsandboxed code (server runs with the daemon user's access); installed via `paseo plugin install/add` or Settings → Plugins, with a global enable switch. API marked experimental; community directory at paseo.cafe. Documented at paseo.sh/docs/plugins/v0.8 and paseo.sh/docs/plugins.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: WebSocket API, TypeScript SDK (@getpaseo/client), MCP server with agent/workspace/terminal/schedule tools, and CLI.

github.description: Orchestrate multiple coding agents from desktop and mobile

top.title: Show HN: Paseo – Beautiful open-source coding agent interface

tools.authorNote: The best of the chat-first ones. If you steer agents by typing at them rather than reading terminals, Paseo’s desktop and phone apps are the most complete pair I’ve used, and the self-hosted relay means you can run 100% of it on your own. The phone app is the specific differentiator - it’s unusually complete and easy to use. If you expect to use your phone often, give this a go.

editorial.reachRationale: 2.28M release-asset downloads over the last five releases, ~91k combined monthly npm downloads across the client and CLI packages, and a well-received 92-point Show HN together support an established, real user base for a solo-maintainer project; the Discord (1,887) and personal X account (1,375 followers) are modest, keeping it below major.
editorial.polishRationale: My call from hands-on use: the most complete desktop and phone pair among the chat-first tools. Five platforms with store listings, a Homebrew cask, staged 36-hour stable rollouts, a beta channel and a dated changelog every week. The 0.8.0 notes still list many crash and sync fixes, and the plugin API is labelled experimental.
editorial.depthRationale: Beyond running agents in parallel it has worktree workspaces with setup hooks and per-worktree service URLs, in-app diff/PR/merge flow, cron schedules and heartbeats, agent-spawns-agent via MCP and CLI, GitHub/Slack/Discord triggers through Hub, local voice, a plugin system, an SDK and an MCP server; few tools in this category document that much.
editorial.feelRationale: My call from hands-on use: fine day to day. It is an Electron desktop app (`packages/desktop`), and its changelog keeps fixing editor and diff sluggishness ('Reduced JS stalls while watching a streaming agent on mobile,' 'Fixed large and many-file diffs stalling or crashing while opening and scrolling,' 'Fixed diff file headers lagging behind while scrolling on web and desktop'), with performance fixes still landing as of 0.8.0, which keeps it short of quick.

tools.name: Poolside
tools.tagline: We're building open-weight foundation models and the systems that refine and improve them.
tools.valueProp: The only entry that is also a model lab: it ships open-weight models and can run the whole loop offline on a Mac, while hosting Claude Code, Codex and Gemini over ACP. Closed-source and Mac-only; the business is on-prem enterprise.

maker.name: Poolside
maker.funding: $500M fundraise announced 2024-10-02; first-party AWS offering (2024-12); acquired Fern Labs (2025-11)

pricing.notes: The desktop app, VS Code and Visual Studio extensions and the pool CLI are free downloads. Poolside-hosted Laguna inference is free 'in Preview' with an API key from platform.poolside.ai; paid access to Poolside models is via OpenRouter (per-token, larger context) or an enterprise Poolside Platform deployment in your VPC or on-prem (contract pricing, Standard/Premium support tiers, no public prices). Third-party harnesses use your own Claude Code, Codex or Gemini subscriptions; local MLX/Ollama models cost nothing.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Poolside Assistant for desktop is a .dmg for Apple-silicon Macs only (docs prerequisite: 'a Mac with Apple Silicon'). The pool CLI also installs on macOS via curl.
featureNotes.platforms.windows: No desktop app. The pool CLI installer for Windows is labelled beta/preview (PowerShell `irm ... | iex`), and the Visual Studio 2022 extension runs on Windows amd64.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: No desktop app. Only the pool CLI (curl installer) and the VS Code extension.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: No app is documented. The desktop app lists 'Remote access: Access the desktop app from your phone (experimental)' with no further detail.
featureNotes.platforms.android: No app is documented; same experimental phone remote access as iOS.
featureNotes.platforms.web: No hosted web client is documented. The experimental phone access to the desktop app may be browser-based but the docs do not say.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: `pool` (interactive), `pool exec` (one-shot, JSON output, `--unsafe-auto-allow` for CI), `pool acp` (ACP server for Zed, JetBrains, Xcode, Neovim), `pool mcp`, `pool --worktree`, `pool -s` (pick another agent server).
featureNotes.platforms.tui: `pool` is a full-screen single-conversation terminal app (repo topic 'tui') with a status line, mouse support, dialogs, session picker and slash commands. The multi-session view is the desktop app, not the TUI.
featureNotes.execution.local: All three surfaces run agents on the machine where they are installed; on-device MLX models make the desktop app work fully offline.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: The pool CLI can connect to a remote ACP server you run yourself over streamable HTTP (`agent_servers: { remote: { url: https://my-vm/acp, headers } }`, then `pool -s remote`), so the agent runs on your VM while the TUI stays local. The desktop app's phone access is experimental and undocumented beyond one bullet.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: No vendor-run sandboxes or cloud runs for the Assistant. The enterprise Platform runs sessions in containers, but inside your own VPC or data centre, not Poolside's cloud.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The Assistant itself has no server component. Enterprise customers can deploy Poolside inference and the Console on AWS EKS, OpenShift, upstream Kubernetes, bare metal or air-gapped hardware (Terraform bundles), but that is a contract product, not a download.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Named in the blog ('bring your existing Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini subscription') and docs (`pool --agent-server claude-agent-acp`); runs via the ACP adapter `@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp`. The desktop app can also import existing Claude Code sessions from Settings > Archive.
featureNotes.agents.codex: Named in blog and docs; runs via `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp`. Existing Codex sessions can be imported into the desktop app.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Named in docs: `pool --agent-server "gemini --acp"`, and 'Gemini' in the desktop announcement.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Not named. The desktop app lists agents 'Tested by Poolside' and 'Other Third-Party Agents' from the public ACP registry, but the tested list is not published in the docs.
featureNotes.agents.opencode: Not named as a hosted agent. docs.poolside.ai/tools/opencode covers the reverse direction: using Poolside models inside OpenCode.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Not named.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Not named as a hosted agent. docs.poolside.ai/tools/pi covers using Poolside models inside Pi.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Custom commands must speak ACP: `assistant.json` `agent_servers` for the desktop app and extensions, `settings.yaml` `agent_servers` for the CLI. Plain CLIs without an ACP mode cannot be attached.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Poolside Agent (pool) with Laguna S 2.1 / XS 2.1 by default, plus 'Poolside Local' running MLX models on-device and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, OpenRouter).
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Desktop: 'Run multiple agent sessions at once in separate Git worktrees and branches'. CLI: `pool --worktree [<branch>]` creates the worktree and branch (auto-generated names with `pool.worktree_prefix`), and `/move` relocates a session to another worktree, optionally carrying uncommitted files.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Optional local Docker sandbox configured in `settings.yaml` (image, read-only or read-write workspace mount, egress allow-list via a proxy container, extra mounts); `--sandbox required` enforces it. Not on by default.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: `pool --worktree <branch>` creates the branch; `--worktree` with no name generates one. The desktop app gives 'each task ... its own isolated checkout and branch'.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Desktop layout keeps 'conversations beside terminals, files, Git status, diffs, and GitHub status'; all surfaces ask you to 'review changes before you keep them'. Read-only sandbox mode stages agent edits for review before they land on the host.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Only 'GitHub integration ... for pull request awareness and status colors' is documented; no create-PR action is described.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Not documented beyond 'You decide which changes are worth merging'.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Conversation-level only: `/rewind` or double Esc rolls back to a previous turn in the CLI. No file snapshot or restore is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Desktop: 'runs multiple sessions in parallel ... Claude Code working in one repository, Codex investigating another, and pool somewhere else, all from the same window', with tabs, splits, a secondary sidebar and a bottom panel; multiple projects per window.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: pool's main agent can delegate to a built-in `general` in-process subagent or named subagents that are another in-process Poolside agent or any command-based ACP server, and can run several at once (they share the workspace). In-process subagents cannot nest or ask you questions; approvals surface in the parent session; `/usage` shows per-subagent cost.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: No scheduler or triggers in the tool. `pool exec` runs headless in scripts, GitHub Actions and n8n with `POOLSIDE_API_KEY`, and hooks fire on six agent lifecycle events.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: pool 'can send notifications when a turn ends, when an approval prompt needs your response, or when the agent asks a question', only when the session is unfocused; inside cmux it also sets status icons. Not documented for the desktop app.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Agent handoff passes one conversation and its context from one harness to another ('Ask Claude Code to review what pool built'); agents do not message each other.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Voice input (dictation) is a listed feature of the desktop app and both extensions.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: The free Assistant and CLI are single-user. The enterprise Platform has a Console, OIDC identity (Okta, Entra ID or a Poolside Keycloak) and an identity-management API, but those docs are behind an access code.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: `/share` returns a link to a trajectory viewer 'when trajectory sharing is available'; it is a read-only replay, not co-steering.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Enterprise only: a Poolside deployment with subscription, Standard/Premium support and account representatives. No self-serve team plan.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: LICENSE.md: '© Poolside. All rights reserved. Use is subject to the Poolside End User License Agreement.' The poolsideai/pool repo holds only README, CHANGELOG, LICENSE and third_party notices; binaries ship from downloads.poolside.ai. Only the Laguna model weights are open.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: There is no server to host: with Poolside Local (MLX) or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the blog says the agent 'can work without sending your code or prompts to a cloud service'. Caveats: closed binaries, the default login goes through platform.poolside.ai, and no telemetry statement covers the apps.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini keep 'the models and configurations they support' and your subscriptions; pool accepts OpenRouter keys and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Poolside-hosted models are free in preview rather than resold.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: No telemetry or crash-reporting documentation for the apps was found. Trajectories and logs are stored locally (`pool config` prints paths); `/share` is opt-in. The privacy policy says data may train models 'unless you opt-out' without a documented switch.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial: `settings.yaml` can define a named subagent with `type: command` (a custom ACP-compatible agent server command) or `type: agent_server` (reusing a top-level `agent_servers` entry), which Poolside then runs, manages permissions/approvals for, and lists in `/usage` alongside its own agent, a config-level custom agent/provider definition, the narrow bar for partial. MCP servers, Skills, AGENTS.md and hooks are agent-side additions and don't count; none of this adds a panel, view or command to the Poolside CLI/UI itself. Documented at docs.poolside.ai/subagents.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: `pool acp` is an ACP server any client can drive (session/list, session/load, steering, config options), and `pool exec -o json` gives scripted runs. It is an MCP client, not an MCP server, and the desktop app exposes no API.

supportedAgents: Any ACP agent from the public registry

github.description: pool is Poolside’s coding agent that runs in your terminal or integrates with any ACP-compatible editor

top.title: Laguna S 2.1

activity.changelogCadence: weekly to biweekly (17 CLI entries 2026-04-28 to 2026-08-14), nothing since; the VS Code extension ships separately, v1.5.10 on 2026-09-18

editorial.reachRationale: The CLI's GitHub repo undercounts the product (it holds no source, only docs), and the actual multiplexer surface, Poolside Assistant, only launched in July 2026 with thin concrete numbers (1,885 release-asset downloads, 504-member Discord); the well-funded company (~$500M raised) and a 416-point HN story were discounted since that story is about Poolside's model, not the assistant app, so this reads as early rather than established.
editorial.polishRationale: My call: a careful, coherent product from a team that trains its own models rather than wrapping someone else's. Judged from docs and the launch post, not hands-on. CLI docs are thorough and versioned, the extensions ship weekly, and the layout and handoff story hangs together. Held back: the desktop app launched July 28, 2026, is Apple-silicon only, has a single docs page and no changelog, phone access is 'experimental', the CLI repo has been quiet since 2026-08-14, and half the docs tree sits behind an access code.
editorial.depthRationale: Judged from docs and the launch post, not hands-on. The desktop app does the core multiplexer job (parallel sessions across harnesses, managed worktrees and branches, diffs and terminals in one layout, cross-harness handoff, connectors, voice, on-device models) and pool adds subagents, hooks, Docker sandboxes and an ACP server. There is no task board, scheduler, PR flow, cloud execution or real multi-user layer outside the enterprise contract.
editorial.feelRationale: GitHub's languages API returns an empty breakdown for poolsideai/pool (a binary-distribution repo), and the desktop/CLI docs never name an implementation language, rendering stack, or performance claim, so the client's stack cannot be determined.

tools.name: QM
tools.tagline: A multiplayer agent harness for work. In Slack and on the web.
tools.valueProp: Not a coding tool but a company-wide deployment: every employee and Slack channel gets its own scoped identity, memory, files, sandbox and security posture, and any of four interchangeable harnesses (Pi, OpenCode, Codex, Claude Code) can drive it. Built and run internally by Y Combinator itself and given away open source, rather than sold as a hosted product, you self-host it on your own AWS or Fly account.

maker.name: Y Combinator
maker.funding: built and run internally by Y Combinator (labs@ycombinator.com); not a separately funded startup

pricing.notes: Open source (MIT) and self-hosted; the maker charges nothing and has no pricing page. You pay your own cloud provider (Fly or AWS) and bring your own model/harness credentials. A third party, Agent37, resells hosting for QM from its general sandbox pricing (from ~$2–5/mo per sandbox, metered).

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Preview build, Apple Silicon/macOS 13+ only; connects to an existing QM deployment (no bundled server), no auto-update as of the v0.1.0 release notes (September 2026).
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The `qm` CLI (published as @yc-software/qm) provisions and deploys the service; it is not an entry point for starting or steering agent conversations, which happen in Slack/web.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: No first-party managed cloud from the maker, deployments run in the operator's own AWS/Fly account. A third party, Agent37, offers a hosted version at agent37.com/qm ('we handle the hosting').
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: The only 'worktree' references in the repo are for QM's own internal dev-instance tooling, not a managed per-task worktree feature for end users.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: No in-app diff viewer found; code changes are made by the agent via shell/git commands in its sandbox and reviewed in the session transcript, not a dedicated diff UI.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Not a dedicated PR button: the first-party github-gitlab skill (skills-seed/github-gitlab/SKILL.md) has the agent run `gh pr create`/`glab mr create` from its sandbox shell.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Provider-native sandbox snapshots (Modal, E2B, Sprites, Smolmachines) with restore-on-failure, per docs/sandbox-preservation.md, recovers the sandbox filesystem/compute, not git-level checkpoints.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Approval-gated tool calls (Strict/Auto security postures) surface as a message in the same Slack or web thread asking a human to approve; no separate push/desktop channel is documented.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Native via shared Slack channels/group messages/projects, where a room has its own scoped memory and multiple people work with the same agent context; the separate 'Share' button only makes a read-only snapshot link (docs/session-sharing.md), not live co-steering.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Self-hosted with no vendor billing plane; 'admin control' covers security/sharing posture and which harnesses/models are available, not billing or seats.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system for QM itself. The `plugins/` directory holds QM’s own first-party surfaces compiled into the app, and the README’s only way to add one is a source fork. `MEMORY_PROVIDER_CONFIG` routes the memory substrate to an external backend, which is provider configuration, not an extension of QM’s interface. Documented at github.com/yc-software/qm/blob/main/docs/memory-providers.md.

github.description: Multiplayer agent harness for work.

top.title: qm – Multiplayer agent harness for work

editorial.reachRationale: A 682-point/163-comment Show HN launch and 15.2k GitHub stars within two months of the July 2026 launch reflect strong product-specific attention, reinforced by independent third-party guides and teardowns (Substack, Medium) appearing within weeks of launch; discounted against modest npm installs for the deploy CLI (~3.7k/month), no Discord, and a small product X account (957 followers), since this is infrastructure a startup deploys once rather than a tool individuals install repeatedly.
editorial.polishRationale: The only end-user client beyond Slack/web is a 'preview' Mac build without signed updates, inbox Loops ship behind a default-off feature flag, and a widely-read Reddit thread flagged real security gaps two months after launch.
editorial.depthRationale: Org-wide security/sharing postures, agent swarms with inter-worker messaging, scheduled/event-triggered Loops, MCP and Composio connector plumbing, and per-scope memory/skills/sandboxes are all shipped, not roadmap. These go well past a tmux wrapper.
editorial.feelRationale: Standard web-app stack: a Fastify/Node core with a Vite + Lit web UI (README architecture section), not GPU-native, but Lit's lightweight web components avoid typical Electron/React weight. No user reports of latency or jank found; third-party discussion (HN, Reddit) centers on security, not responsiveness.

tools.name: Sculptor
tools.tagline: Extensible, parallel coding workspace you own
tools.valueProp: Shipped per-agent Docker containers first and walked them back: agents now live in plain worktrees, and the weight has moved to a bundled spec-to-review skill pipeline and a JavaScript extension SDK. MIT, local-only, Mac and Linux.

maker.name: Imbue, Inc.
maker.funding: $200M Series B at a $1B+ valuation (Sept 2023), Astera Institute, NVIDIA and angels

pricing.notes: Free and MIT-licensed; no pricing page. Homepage FAQ: 'Sculptor uses your existing Claude or Claude Max plan. We do not resell tokens or cap your usage.' The Pi harness uses your own provider logins or API keys. Show HN: 'Sculptor itself is free to use'.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Apple Silicon only. Intel Mac was 'on the way' in the Sept 2025 launch post and has not shipped; the homepage FAQ lists Mac (Apple Silicon) and Linux only.
featureNotes.platforms.windows: Homepage FAQ: 'No Windows or mobile support currently.'
featureNotes.platforms.linux: x64 and arm64 AppImage; the product spec calls arm64 a best-effort, non-blocking build target.
featureNotes.platforms.web: Electron desktop only. The product spec names the desktop GUI and the sculpt CLI as the two surfaces; docs/competitors.md says 'you can self-host it if you want to access it remotely' but no user doc describes a browser client.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The `sculpt` CLI ships with the app and drives the same local backend: create workspaces and agents, send messages with --follow, read status as JSON, signal state from inside an agent.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Experimental 'custom backend command' (Settings > Experimental) relocates the whole backend; the docs describe Docker, SSH and VM targets but only ship a Docker recipe, with SSH/VM recipes 'planned'. Flagged unstable.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The backend is a local HTTP server that the Electron app and sculpt CLI both talk to; the experimental container recipe runs it off-host. No relay component exists.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Two forms: the integrated chat harness (Claude Code run as a streaming-JSON process with tool permissions auto-approved, Sculptor substitutes its own ask-question and plan tools) and the bundled 'Claude CLI' terminal agent, which runs the Claude Code TUI in a PTY.
featureNotes.agents.codex: The launch post's Dec 2025 update says Codex support was added via an OpenAI API key, but the README, help docs and product spec list only Claude and Pi as harnesses; Codex would run as an unintegrated terminal agent.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Integrated harness run in RPC mode with a Sculptor-pinned extension set; the model picker is populated from whichever Pi providers you authenticate, with mid-session model switching. Fast mode and the context-usage chip are unavailable for Pi.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: A plain Terminal agent or a TOML-registered terminal agent (display name, launch command, optional resume command); registered agents can call `sculpt signal` to light busy/idle/waiting dots. No chat rendering for these.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Product spec non-goal: 'Not a model provider; it orchestrates agent CLIs (Claude, Pi), it doesn't serve models.'
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Default workspace mode; experimental clone and in-place modes exist behind Settings > Experimental. Workspaces live under ~/.sculptor/workspaces/ with an optional per-repo setup command.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Per-agent Docker containers (the Sept 2025 launch architecture) were removed; docs/history.md explains why. What remains is the experimental custom backend command that runs the entire backend in a container or VM, not one sandbox per agent.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: New branch per workspace using a `<user>/<slug>` pattern, configurable globally and per repo; experimental auto-naming of branches from the first message.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Files panel with Changes (uncommitted or against target branch), side-by-side or unified diff, per-file discard, commit graph; an experimental 'Review All' combined diff.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: GitHub only, through the gh CLI. The PR button tracks open/merged/closed, approvals, unresolved comments and CI status.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Only through the experimental, off-by-default CI Babysitter, which asks an agent to rebase and resolve conflicts on an open GitHub PR. There is no in-app merge action; you merge on GitHub.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: No snapshot or rollback of agent state. Forking agents was listed as 'next' in the Sept 2025 launch post and is not in the docs or spec; per-file 'Discard changes' is the only revert.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Workspaces as tabs, several agents per workspace as sub-tabs, status dots per tab and a hover 'peek' popover across workspaces.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: The bundled Linear extension adds a board-style home view of your assigned issues grouped by status and links issues to the current branch/PR; nothing documents creating workspaces from that board.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: An agent's shell has the sculpt CLI: `sculpt run` and `sculpt agent create` spawn workspaces and agents, `agent send --follow` waits on them. The handoff and stack skills do this from inside a session.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: CI Babysitter (experimental, off by default) reacts to failed CI runs and merge conflicts on open PRs, up to a retry cap, only while the app is running. No scheduler; the spec suggests driving `sculpt` from your own cron.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: In-app only: status dots on workspace and agent tabs (ready, waiting, error), mark-as-unread, and the integrated harness raises a notification when Claude asks a question. No OS desktop or push alerts are documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: `sculpt agent send <id>` addresses agents in any workspace; answering an agent's question is reserved for the human in the UI.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Product spec: 'Sculptor is local-first and single-user.' The onboarding email is only used for telemetry identity and can be skipped.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Runs entirely on your machine with no Imbue server in the path; the only vendor traffic is opt-out PostHog/Sentry telemetry.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Claude harness uses your Claude / Claude Max login; Pi harness uses your own provider keys. Imbue resells nothing.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: On by default; a checkbox on the onboarding screen and a switch under Settings > Privacy turn PostHog analytics and Sentry error reports off together. Prompts, file and branch names are masked when on.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: True: third-party JavaScript/TypeScript extensions loaded at runtime from ~/.sculptor/extensions or a URL can add panels, widgets, home views, overlays and settings screens to Sculptor's own app; four are first-party/bundled (Linear, Sculpty, Pomodoro, Buster) but the loader accepts any local or URL-hosted extension, and agents can install one via `sculpt extension load` once a user opts in. This is app-level UI code, distinct from Sculptor's separate agent-side Skills. Documented at github.com/imbue-ai/sculptor/blob/main/docs/help/extensions.md.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Local HTTP API with an OpenAPI spec and a live update stream; the sculpt CLI is a generated client of it. No MCP server is offered.

supportedAgents: Codex (per Dec 2025 launch-post update; not in current docs)

github.description: Build product with grounded, parallel coding agents.

top.title: Show HN: Sculptor – A UI for Claude Code

editorial.reachRationale: A well-received 176-point Show HN ('A UI for Claude Code') shows real initial attention, but concrete install signals are very thin, GitHub release assets show 0 downloads (binaries ship via S3) and the Homebrew cask is stale at 1 install/30d, and the 10k X followers belong to the company account (Imbue), not a product-specific one, so this lands as early rather than established.
editorial.polishRationale: It ships as a signed, notarized DMG and AppImage with in-app auto-update and stable/latest channels, customisable keybindings, a theme builder, and help docs that are re-audited with fresh screenshots each release, on a roughly weekly stable cadence (0.44 to 0.47 between 14 Aug and 8 Sep). Held back because the README and product spec self-describe it as an 'experimental research preview' at 0.x, there is no Windows or Intel Mac build, PRs are GitHub-only, the marketing site carried, as of September 2026, the Sept 2025 launch post describing per-agent containers and Pairing Mode that docs/history.md says were dropped, the homebrew-core cask is frozen at 0.7.0, and the repo has 233 stars with gated external PRs.
editorial.depthRationale: Well past a session switcher, with worktree workspaces plus per-repo setup commands, a Files panel with commit graph and PR status tracking, a bundled six-stage spec-to-review skill pipeline and TDD fix-bug skill, a CI Babysitter that dispatches agents at failing checks and conflicts, a runtime JS extension system with a Linear board view, terminal agents, and a JSON-emitting CLI that lets agents create and message other agents. Held back because there are no checkpoints, no scheduler, no OS-level notifications, no task queue of its own, and no cloud or multi-user path, and several of the listed pieces (clone mode, babysitter, container backend, handoff/stack) are behind the Experimental toggle.
editorial.feelRationale: Packaged with Electron Forge (Electron 42.4.1, per requirements.md REQ-COMPAT-012) with a React/Jotai/Radix renderer talking to a Python FastAPI backend; the requirements doc explicitly leaves end-to-end interaction-latency and streaming-latency budgets 'Unspecified' (REQ-NFR-004) and only pins UI debounce/throttle windows of 100ms-2s for things like auto-scroll and mark-read, and no user reports of jank or praise for speed turned up in search.

tools.name: Solo
tools.tagline: The meta-harness for coding agents
tools.valueProp: Solo keeps coding agents beside the live dev stack they share, with one solo.yml for servers, logs, and commands. Its MCP tools let a lead agent inspect processes and launch workers from different harnesses.

pricing.notes: Free forever for up to 4 projects and 20 processes, with every feature. Pro is $99/year for unlimited projects/processes and 3 devices. Team seats use centralized billing at $99–$69 per seat/year by quantity; agent subscriptions are separate.

featureNotes.platforms.linux: The download page shows a Linux label, but only macOS and Windows beta installers; installation docs say public builds are packaged for macOS and Windows.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Pi appears in the homepage headline, but the supported-agent docs do not list Pi as a built-in tool; it can run as a custom CLI agent.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: The changelog mentions linked checkouts and a schema foundation for existing worktrees, copy-on-write checkouts, and full clones; no first-party page says Solo creates or manages Git worktrees.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Todos have blockers and locks and are shared with agents, but there is no kanban or automatic task queue feeding sessions.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Delayed prompts through Solo timers and file-watch process restarts are documented; no general cron-run workflow is shown.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Native macOS notifications, in-app toasts, unread badges, and agent recap notices are documented; Windows native delivery is not described.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Privacy policy documents anonymous Aptabase analytics and possible Sentry diagnostics; no opt-out is documented in privacy or settings pages.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, config and external control only: Settings → Agents adds custom CLI agent commands and the local HTTP API/CLI/MCP can drive projects, processes, and workspaces. The agent setup and integration docs do not document a loader for third-party code that adds Solo panels, commands, or lifecycle hooks.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Local bearer-token HTTP API and bundled MCP stdio helper control the running desktop app; the HTTP listener binds to 127.0.0.1.

top.title: The meta-harness for coding agents

activity.changelogCadence: irregular: 4 releases in about 3 months (June 5–September 3), including an 8-day gap and a 67-day gap

editorial.reachRationale: Product-specific HN query has three stories, with the top at two points. Several third-party Solo companions exist on GitHub, showing early users, but no product download or community counts are published; the 1,289-star soloterm/solo Laravel package belongs to a different product and is excluded.
editorial.polishRationale: Signed macOS and Windows installers, built-in updates, a detailed docs tree, project/workspace management, keyboard shortcuts, and a paid tier, though the download page labeled the app beta as of September 2026, and Linux has no public installer.
editorial.depthRationale: Solo adds process-aware MCP, a local HTTP API/CLI, cross-harness spawning, shared todos and scratchpads, timers, and dev-stack command lifecycle, but lacks managed worktrees, integrated diffs, and PR flow.
editorial.feelRationale: The installation docs identify a Tauri desktop app with a webview; v0.10.0 says terminal output now bypasses up to 20 ms of batching latency, reduces rendering work, and starts faster. These are maker claims and release fixes, with no independent latency measurement.

tools.name: stagewise
tools.tagline: The Agentic IDE for Open-Source Models
tools.valueProp: An Electron IDE with its own agent and an embedded Chromium, so the agent can pick DOM elements and read console state as context. It wraps no third-party CLI agent; instead it switches between ten-plus model providers, hosted, BYOK or local.

maker.name: stagewise GmbH
maker.funding: YC S25; backed by Y Combinator, TwentyTwo Ventures, Blast Club, Teuto Seed Club

pricing.notes: Hobby: free, limited to 3 standard models via stagewise Account, or unlimited via BYOK. Individual: $20/mo Pro or $200/mo Ultra for stagewise-hosted access to frontier + open-weight models. Enterprise: custom, SSO/SCIM, EU inference, optional self-hosting of the stagewise Cloud.

featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: Enterprise tier offers 'optional self-hosting of the stagewise Cloud' (the account/model-routing layer); the desktop app itself needs no server when run with BYOK or local models, but self-hosting the full stack (incl. stagewise Cloud Inference) is not offered, that's their managed service.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: The workspace selector lets you create a worktree or branch per workspace (screenshot: 'create worktree, use existing worktree, create branch, use existing branch'), but this is a manual choice per connected workspace, not automatic per-task branching.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Undo/redo is tracked at the tool-call level ('Undo, Roll back all changes from a specific agent action'), which restores file state per action; there is no full session/state snapshot beyond file diffs.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: No accounts system for solo use beyond a single stagewise Account; Enterprise adds 'centrally manage accounts, users, permissions' via SSO/SCIM, multi-user exists only at that tier.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Enterprise plan is custom-priced with org-level SSO/SCIM and centralized model/inference configuration; no self-serve 'Team' tier separate from Individual and Enterprise.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The app runs with zero stagewise infrastructure when configured with BYOK or local/custom model endpoints (no account required). The stagewise Cloud (account, hosted model library, org admin) is vendor-run; only Enterprise customers can self-host that layer, and even then not the managed inference.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin system for stagewise itself: the docs state “stagewise does not load community plugins”, and the six listed plugins (Figma, GitHub, Supabase, PostHog, Vercel, Remotion) are built in. Custom Providers only register a model endpoint, which is configuration, not extension. Documented at docs.stagewise.io/reference/custom-providers.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: No MCP server or public API found across the full docs sitemap (27 pages read); built-in plugins call out to Figma/GitHub/Supabase/etc., but stagewise does not expose itself as an MCP server or document an external API.

github.description: The Open Source Agentic IDE. Create and orchestrate coding agents, show app previews and run git workflows. Use your favorite models across all providers.

top.title: Show HN: Stagewise (YC S25) – Front end coding agent for existing codebases

activity.changelogCadence: weekly (public newsroom); GitHub tags cut far more often (near-daily nightlies)

editorial.reachRationale: Product-specific community signals were small, as of September 2026, for a tool with this much engineering output: a 655-member Discord, 1,499 X followers with no post since June 2026, and a single Show HN (46 points, Aug 2025) predating the product's April/May 2026 pivot from a browser toolbar into a full agentic IDE. Discounted the 6.8k GitHub stars (attention, not use) and the 266k/month npm downloads on the legacy @stagewise/toolbar package, which measures the old, now-superseded browser-extension product rather than the desktop IDE that replaced it, landing at emerging rather than established.
editorial.polishRationale: Native installers for all three desktop OSes, a 27-page docs site with a consistent reference section, SOC 2 Type 1 compliance, nightly self-updating builds alongside production releases, and a built-in open-source-licenses browser; held back because the product's core boundary (browser-toolbar vs. full IDE) only settled in May 2026 and SOC 2 Type 2/ISO 27001/pen-testing were on the roadmap as of September 2026.
editorial.depthRationale: Goes past a plain terminal wrapper with a full embedded Chromium browser for DOM/console context and design previews, per-workspace worktrees, tool-call-level undo/redo, skills (SKILL.md) and six built-in plugins (Figma, GitHub, Supabase, PostHog, Vercel, Remotion), but has no task board, automations, subagent spawning, PR creation, or merge assistance documented anywhere in its docs.
editorial.feelRationale: Built on Electron (electron-forge in apps/browser/package.json) with a full embedded Chromium engine running alongside the agent chat, not a native-rendered UI. Multiple release-week notes ('UI performance improvements', 'a more responsive UI', 'UI zoom') show recurring perf work rather than a settled instant feel, and no first-party performance claims or user reports of speed/lag turned up in a targeted search, scored as a typical, unremarkable Electron app rather than notably fast or notably janky.

tools.name: Supacode
tools.tagline: The command center for coding agents.
tools.valueProp: A native libghostty terminal that does what cmux doesn’t: a git worktree and live PR/CI state per task, with sessions surviving app quits and dropped SSH via its own daemon. Free and source-available; “remote” means a machine you own.

pricing.notes: Free macOS app (labelled BETA); no Supacode pricing tiers found. You bring your own Claude Code/Codex/Copilot/etc. CLI subscriptions to run inside it.

featureNotes.openness.openSource: Repo is public and homepage says "Open source," but LICENSE is Functional Source License 1.1 (FSL-1.1-ALv2), which is source-available, not OSI-approved; it converts to Apache-2.0 two years after each version's release.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: The `supacode` CLI and `supacode://` deeplinks give scriptable external control, but there is no documented network API or MCP server.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial: 'Custom scripts' are named shell commands (with an icon/tint, per-repository or global) that a user defines and Supacode then surfaces as first-class items in its own Script Menu, command palette and deeplinks, running in their own tab, a config-level custom command/action definition on Supacode's own surface, the narrow bar for partial. It falls short of true: the README documents no plugin API, extension SDK, MCP support, or any mechanism for third-party code to register a new panel, view or provider. Documented in the README's Custom scripts section (github.com/supabitapp/supacode).

github.description: worktree coding agents command center.

editorial.reachRationale: Real but early-stage usage signals: 61,683 release-asset downloads across the last 5 releases, 252 brew cask installs/30d, 2,390 stars and 56 contributors, plus organic third-party coverage (a YouTube "new daily driver" review, a daily.dev repost, a Facebook workflow writeup, an independent Verdent.ai guide). Discounted the maker's personal X account (no dedicated product handle or follower count found) and found no Discord and no Show HN/HN story at all, so this reads as attention without a known-quantity community.
editorial.polishRationale: A genuinely broad feature list (command palette, custom scripts, Sparkle auto-updates, PR tracking) but the app itself and its flagship remote-SSH feature are both explicitly labelled BETA, there's no docs site or pricing page, and the README notes "some local-only features reduced" over SSH.
editorial.depthRationale: Goes beyond a plain terminal multiplexer with managed worktrees, live PR/CI state and merge-conflict help, notifications, a CLI/deeplink automation surface and SSH-remote worktrees, but there's no task board, no containers/sandboxing, no subagent orchestration and no checkpoints/rollback.
editorial.feelRationale: Fully native Swift app (Composable Architecture) rendering every session through libghostty, not Electron; the maker's own claim is "Pure macOS performance you can feel in every keystroke," and a targeted search for slow/laggy reports turned up none, only positive "daily driver" coverage.

tools.name: super.engineering
tools.tagline: Don't run an agent. Command a fleet.
tools.valueProp: A 100%-Rust, GPU-rendered native Mac app, not Electron: every task gets its own git worktree with its own terminal, chat, diff and PR context, and an SSH-backed remote workspace runs the same setup on a host you own. No web or Linux build, and no Windows.

maker.name: Super Dot Engineering LLC
maker.funding: Self-funded / sponsorship-supported; Terms of Service name the maker as "Super Dot Engineering LLC, a Delaware limited liability company." No investment round disclosed. Footer: "Designed by humans in New York & Colorado." The only paid offering is a voluntary, feature-unlocking-nothing Stripe sponsorship.

pricing.notes: The app is free to download and use. Per its own Terms of Service: "Sponsorship is voluntary financial support for our work, and it is currently the only thing we charge for. The software is free... Sponsoring does not unlock features, remove limits, provide priority support, grant influence over the roadmap." Sponsorship is one-time or monthly via Stripe. You bring your own coding-agent CLI accounts/subscriptions (Claude, Codex, Cursor, etc.), the app does not proxy or resell model access. Teams/Enterprise is custom-quoted via a "Talk to a human" contact flow; no published price.

featureNotes.platforms.windows: Docs, CLI automation page: a "Windows migration helper uses a directory junction; this does not imply Windows desktop app availability", an explicit first-party disclaimer that Windows is not a supported platform, only referenced in internal migration tooling.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: Homepage: "Coming soon to Linux" with a "Notify me" waitlist. Not available as of September 2026.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The bundled `sc` CLI controls the running desktop app (worktrees, chats, orchestration, reviews), it is a companion to the native app, not a standalone headless mode.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Docs (docs/): "an SSH workspace intentionally runs repository and provider work on the host you chose", a documented Remote Workspaces (SSH) feature for attaching to a machine you control; docs/cli-local-api also references a "Remote SSH → Install / Update CLI" flow.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: No server component: this is a local-first native desktop client with an optional SSH-connected remote host for execution, not a self-hosted service you deploy.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Install docs list supported providers including "the legacy Gemini integration", worded as legacy/deprioritized rather than a first-class integration like Claude Code or Codex.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: The provider list is long and named (Claude, Codex, Cursor, Grok, Pi, Oh My Pi, OpenCode, Kimi Code, Antigravity, Gemini, Copilot, Factory Droid, Hermes, Kiro, Qwen Code) but nothing in the docs read describes a generic/custom-CLI escape hatch the way some competitors do.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Docs landing page: "It keeps each task in its own Git worktree, connects terminals and chats to the code they change." Homepage: "Worktrees, Isolated by task." This is the app's core mental model (Workspace > Project > Worktree > Tab), not an optional feature.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Docs: "Review changed files and the diff against the worktree's target branch" as a standard step in every task, plus a dedicated review-comment CLI surface (`sc worktree review-add/review-list`).
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Docs: built-in Git actions include "Create PR/MR"; GitHub (PRs, checks) and GitLab (MRs, pipelines) are both first-class forge integrations.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Docs: the adaptive Git action flow runs "commit, push, create a PR or MR, fix blockers, merge, then delete the finished worktree" end to end.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Workspaces "resume where you stopped" (restore tabs, terminal sessions, diffs, sidebars), a session/UI-state restore, not a documented file/agent-state snapshot-and-rollback mechanism, so left unconfirmed rather than guessed.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Homepage orchestration section: "Put Fable 5 in the lead. Agents message one another, share coordination state, and hand work off"; CLI has dedicated `sc team run`, `sc agent send`, and `sc coordination-state` commands.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: The bundled `sc` CLI drives scripts and recipes, and per-project setup/dev-server/watcher/cleanup scripts run on worktree lifecycle events (`.super.engineering/config.json`), event-triggered, not cron-scheduled.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Dedicated Notifications & Approvals system: an inbox with Running/Queue/Timeline views, plus banner, toast, and macOS notification surfaces for approvals, questions, completions, and errors across all open workspaces.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Config-level/control-protocol only, not code-loading extensibility: there is no plugin/extension SDK or marketplace that lets a third party add a panel, view, command or provider to the app itself. The bundled `sc` CLI (docs/cli-local-api) is a documented, JSON-output control protocol that can drive the app's own surface from outside, creating/closing/retargeting worktrees, splitting tabs and panes, saving/applying layouts, and sending/observing agent sessions, which meets the 'scripting or control protocol that can drive the app from outside' bar for partial. "Custom commands and action routing" (docs/custom-commands-and-routing) is separately config-only (named prompts, Git-action provider/model routing).
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Privacy Policy: "You can opt out at any time in Settings → Privacy by turning off Share anonymous usage data," which also deletes local session-state; a separate, non-personal hourly update/active-install check is described as independent of this setting.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: The bundled `sc` CLI exposes JSON-output programmatic control of the running app (`sc chat send`, `sc workspace open`, `sc worktree status --json`, orchestration commands), a local control-plane interface, not a network API or MCP server.

activity.changelogCadence: No public changelog or version-history page was found; the app ships on a single "Nightly" update track (Settings → General → Updates) that the docs say "can include newer behavior that changes quickly." Used the product X account's last post (Sep 25, 2026) as the freshest first-party activity signal, since the product is closed source.

editorial.reachRationale: No GitHub repo (closed source) and no stars to measure. Product-specific signals are modest but real: a 676-member Discord (81 online) and 6,195 X followers with a post as recent as October 16, 2026, plus several independent third-party X testimonials praising its speed. No Hacker News discussion turned up under multiple query variants. The product itself (formerly named "Superconductor") is macOS-only, Nightly-only, with Linux "coming soon" and no Windows plan, consistent with a product with early users and real but limited attention, not a name most practitioners know.
editorial.polishRationale: A fully custom design system (native GPUI interface, dedicated install/download flow with architecture detection, a detailed multi-page documentation site, and a Discord support community) reads as a deliberately finished, professionally presented product, docked slightly for shipping only a single 'Nightly' release channel with no stable track.
editorial.depthRationale: The full task lifecycle (worktree creation, terminal/chat sessions, file/diff context, custom command routing, multi-agent orchestration with a lead/specialist model, Git-action automation through PR/MR and merge, remote SSH workspaces) goes well beyond a tmux wrapper, though it lacks some organizational features (no task board/queue, no team billing, no plugin SDK) that the deepest tools in this dataset have.
editorial.feelRationale: First-party: "100% Rust, rendered with Metal on your GPU. No Electron, no embedded browser" and quoted performance figures (sub-0.7s cold start, ~226MB idle memory, one native process); the app is built on GPUI (the Zed editor's GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework, per its own X account: "GitHub reviews, now in GPUI"). Multiple independent third-party X posts surfaced via search call it explicitly "FAST" / "fantastic and fast." That fits a native, GPU-rendered app, and no counter-evidence turned up.

tools.name: Superconductor
tools.tagline: Superconductor is the multiplayer AI workspace for teams and coding agents.
tools.valueProp: The only tool here that turns customer emails and meeting transcripts directly into tickets and shipped code, via dedicated Email and Meeting Assistant agents. It also ships a built-in benchmark that reruns every supported agent against your team's own merged pull requests to rank them by quality, cost and speed on your codebase.

pricing.notes: Free: 32 sandbox hours/mo, up to 4 vCPU/8GB, 4 members, 4 concurrent agents. Pro: $128/mo, sandbox-hour tiers from 128 up to 2,048/mo, up to 8 vCPU/32GB, 32 members, unlimited concurrent agents, overage $30/100 sandbox-hours. Enterprise: custom, unlimited hours/members, own-cloud sandbox deployment, SLAs, forward-deployed engineer option. Every plan is bring-your-own agent tokens (Claude/ChatGPT/SuperGrok plans or API keys), Superconductor bills only for sandbox compute, never per seat. YC and ed-tech startups get 20% off paid plans.

featureNotes.platforms.windows: Docs and download page both say "Windows support is coming soon"; not shipped.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Installed as a Progressive Web App via Chrome's "Add to Home screen," not a Play Store app or APK.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: A Gemini API key can be added, but only to power Superconductor Skills (image/video generation); docs explicitly say to use OpenCode, Factory Droid or Cursor to run coding agents or benchmarks with Gemini models.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Fixed roster of 8 named agents (Claude Code, Codex, Amp, OpenCode, Pi, Factory Droid, Grok Build, Cursor); no generic "point at any CLI" adapter, unsupported agents require emailing the team.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Isolation is per-implementation cloud containers (via Runloop), each with its own dev environment and branch; not git worktrees sharing one machine.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: iOS docs only point to the phone keyboard's built-in dictation as a "pro tip" for composing tickets; no native voice-control feature in the app itself.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Enterprise tier can "deploy sandboxes in your own cloud or private infrastructure," but the core web/mobile app and ticket data remain on Superconductor's hosted control plane, no fully self-hosted path.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: No public API or developer docs found in the full docs site map (150+ pages read); agents can consume external MCP servers/Connectors, but nothing indicates Superconductor exposes its own API or MCP server for outside control.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Agent-side only, nothing for Superconductor itself: Skills (docs/project/mcp-and-skills) follow the open agentskills.io standard and explicitly work "with any Superconductor agent," and MCP servers (Connectors, custom-mcp-servers) likewise extend what the agent can call, not the app's own panels, views or commands. Automations (docs/project/automations) are a fixed trigger (schedule or PR-merged) wired to one of exactly three built-in action types (create ticket / launch implementation / send message) with no way to add a new action, panel or provider, configuration of existing behavior, not an extension point. No plugin/extension SDK or marketplace for Superconductor's own interface is documented anywhere in docs.superconductor.com.

top.title: Why coding agents belong in remote sandboxes

editorial.reachRationale: Product-specific X account has just 1,203 followers (last post on October 14, 2026, so not abandoned) and no public Discord was found; the disambiguated HN query returns only two stories, topped by a first-party security post at 14 points with zero comments, thin community signal, and there is no GitHub/download data to weigh since it is closed-source. Set against 14+ months of weekly changelogs, a real Free/Pro $128/Enterprise pricing ladder, and YC/ed-tech discounts implying some paying teams; discounted the site's own "well-funded" claim since no funding round or size is disclosed anywhere found.
editorial.polishRationale: The docs, security page, pricing page and comparison pages are extensive and internally consistent and the product ships weekly, but several core flows were labelled Beta (QA Checks, Email triage, Meeting assistant, Implementation Recommendations) as of September 2026, Windows is 'coming soon', and the Pro tier wasn't self-serve checkout as of September 2026; the pricing page says Pro is 'rolling out ... with hands-on onboarding,' requiring a booked call.
editorial.depthRationale: Well past a session switcher: Guided Review and beta QA Checks, a custom benchmark that reruns agents against your own merged PRs (no competitor in Superconductor's own comparison table has this), scheduled and PR-merge-triggered Automations, a Meeting Assistant that turns call transcripts into tickets, Email triage that drafts replies, per-project network-sandbox rule engine, and multiplayer sessions teammates can join and steer together.
editorial.feelRationale: No first-party claims about interface speed were found, the site's only "fast" language ("Fast isolated sandboxes," "snapshots built fast") describes ~30-second sandbox boot time, not UI responsiveness. The desktop app docs describe it as opening the same web app "in its own window instead of another browser tab" (i.e. a webview wrapper, not a native Rust/Swift/GPU renderer), and a targeted search for user reports of it being slow, fast or laggy turned up no sentiment either way.

tools.name: Superset
tools.tagline: Bring Any Agent. Orchestrate Them All.
tools.valueProp: The team platform: cron automations that spawn workspaces, a hosted MCP server and SDK, SSO and audit logs. macOS-first, source-available rather than open source, and signed into Superset's cloud even when running locally.

maker.name: Superset
maker.funding: YC-backed (Launch HN: Superset (YC P26)); team page says $11M raised; three ex-YC CTO founders, San Francisco

pricing.notes: Free: 1 user, local workspaces, desktop app, GitHub integration, CLI. Pro: $20/user/month ($15 billed yearly) adds unlimited users, remote access, automations, Linear and Slack integrations. Enterprise: custom, annual, adds SAML SSO, SCIM, audit logs, SOC 2 report, SLA. Agents run on your own subscriptions or API keys; Superset never proxies model calls. README: the desktop app is free forever for local parallel agents.

featureNotes.platforms.windows: README and FAQ: Windows desktop app not available, planned with no date. The standalone CLI has no Windows build either (macOS and Linux only).
featureNotes.platforms.linux: A Linux x64 AppImage ships with each release but the FAQ calls it experimental and untested; macOS is the primary target. The CLI supports Linux x64 and arm64.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: An iOS app exists (apps/mobile in the repo; the 2026-09-13 changelog documents iOS features such as Pages on your phone, an iOS paywall and Sign in with Apple; the repo's mobile RELEASE.md ships via TestFlight/App Store Connect). But README, pricing page and FAQ, as of September 2026, say the mobile app is 'coming soon' / 'in progress, no date yet', and no App Store link is published.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Mobile release notes in the repo say iOS only; no Android app announced.
featureNotes.platforms.web: FAQ: 'There's no supported web dashboard today.' app.superset.sh exists only for sign-in and Pro billing.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: Bare `superset` opens an interactive command browser for picking commands and flags; it is not a full-screen session UI.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Pro feature. Run `superset start --daemon` (or toggle Remote Access in the desktop app) on a machine you own; it registers with the Superset Relay and other devices in your org reach its workspaces, terminals and ports through the relay. Headless hosts authenticate with an API key.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: superset.sh/cloud is a 'Cloud is coming. Become a design partner' waitlist form; no vendor-managed sandboxes are shipping as of 2026-09-14.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The API, relay and web apps are in the ELv2 monorepo and the README says 'self-host it for your team'; DEVELOPMENT.md brings up a local Postgres + Electric stack. There is no user-facing self-hosting guide, and the shipped product signs into api.superset.sh and routes remote traffic through Superset's relay.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: README: 'Any other CLI agent, works without configuration'; custom agents get their own icon, launch command, prompt template and resume args under Settings → Agents. Status/notification hooks only work for agents launched through Superset.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: A built-in chat pane with a model picker, reasoning-effort control, inline tool approvals and plan review; it uses your own provider keys (Anthropic, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry).
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: The Pull Requests view merges a PR from inside the app (squash, merge commit or rebase) through your GitHub connection. No conflict-resolution helper is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Isolation is git worktrees on the same machine; no per-task container or microVM is documented. 'Sandbox Access' in the docs refers to an agent asking permission for files outside its workspace.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Tasks view pulls Linear issues and GitHub issues (plus native tasks) into a list or kanban board; 'Run in workspace' creates a workspace per task with the agent already working. The Workspaces page also has a board layout with Idle / Working / Needs attention / Needs review / Merged lanes.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: The bundled `superset:orchestrate` skill lets Claude Code or Codex act as a coordinator: it creates a workspace per worker, launches agents and sends follow-ups over their terminals via the Superset CLI (or MCP). Claude Code/Codex native subagents are also shown nested in the sidebar, but that is display only.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Pro feature. RRULE-scheduled agent sessions dispatched to a chosen device; each run produces a live workspace. No agent-outcome tracking: a run counts as successful when its workspace was created.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Desktop notifications, completion chimes and a macOS dock badge when an agent finishes or waits for input; the docs say waiting-for-input detection varies by agent (Claude Code reports both, some agents only completion).
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Only coordinator-to-worker: the orchestrate skill sends follow-ups and dependency results into worker terminals with `superset terminals send`, and the docs describe handing a branch from one agent to another with its terminal context. No peer-to-peer inbox between sessions.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Members granted access to a remote host open its workspaces with 'the full Superset experience (terminals, agent runs, the diff viewer) proxied through the relay', and Pages lets teammates comment straight to the agent watching a page. Simultaneous co-steering of one terminal is not described.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Organizations with members and owners; Pro is per user per month; Enterprise adds SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, audit logs, IP restrictions.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: Source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, which is not OSI-approved. The Homebrew formula's metadata says MIT but the repo LICENSE.md and package.json say Elastic-2.0.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: See execution.selfHostServer: possible from source under ELv2 but undocumented; the default product depends on Superset's API for sign-in and on its relay for remote access.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Homepage: 'Use your existing agent subscriptions and API keys. Superset never proxies model calls.' The Usage page even shows Claude/Codex subscription quota meters and supports multiple accounts per provider.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: The desktop app sends PostHog analytics, on by default (DEFAULT_TELEMETRY_ENABLED = true). The source has a settings.getTelemetryEnabled query and TelemetrySync component, so a toggle appears to exist, but no docs page mentions telemetry or how to turn it off.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Config-level and external-API only, nothing that loads third-party code into the app itself. Extension points: importable/marketplace theme JSON (docs/custom-themes); per-agent command-template customization for the fixed built-in agent list (Settings -> Agents, docs/agent-integration), not adding a new agent type; and an alpha @superset_sh/sdk TypeScript SDK (docs/sdk/getting-started) that drives workspaces/tasks/projects/automations from outside via API key, a control-plane rather than in-app code. Superset's own "plugins" (repo docs/plugins.md: "a bundle of skills and MCP tools an agent can use... ships no code") are an agent skills/MCP marketplace (plugins/slack, plugins/notion, etc.), agent-side, so it doesn't count. The Marketplace's "Agent Configs" section is an explicit placeholder ("Future home for reusable agent configs").
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Hosted MCP server at api.superset.sh/mcp (OAuth 2.1 or API key) with tools for tasks, workspaces, agents, terminals, pages, automations, hosts; a `superset` CLI with --json output; a TypeScript SDK (@superset_sh/sdk).

github.description: Superset is an agentic IDE to orchestrate 100+ coding agents in parallel. Run any agent with your own subscription.

top.title: Launch HN: Superset (YC P26) – IDE for the agents era

tools.authorNote: Probably the most polished of three open source multiplexers (Paseo, Orca and Superset). It sits between the other two: more terminal-focused than Paseo, more workflow-focused than Orca, and the whole experience is super clean. The team-focused features are pretty great too.

editorial.reachRationale: 249,601 release-asset downloads, 116 contributors, and a well-received 108-point Launch HN together support a real, established user base for a YC-backed product; the 1,239-member Discord and 6,873 X followers are modest, keeping it short of major.
editorial.polishRationale: My call from hands-on use: among the most finished tools here. The docs are thorough and the changelog is weekly with a daily release train. The rough edges are at the margins: macOS is the only supported desktop target, Linux is labelled experimental, the CLI is in beta, the FAQ referenced a v1/v2 UI split as of September 2026, and the marketing site, README and changelog disagree about whether the iOS app exists.
editorial.depthRationale: The top of the dataset: beyond worktrees and terminals it has a Tasks board fed by Linear and GitHub issues, a full PR review-and-merge screen, RRULE automations, Pages for agent-published docs with comment-to-agent loops, per-account subscription quota meters, a hosted MCP server, a CLI and a TypeScript SDK.
editorial.feelRationale: My call from hands-on use: fine day to day. It is Electron (README badge, `desktop-analytics.ts` imports `electron`), and the changelog keeps fixing freezes and stalls ('the app no longer freezes after closing a dialog,' 'the terminal viewport no longer freezes when Pi clears its scrollback,' 'deleting many workspaces no longer stalls the app,' plus a WebGL terminal-renderer fallback bug), which keeps it short of quick.

tools.name: Synara
tools.tagline: Run every coding agent in one workspace
tools.valueProp: Synara keeps provider-native sessions, task-owned worktrees, live terminals, browser and iOS simulator previews, and GitHub review in one local workspace. Its headless server and scoped MCP bridge let the same task system run from another machine or client.

pricing.notes: Synara is free and MIT-licensed; supported provider CLIs, accounts, subscriptions and model limits remain provider-owned. No Synara model plan.

featureNotes.platforms.ios: Install and docs list desktop builds and remote browser access, but no native phone app.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Install and docs list desktop builds and remote browser access, but no native phone app.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The release includes a headless server CLI and external MCP bridge; task control is chiefly through the web UI or MCP rather than a documented general-purpose terminal client.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Headless server tarball can run on a machine you control; remote binding requires a token and transport safeguards (Headless server guide).
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Docs and privacy page describe local/self-hosted execution and no Synara-hosted workspace account.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: README names nine supported provider integrations; a custom executable path changes a supported provider binary, not an arbitrary agent adapter.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Synara uses locally installed provider runtimes and does not include model access or its own agent loop (README and installation guide).
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Synara creates and owns task worktrees, binds task terminals and Git actions to them, protects active environments and prunes archived ones (Worktrees guide).
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: The PR workspace can merge a reviewed PR and Git actions check conflicts; the docs instruct a human to resolve worktree integration conflicts and do not describe automatic conflict resolution.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Projects and tasks have status and visible ownership; no primary Kanban queue is claimed in the workspace docs.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Agent Gateway allows a Synara task to create, wait for, read, steer and interrupt ordinary Synara tasks; native provider subagents are separately projected in the UI.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Agent Gateway synara_send_message steers another Synara task; scope and capability checks apply.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Privacy page says there is no Synara account; docs position remote access as self-hosted access to one workspace, not team accounts.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Product is free, uses provider accounts, and has no team plan; sponsorship on the marketing site is separate.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, External MCP lets approved local third-party clients create, wait for and read Synara tasks, so code can drive app behavior from outside. The External MCP and Customization docs document no loader for third-party panels, commands, providers or lifecycle hooks inside Synara; agent skills and MCP clients are not in-app plugins.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Stable anonymous PostHog analytics are off by default; SYNARA_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=true opts in. Beta separately shares crash and usage diagnostics (privacy and Beta docs).
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Scoped External MCP bridge exposes overview, capabilities, project listing, task creation, wait and read to approved local clients; Agent Gateway is internal to provider sessions.

github.description: The best place to build with your AI sub

activity.changelogCadence: frequent: 8 stable entries Sep 1–25, 2026; 29 GitHub releases in 90 days

editorial.reachRationale: The official install page claims 19,268 downloads; GitHub shows 77,266 asset downloads across the latest five releases, 140 contributors and 1,980 stars. These support an established user base, but asset counts include repeat downloads and stars are attention rather than active users.
