top.title: Show HN: Vibe Kanban – Kanban board to manage your AI coding agents

editorial.reachRationale: Sunset (bloop shut down April 2026), so this reflects the reach it had: a well-received 195-point Show HN, 28k stars, a 2,227-member Discord and steady npm downloads (8,122/month) that persist even post-shutdown are evidence of a real established user base and community while it was active, noted in the past tense.
editorial.polishRationale: A signed Tauri desktop app on three OSes, a VS Code/Cursor/Windsurf extension, an embedded preview browser with devtools and device emulation, localisation, and a homepage counting 100,000 PRs created; docked a point because the June 2026 community thread cites bugs and untested code, and the UI routed to cloud features that no longer exist, as of September 2026.
editorial.depthRationale: Issues with sub-issues and parent/child links, batched inline diff comments fed back to the agent, PR creation with AI descriptions, merge/rebase prompts, dev-server preview with click-to-component, an MCP server and phone remote access; no automations, containers or agent-spawns-agent orchestration.
editorial.feelRationale: It's Tauri (Rust core, TS webview UI per gh api languages: Rust 3.7M/TS 3.4M) rather than full Electron, but a closed GitHub issue (#2842, Feb 2026) reports the Projects page was 'very slow to load' - traced to an ElectricSQL sync bug and fixed the same day - and the official troubleshooting docs carry a dedicated 'Everything is slow' section, so real if isolated sluggishness has been reported alongside no praise for speed.

status.overrideReason: bloop announced its shutdown on 2026-04-10; hosted Vibe Kanban Cloud (issues, comments, projects, organisations, relay) was withdrawn 30 days later and subscriptions terminated. The Apache-2.0 repo remains, a maintainer opened a 'community edition' discussion in June 2026, and seven maintenance commits landed in September 2026, but there has been no release since v0.1.44 (2026-04-24).

tools.name: Vorflux
tools.tagline: Autopilot for software engineering.
tools.valueProp: Vorflux puts parallel cloud coding sessions in a shared web workspace, with status filters, per-session machines, and an agentic merge queue. Unlike Cursor’s editor, Devin’s chat fleet, and Amp’s threads, its session groups and duplicate-task warning organize overlapping team work.

pricing.notes: Pay-as-you-go machine compute and model usage; BYOK pays providers directly plus Vorflux platform and machine fees. Signup credits are offered after connecting a Git provider.

featureNotes.platforms.ios: The phone experience is a PWA, not an App Store or TestFlight app.
featureNotes.platforms.android: The phone experience is a PWA, not a Play Store or APK app.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: An ACP bridge runs from editors, but the documented session launcher is the web app or REST API, not a standalone CLI.
featureNotes.agents.codex: A Codex subscription can pay for GPT model use, but the docs do not establish whether Vorflux runs Codex CLI as a managed agent.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: The session docs specify a separate cloud machine and repo clone per session; they do not document creating or managing Git worktrees.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: PR settings document Vorflux agent branches and a configurable branch prefix for session-created PRs.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: Sessions have status and Groups views, but the docs do not describe a kanban task queue.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: The pricing page lists a Codex subscription path for GPT models; BYOK model API keys are also offered with a platform fee.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, config-only: the Harness Builder changes the app’s agent roles, models, and instructions, but the Skills and Harness Builder docs do not document loading third-party code into Vorflux panels, commands, or lifecycle hooks.

tools.authorNote: Another one where I have a bit of personal experience. Alongside Capy, Tembo and the others, it's pretty similar in that it just works and it's pretty slick. To be fair, they have a slightly less phenomenal eye for design. But I think they offset that with the actual usability and performance of the platform, and their thoughtful execution of things like automations.

editorial.reachRationale: The first-party site offers public signup and a working app login, but publishes no product usage figure or customer count. With no official product repository or package metrics found, reach remains a provisional niche tier.
editorial.polishRationale: A public signup flow, detailed docs, and interactive first-party demos show a coherent session workspace, status filters, plan approval, PR review, and phone PWA; authenticated product use was not verified.
editorial.depthRationale: Per-session cloud machines, session groups and duplicate detection, subagent dispatch, schedules and webhooks, in-app diffs, and a merge queue go well beyond a terminal wrapper.
editorial.feelRationale: Vorflux ships only as a browser-based web app, with no desktop or native client in its own platform list, a typical web-app rendering stack; no performance claims or user reports of lag were found.

tools.name: VS Code Agent Sessions
tools.tagline: We've also made updates to the Agent Sessions view, your single place to manage your agents.
tools.valueProp: One pane inside the world’s most-used editor that lists and switches between sessions from four harnesses (its own local agent, Copilot, Claude, Codex) across local, remote, dev-container and GitHub cloud execution, and picks up sessions started outside VS Code. The deeper multi-agent features sit behind a paid Copilot tier.

maker.name: Microsoft
maker.funding: Public company (NASDAQ: MSFT). VS Code is a free, MIT-licensed editor; Agent Sessions and the underlying agent harnesses are funded as part of GitHub Copilot, Microsoft's paid AI coding subscription, no separate funding event for this feature.

pricing.notes: VS Code itself is free (MIT). Agent Sessions works with the free GitHub Copilot tier (2,000 completions/mo, limited agent use) but access to the Claude and Codex harnesses, cloud agents, and code review requires Copilot Pro ($10/user/mo) or above; Pro+ ($39/user/mo) adds premium models including Opus; Max ($100/user/mo) adds priority access and the largest usage allowance. Business/Enterprise tiers add audit logs, policy and org billing. The Agents window also accepts a BYOK Anthropic API key or a ChatGPT sign-in as experimental, GitHub-account-free alternatives for the Claude/Codex harnesses specifically.

featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: One of the four agent harnesses VS Code documents as supported: "Visual Studio Code supports the Local, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic Claude, and OpenAI Codex agent harnesses" (docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses). Usable via a Copilot subscription or a BYOK Anthropic API key in the Agents window.
featureNotes.agents.codex: Same exhaustive four-harness quote as claudeCode; usable via Copilot subscription or an experimental ChatGPT sign-in in the Agents window. Also the first third-party agent brought into VS Code, announced in the Nov 2025 launch post.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Not among the four documented harnesses. Google's agent (Jules) is named as a GitHub-platform-wide Agent HQ partner (github.blog, Oct 2025) but no VS Code-specific harness integration is documented as of Sept 2026.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Not a fifth harness; VS Code's Agent Sessions view discovers and lets you adopt local sessions already running in the external Copilot CLI, alongside the GitHub Copilot mobile app and Claude Code/Codex CLIs run outside VS Code (docs/agents/concepts/sessions).
featureNotes.agents.opencode: Not documented; the four-harness list is stated as exhaustive by VS Code's own docs.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Not documented; excluded by the same exhaustive four-harness statement.
featureNotes.agents.amp: Not documented; excluded by the same exhaustive four-harness statement.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Not documented; excluded by the same exhaustive four-harness statement.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: No generic "bring any CLI/ACP agent" mechanism is documented; the harness list is closed to Local, Copilot, Claude and Codex.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Worktree isolation gives a session "a separate Git worktree based on committed Git state" and cloud/PR-backed sessions work against a branch, but no VS Code doc states an automatic, guaranteed branch-per-task naming convention for local worktree sessions the way some competitors document.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: The Changes view offers one-click Commit, Merge, Checkout, or Discard actions on a session's edits (docs/agents/run/review-code-edits), plus PR checkout/review for cloud sessions. No conflict-resolution assistance beyond that is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: The Agents window and Agent Sessions view are a session list/sidebar (grouped by Local/Background/Cloud), not a drag-and-drop kanban board.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Handoff carries a session's conversation history and context when you switch harness or execution environment mid-task (docs/agents/concepts/agent-harnesses), and parallel Subagents are coordinated by a lead agent via a documented runSubagent tool. No general agent-to-agent messaging protocol between independent sessions is documented.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: The browser-based Agents window (insiders.vscode.dev/agents) lets the same signed-in user reach their own sessions from any device over a dev tunnel; this is cross-device access, not multiple people concurrently steering one live session.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: VS Code's own "code tunnel" lets you reach a machine you control remotely, but that is remote-own execution, not a separate self-hostable Agent Sessions server product; the Copilot/Claude/Codex harnesses depend on the vendors' managed backends.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: VS Code itself (microsoft/vscode) is MIT-licensed with ~192,900 GitHub stars. The GitHub Copilot Chat extension was previously open-sourced as a mirror (microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat, MIT, ~9,970 stars) but that repo is archived (last push 2026-05-20). The Agent Sessions feature's actual harness backends (GitHub Copilot, and the Claude/Codex integrations) are proprietary, subscription-gated services, not open source.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The editor runs anywhere, but Agent Sessions' cloud target and the Copilot/Claude/Codex harness backends are vendor-managed services with no self-hosted deployment option; Copilot Business/Enterprise adds policy and audit controls, not on-prem hosting.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Setting telemetry.telemetryLevel to "off" fully disables telemetry reporting, per docs/configure/telemetry.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, not true, specifically for the Agent Sessions view (the general VS Code extension ecosystem is irrelevant here unless an extension can actually touch this surface): the official 'AI extensibility in VS Code' overview (api/extension-guides/ai/ai-extensibility-overview) documents exactly four stable ways to extend AI -- Language Model Tools, MCP Tools, Chat Participants, and the Language Model API -- and all four extend the chat/agent-mode conversation, not the Agent Sessions list; none can add a new session source, harness entry, panel or command to that view. The stable chat contribution points (chatAgents, chatInstructions, chatPromptFiles, chatSkills; api/references/contribution-points) likewise only bundle custom personas/instructions/prompts/skills for Copilot Chat, not sessions-view entries -- a general extension API that cannot touch the sessions view, a case that counts as partial at most. A real mechanism that *would* touch the sessions view -- `vscode.chat.registerChatSessionItemProvider` / `createChatSessionItemController` plus a `chatSessions` manifest contribution, which lets a provider appear as a session source alongside Local/Copilot/Claude/Codex -- exists only as an unstable, undocumented proposed API (`vscode.proposed.chatSessionsProvider.d.ts`, `vscode.proposed.agentSessionsWorkspace.d.ts` in the microsoft/vscode source tree) that, as of Sept 2026, is used exclusively by Microsoft's own bundled `extensions/copilot` (its Copilot CLI and Copilot Cloud session providers) and is absent from the stable, documented contribution-points reference -- a real but experimental/undocumented extension point for third parties, meeting the partial bar rather than true.

top.title: Show HN: DevSwarm 2.0, fix parallel Claude Code sprawl

editorial.reachRationale: Scored for VS Code + GitHub Copilot's real installed base, not for Agent Sessions as an isolated product: VS Code is the default code editor for a large majority of professional developers, Copilot is the market-leading AI coding subscription, and Agent Sessions ships as a built-in, on-by-default surface of that combination rather than an opt-in extension. Evidence: the product's own @code X account (distinct from @github/@Microsoft) has 816k followers with same-day posting activity; monthly stable releases (19 GitHub releases/tags in the last 90 days alone) plus weekly doc/blog updates; a public, multi-tier Copilot pricing ladder up to a dedicated Max plan for "sustained, high-volume agent workflows"; and first-party GitHub Agent HQ messaging aimed at bringing Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Cognition and xAI agents to "millions more developers who use GitHub and VS Code." This is a dominant, default choice by virtue of the host platform; it does not mean Agent Sessions specifically is the most-used multi-agent workflow among power users.
editorial.polishRationale: An extremely mature, extensively documented product (dedicated docs site with 60+ agent-specific pages, monthly release notes, in-product screenshots and settings references) shipped by a team that iterates weekly, but several Agent-Sessions-specific pieces were, as of September 2026, explicitly labeled Preview or Experimental: the Agents window itself ("Preview"), agent sandboxing ("Preview on macOS/Linux/WSL2, Experimental on Windows"), automations ("rolling out gradually"), and the artifacts panel ("Experimental"), so the newest multi-agent layer was visibly less finished than the 10+ year old core editor around it.
editorial.depthRationale: Four distinct harnesses (Local, Copilot, Claude, Codex) across four execution environments (local, connected host, Dev Container, GitHub-managed cloud) with worktree or container isolation, checkpoints with restore, inline diff review with per-range feedback that round-trips to the agent, PR-integrated review comments, scheduled/triggered automations, parallel lead-agent-coordinated subagents, MCP and Agent Plugin extensibility, OS-level terminal sandboxing (Seatbelt/bubblewrap/MXC), and a remote protocol (Agent Host Protocol) for browser access to sessions on another machine. This goes far beyond a tmux-style wrapper.
editorial.feelRationale: VS Code's core editor (Monaco, native rendering) is broadly regarded as fast for an Electron app, but the chat/agent-session UI specifically has recurring, independent reports of sluggishness under real use: a Reddit thread titled "Long Copilot agent sessions cause severe UI lag and forced reloads," a GitHub Community discussion "Everything becomes slow in VS Code when Copilot is enabled" (advice to delete old chat history to recover performance), and a Visual Studio Developer Community report "GitHub Copilot agent mode is extremely slow." VS Code's own September 2026 release notes list "Faster session list loading" as a fix, which is first-party acknowledgment that the sessions list had a real performance problem. Net: a fast core editor wrapped around an agent-session UI that degrades over long sessions and has needed repeated first-party performance fixes, consistent with known sluggishness rather than isolated complaints, but not as uniformly poor as products with no acknowledgment or fixes.

tools.name: Waku
tools.tagline: One native app for all your coding agents.
tools.valueProp: A Rust/GPUI native app, not Electron, driving Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Amp, OpenCode, Pi, Grok and more through each CLI's own protocol in one timeline. Every task gets a daemon-owned git worktree and per-prompt checkpoint that rewinds code and conversation together, with the same daemon also serving companion web and mobile clients.

maker.name: EGOIST
maker.funding: GitHub Sponsors (README Sponsorship section); maker also runs ChatWise.app

pricing.notes: Free and open source (GPL-3.0-only); no Waku account, telemetry or billing. You install and authenticate your own agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, etc.), each with its own subscription or API key.

featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: `crates/waku-core/src/worktree.rs`: 'Daemon-owned isolated Git worktrees for tasks', the daemon creates one under `~/.waku/worktrees` per task (project id + session id), requires the project be a Git repo, and returns the path for the task's lifetime.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Config/control-protocol only, not code-loading: there is no plugin/extension SDK for adding a new panel, view, command or provider to Waku itself, the provider list is a fixed set of 11 named drivers (docs/providers.md) with no generic/custom adapter, and the Skills settings page (`crates/waku-core/src/skills.rs`) only discovers and toggles SKILL.md files already sitting in each underlying agent's own directory (~/.claude/skills, ~/.codex/skills, etc.), not a Waku extension point. But `waku-protocol` (README `## Architecture`; `crates/waku-protocol/README.md`) is a documented, versioned, transport-neutral WebSocket RPC contract, 'the authenticated, versioned WebSocket contract' the desktop, web and mobile clients all speak, with a generated TypeScript contract (`bun run protocol:generate`) so any external client can drive tasks, checkpoints, files/diffs, Git, skills and settings on the daemon; the desktop Settings -> Daemon page can expose this beyond loopback with a copyable auth token that 'grants full control of the daemon host' (apps/mobile/README.md). That is exactly the 'scripting or control protocol that can drive the app from outside' bar for partial, it drives existing daemon state, it does not let a third party add new surface to the app.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: `apps/mobile` is an Expo/React Native client you build and run yourself (`bun --filter @waku/mobile ios`); no App Store listing found. It connects to a remote Waku daemon you already run, not a hosted service.
featureNotes.platforms.android: Same Expo client as iOS (`apps/mobile`); no Play Store listing found, run from source.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: README architecture section + `apps/mobile/README.md`: the desktop's Settings -> Daemon page exposes the child daemon on a fixed port over an authenticated WebSocket; mobile and web clients connect to 'one or more remote Waku daemons' via ws/wss with a copied token. Loopback-only by default.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The `waku-daemon` process (bundled with the desktop app) is the server the web and mobile clients depend on; there is no vendor-run alternative.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: `src/review_diff.rs` and `src/app/activity_diff.rs` implement an in-app diff view over session/task changes.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: No PR-creation feature found in docs, README or changelog; opening a PR would be up to the agent's own tool use inside a session.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Search hits for 'subagent' are Waku rendering Claude Code's and Codex's own built-in subagent/background-work activity in the transcript, not a cross-provider orchestration feature Waku itself provides.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: No desktop/push notification feature for turn completion or permission requests found in docs, README or CHANGELOG.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Homepage states architecture-level absence, not just a toggle: 'No account, no telemetry, no Waku cloud between you and your agents.'
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: The daemon exposes an authenticated, versioned WebSocket RPC protocol (`waku-protocol`) that the desktop, web and mobile clients all use, and that Settings -> Daemon can expose beyond loopback, an external programmatic control surface.

github.description: ⚡ A native app for all your coding agents.

top.title: Launch HN: Twill.ai (YC S25) – Delegate to cloud agents, get back PRs

editorial.reachRationale: Repo created in July 2026, with fast, sustained development (1,539 stars, 16 contributors, 481 commits/90d, 14 releases/90d) and a real maker following (EGOIST, indie dev/ChatWise founder, ~17.5K personal X followers who posted the launch). Its actual Show HN ('I built a native app for coding agents with Rust and GPUI') scored a modest 39 points. Discounted GitHub stars as attention rather than use, and found no Discord, install/download counts, or third-party plugin ecosystem, so this reads as early but growing rather than an established user base.
editorial.polishRationale: A signed, auto-updating macOS build, a Linux install script and a Windows installer/portable zip, unusually meticulous architecture docs (protocol codegen checks, a cross-platform CI matrix, detailed computer-use platform notes) and sustained solo-maintainer velocity (1,539 stars, 481 commits/90d) show real engineering care; held back because the mobile/web clients are build-it-yourself with no store listing and computer-use is explicitly a dev-only, macOS-first feature.
editorial.depthRationale: A little beyond a plain session switcher: a daemon-owned worktree per task, per-prompt checkpoints that rewind code and conversation together, an in-app diff view, and companion web/mobile clients sharing the same daemon protocol, but there is no plugin system, no automations, no cross-agent messaging, no PR creation, and no task board, so it doesn't reach orchestrator territory.
editorial.feelRationale: Built in Rust with GPUI, the GPU-accelerated framework behind Zed (a basis for an instant feel). Homepage: 'Native down to the frame... Instant launch, smooth scrolling through years of transcript, no Electron'; maker's own launch post on X makes the same Rust+GPUI/fast claim. No jank or slowness reports found.

tools.name: Warp
tools.tagline: Warp is an open agentic development platform that was built to work wherever and however you work.
tools.valueProp: The terminal itself rather than a wrapper: an AGPL Rust app on all three desktops that auto-detects fifteen CLI agents and adds notifications, diff review and phone remote control. Its own agent and the cloud platform behind it stay proprietary and credit-metered.

maker.name: Warp, Inc.
maker.funding: VC-backed: $50M Series B led by Sequoia Capital (Andrew Reed on the board); earlier backers include GV, Neo, BoxGroup and Dylan Field, with Sam Altman and Tobi Lutke as angels. OpenAI is the 'founding sponsor' of the open-source repository. The open-source post calls Warp 'a VC funded startup'.

pricing.notes: Free $0: the terminal, Warp Agent CLI, bring-your-own inference (API keys, SuperGrok, OpenAI-compatible endpoint), limited cloud agents (Warp Agent harness only, 'limited' concurrency and compute), 3 indexed codebases, 30 stored cloud conversations, 5 shared sessions; telemetry must stay on to use AI. Build $18/mo annual ($20 monthly): 1,500 credits (~$20 of agent usage at API rates), all frontier and open models, 20 concurrent cloud agents at 2 vCPU/4 GiB, third-party cloud harnesses, unlimited Drive and session sharing, up to 10 seats. Max $180/mo annual ($200 monthly): 18,000 credits, 4 vCPU/8 GiB cloud agents. Business $45/user/mo annual ($50 monthly, up to 25 seats): per-seat credits, 80 concurrent cloud agents at 8 vCPU/16 GiB, SAML SSO, admin-configured data controls, BYOK for orgs larger than 10 people. Enterprise: custom; unlimited seats, self-hosted cloud agents, BYOLLM (Bedrock, Vertex), ZDR, analytics API. Cloud runs meter inference plus compute plus platform credits; Claude Code and Codex harnesses bill their own provider while Warp meters compute and platform credits. Warp Factories (Early Access) is usage-based per agent run, 20% markup on the pay-as-you-go tier. Cloud agents and integrations for a team require Build, Max or Business with at least 20 credits.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Native Rust app (Metal), macOS 10.14+, Intel and Apple silicon; `brew install --cask warp`.
featureNotes.platforms.windows: Windows 10 1903+ / Server 2022, x86_64 and ARM64; `winget install Warp.Warp`. The SSH extension is not available from the Windows client.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: .deb, .rpm, Arch .tar.zst and AppImage for x64 and ARM64; needs glibc 2.31+ and OpenGL ES 3.0+ or Vulkan.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: No App Store app is documented. Mobile access is the Oz web app (oz.warp.dev) and shared-session links opened in a phone browser.
featureNotes.platforms.android: No Play Store app is documented; same browser-only mobile path as iOS.
featureNotes.platforms.web: The Oz web app at oz.warp.dev starts runs, manages schedules, environments, secrets and integrations, and 'works on mobile devices'. Shared and Remote Control sessions open in any browser with no install. The 2026.09.09 changelog and build.warp.dev also reference a web-compiled 'Warp on Web' terminal.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: Two CLIs: the Warp Agent CLI (`warp`, `curl -fsSL https://app.warp.dev/download/agent-cli | bash`, macOS and Linux) runs the built-in agent in any terminal, and the `oz` CLI (`oz agent run`, `run-cloud`, `schedule`, `integration create`) drives cloud runs. `oz` commands are supported through the end of September 2026 before folding into `warp`.
featureNotes.platforms.tui: The Warp Agent CLI is an interactive single-conversation terminal program with a footer, slash commands and approval cards; it is not a multi-session full-screen multiplexer. The Warp app itself is a GPU-rendered desktop window, not a TUI.
featureNotes.execution.local: Local agents (Warp Agent and third-party CLIs) run in your checkout on your machine; local orchestration spawns child Warp Agent conversations on the same machine.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: Two paths. The SSH extension installs a companion server under `~/.warp*/` on a remote macOS or Linux host over your existing SSH connection (no open ports, no root) and gives the file tree, code review, indexing and native diffs on that host. Separately, the Automation Platform's self-hosted runners (`oz-agent-worker` daemon, or unmanaged `oz agent run` on any host with session tracking) are Enterprise-only.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Warp-hosted Docker environments; concurrency and size scale by plan (Free 'limited', Build 20 x 2 vCPU/4 GiB, Max 20 x 4 vCPU/8 GiB, Business 80 x 8 vCPU/16 GiB). Started from the Warp app's Cloud Mode, the Oz web app, the CLI, the API/SDK, schedules, or Slack/Linear/GitHub/Jira triggers. Third-party harnesses in the cloud require Build or higher.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: Enterprise plans can run the `oz-agent-worker` daemon on Docker, Kubernetes or bare hosts so code and execution stay in your network, but orchestration, session storage and inference route through Warp's backend, which is proprietary. Managed workers were Linux-only as of September 2026 (macOS/Windows planned); the unmanaged path runs on any OS.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: Auto-detected in the app with the full toolbelt (rich input, notifications via a Warp plugin, code review comments, Remote Control), and available as a cloud harness (`claude`) on Build+ using your Anthropic API key or Bedrock credentials.
featureNotes.agents.codex: Auto-detected with the full toolbelt (notifications via a native config change), and available as a cloud harness (`codex`) on Build+.
featureNotes.agents.geminiCli: Auto-detected with the toolbelt but without agent notifications. `gemini` is accepted as a harness type in Warp Factories definition files only, not in the cloud agent API.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Auto-detected with the toolbelt; no agent notifications.
featureNotes.agents.opencode: Auto-detected with the full toolbelt including notifications via a Warp plugin.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Cursor CLI is auto-detected with the toolbelt; no agent notifications.
featureNotes.agents.amp: Auto-detected with the toolbelt; no agent notifications.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Auto-detected with the toolbelt; no agent notifications.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Any CLI agent runs in a Warp pane like any process, but the agent toolbelt only activates for the fifteen auto-detected agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Amp, Auggie, Copilot CLI, Cursor CLI, Gemini CLI, Droid, Pi, Goose, Antigravity, Hermes, Mistral Vibe, Grok Build). There is no generic adapter; ACP support is on the public roadmap (issue #9233).
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Warp Agent: multi-model (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, GLM, Kimi, DeepSeek on Fireworks, plus Auto routing), reachable in the app, as the standalone Warp Agent CLI, and as the default cloud harness (`oz`). Its harness runs server-side and is not in the open-source repo.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Warp detects worktrees you create (`git worktree add ...`) and gives each its own Code Review panel, git chip, file watching and codebase index; the docs recommend one worktree per local agent. It does not create or remove worktrees for you.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: Cloud environments are a Docker image plus repositories plus setup commands, giving each cloud run a fresh workspace on Warp-hosted or self-hosted (Docker, Kubernetes or direct-host) runners. Local runs are not sandboxed.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Cloud runs push branches and open PRs as tracked artifacts under the triggering user's GitHub identity. Local agents work in whatever checkout the tab is in; no automatic branch creation or naming is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Code Review panel (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift++): uncommitted or branch-vs-main diffs, edit or revert hunks, attach diffs as context, and Interactive Code Review where inline comments are batched and sent back to the agent, including third-party CLI agents.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Cloud agent runs produce pull requests as artifacts (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps integrations) and a guide covers attaching session links to PRs. No dedicated 'create PR' button for local sessions is documented; the agent does it via git/gh.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Only as a prompt: the Code overview lists 'Resolve this merge conflict by keeping backend changes...' as an example task for the agent. No dedicated merge or conflict-resolution feature is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: Partial: the Code Review panel can revert individual hunks or discard changes, conversations can be forked, and handoff snapshots carry uncommitted workspace state between cloud runs. No per-turn checkpoint/restore of agent state is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Vertical tabs with git branch, worktree and PR metadata per session, per-tab agent status icons, an Agent Management Panel listing local and cloud runs, and plan-based concurrent cloud agent limits (20 to 80).
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: The Oz web app Runs page and the in-app Agent Management Panel list runs filtered by status, source and creator, and Warp Factories has a factory inbox and dashboard, but there is no kanban or queue you drag tasks into; work enters through triggers (Slack, Linear, Jira, GitHub, schedules, API).
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Multi-agent orchestration: a parent agent spawns child agents (local to local, local to cloud, cloud to cloud, or cloud children sharing the parent's environment) with their own prompt, model and harness (a Warp Agent parent can spawn Claude Code or Codex children). Exactly one level deep; children cannot spawn children. Spawning needs approval unless the profile allows it.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: Scheduled agents (cron via `oz schedule` or the web app), integration triggers (Slack and Teams mentions, Linear and Jira issues, GitHub mentions and Actions, custom webhooks via the API), and Warp Factories automations defined as code.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Complete / Request (blocked on approval, permission or idle prompt) / Error notifications as in-app toasts, a notification mailbox, per-tab status badges and native desktop alerts. Supported for Warp Agent, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode after a one-time plugin or config setup; the other eleven detected agents do not support notifications.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: Parent agents receive child state transitions and results in their transcript and can send follow-ups to children; runs can be steered via follow-up messages from Slack, Linear, the API or shared sessions. Children do not talk to each other.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Push-to-talk voice input (Fn on macOS, Alt+Right on Windows/Linux, or a mic button in Agent Mode), transcribed by Wispr Flow; works in all input editors.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: Warp teams with admin/member roles, domain-restricted invites, an admin panel, shared Drive objects, team environments and secrets. Teams can be created on any plan including Free; each user belongs to one team at a time.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Agent Session Sharing publishes a live session to Warp's servers; multiple viewers with their own cursors can watch prompts, tool use and terminal output, and can be granted edit access to send queries and run commands. Remote Control does the same for third-party CLI agents for async steering from a phone or browser. Free plan: up to 5 shared sessions; shares expire after about a week.
featureNotes.collaboration.teamBilling: Business ($45/user/mo, up to 25 seats) adds team usage metrics, admin data controls and SAML SSO; Enterprise adds shared credit pools, spend controls, multi-admin, domain capture and an analytics API. SOC 2 Type II.
featureNotes.openness.openSource: The desktop client (app and most crates) is AGPL-3.0 and the `warpui_core`/`warpui` UI crates are MIT since the 2026-04-28 public release. The server, Warp Drive backend, hosted auth, the Warp Agent harness and the Automation Platform (cloud agents, orchestration, Oz) are proprietary and not in the repo.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: FAQ: 'Some functionality works fully locally; other features (Drive sync, hosted-model agents, team features) require Warp's backend.' Even Enterprise self-hosted runners need outbound access to Warp for orchestration, session storage and inference. The server is not open and there is no self-hosted control plane.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Third-party CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) run inside Warp with their own logins. For Warp Agent you can bring OpenAI, Anthropic or Google API keys, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a SuperGrok subscription, but explicitly not a ChatGPT or Claude subscription; BYOK is limited to individuals and orgs of 10 or fewer unless on Business/Enterprise. Warp also resells inference as credits, and platform credits still apply to cloud runs.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: Settings > Privacy toggles 'Help improve Warp' and crash reports; an exhaustive telemetry event table and a Network Log are published; Sentry and Rudderstack are named. Caveat: on the Free plan telemetry must stay enabled to use AI features; paid plans can opt out and keep AI.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, config-level only: there is no plugin/extension SDK for adding a new panel, view or command to Warp itself, and agent-side items (MCP servers, skills, rules, saved prompts) don't count since they extend the CLI agents, not Warp. Three genuine app-own-surface, config-level mechanisms qualify: (1) custom theme `.yaml` files dropped into `~/.warp/themes/` (or the Windows/Linux equivalents) that Warp discovers and renders, matching the 'theme files' example (docs.warp.dev/terminal/appearance/custom-themes); (2) YAML Workflows -- `.yaml` files with `name`/`command`/`arguments` that Warp auto-loads from `~/.warp/workflows/` or a repo's `.warp/workflows/` into its own Command Search/Workflow Search UI, i.e. custom command definitions the app itself runs (docs.warp.dev/terminal/entry/yaml-workflows); (3) a custom OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint (OpenRouter, LiteLLM, z.ai, internal gateway) that repoints the built-in Warp Agent at a third-party provider by config (docs.warp.dev/agents/inference/custom-inference-endpoint). None of these let a third party add new code-driven surface to Warp, so it stays partial rather than true.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: REST API at app.warp.dev/api/v1 (create, list, follow up, cancel runs), official Python and TypeScript SDKs (`oz-agent-sdk`), the `oz` CLI, a Factory MCP server (`send_task`), a `warp://` URI scheme and launch configurations.

github.description: Warp is an agentic development environment, born out of the terminal.

top.title: Show HN: Warp, a Rust-based terminal

editorial.reachRationale: A clear major-tier case: 65k GitHub stars (discounted but the largest OSS terminal here), a 17.9k-member product Discord, brew cask 4,249 installs/30d, and a long track record since 2021 support 'a name most practitioners know'; GitHub release tags are noise (dev builds) so this leans on commits, changelog cadence and the community numbers instead.
editorial.polishRationale: Judged from docs and the changelog rather than hands-on. A native Rust app on all three desktop OSes with weekly dated releases since 2021, SOC 2 Type II, an exhaustive telemetry table and unusually thorough docs. Held back from finished: the product is mid-rename (Oz became the Automation Platform on 2026-08-18 and the `oz` CLI is being folded into `warp` in October), the public FAQ page quotes retired plans and request quotas, warp.dev/changelog 404s, notifications only work for four of the fifteen supported agents, and Factories is early access.
editorial.depthRationale: Far past a session switcher. On the local side it auto-detects fifteen CLI agents and gives them a rich input editor, three-way notifications, inline review comments that go back to the agent, worktree-aware tabs and one-click Remote Control from a phone. Behind that sits a full cloud platform: Docker environments, scheduled and Slack/Linear/GitHub-triggered runs, parent/child orchestration across local and cloud with mixed harnesses, local-to-cloud handoff with workspace snapshots, a REST API with Python and TypeScript SDKs, a Factory MCP server, multi-viewer shared sessions, and Enterprise self-hosted runners.
editorial.feelRationale: My call from daily use: slow and sluggish. GitHub issues and an active r/warpdotdev thread ('is it me or warp is really slow lately') report the same input lag and high CPU use, worst on integrated and older GPUs like Intel UHD. The renderer itself is fast: a custom Rust UI framework (warpui_core/warpui) on the GPU, and the docs' own VTE/Termbench benchmarks put raw throughput near Alacritty and WezTerm. Throughput is not how it feels to use.

tools.name: Workmux
tools.tagline: Terminal-first workflow for parallel AI agents.
tools.valueProp: A tmux plugin, not an app: every task gets a worktree and a tmux or Zellij window, with status icons in the window title showing which agents are working, waiting or done. Sandboxes agents in Docker, Podman or Lima, and skills let one Claude Code drive the rest.

maker.name: Raine Virta
maker.funding: bootstrapped (solo freelance developer, ex-Reaktor)

pricing.notes: Free, open-source CLI (MIT). No hosted tier; you bring your own agent CLI logins/API keys.

featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: No built-in `pr create` command; the optional `/open-pr` Claude Code skill writes a PR description from conversation context and the agent runs `gh pr create` itself.
featureNotes.isolation.checkpoints: `workmux resurrect` restores worktree windows and resumes agent conversations (`--continue`) after a tmux/computer crash, and `add --fork` forks a prior conversation; this is conversation-state recovery, not a file/workspace snapshot-and-rollback system.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: The `/coordinator` skill lets one agent use workmux CLI commands to spawn, prompt and monitor other workmux-managed agents; separately, Pi's `pi-suba` extension reports child-agent activity so workmux tracks parent+child status as one unit.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Tmux window titles (and Zellij tab titles) show live 🤖 working / 💬 waiting / ✅ done icons, `workmux last-done` cycles to agents needing attention, and `merge --notification` fires a one-off system notification on successful merge; there is no generic desktop/push alert for every blocked state.
featureNotes.orchestration.crossAgentMessaging: `workmux status --all` / `project:handle` targeting query agent state across worktrees and repositories, and skills can prompt other agents' panes via CLI, but there is no direct agent-to-agent message-passing API.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, config-level only, not code-loading: the README's 'plugin' references (a small status-tracking plugin/skill workmux ships FOR Claude Code via `claude plugin install workmux-status`, and for OpenCode via a `.ts` file dropped in `~/.config/opencode/plugins`) all run the other direction and are agent-side, not workmux's own surface. But `.workmux.yaml` documents real lifecycle hooks on workmux's own worktree lifecycle -- `post_create` (after worktree creation, before the tmux window opens), `pre_merge` (before merging, aborts on failure) and `pre_remove` (before worktree removal, aborts on failure) -- each an arbitrary shell command list the app itself runs at a fixed point, with dedicated env vars (`WM_HANDLE`, `WM_WORKTREE_PATH`, `WM_PROJECT_ROOT`, `WM_BRANCH_NAME`, etc.) (README.md '#### Lifecycle hooks'). That is the same documented, narrow-scope shell-hook pattern already treated as partial for Vibe Kanban's Setup/Cleanup Scripts -- it lets a user run their own code at fixed points in workmux's own worktree lifecycle, but adds no new panel, view, command or provider to the app.

github.description: git worktrees + tmux windows for zero-friction parallel dev

top.title: Show HN: back2vibing – instantly jump back to your agent's tmux pane / terminal

editorial.reachRationale: 43 contributors, 118 commits/30d and 52 releases/90d since a 2025-11-04 creation date show a real, fast-growing user base, and Homebrew accepted the formula into homebrew/core (not just the author's own tap), with crates.io downloads (1,851) and 31 Homebrew installs/30d as independent corroboration. Discounted the 2,716 GitHub stars as attention rather than use, and discounted HN reception (best Show HN only 4 points across five attempts) and the absence of a confirmed product X/Discord account, those limit its reach.
editorial.polishRationale: My call: capable, but not more polished than the desktop apps it used to outrank. Documentation is unusually deep (full CLI and config reference, hooks, skills, sandbox guide, per-agent status matrix) and it ships real safety nets (crash resurrection, interrupted-agent detection, several installers). It is still a layer over tmux and Zellij with a light TUI, so the finish stops at solid.
editorial.depthRationale: It goes well past a worktree wrapper into diff review via the dashboard, container/Lima sandboxing, lifecycle hooks, agent status tracking across 10+ CLIs, and skill-driven cross-agent orchestration. There is no PR-creation or true rollback built into the core CLI itself; both are delegated to optional skills.
editorial.feelRationale: Workmux is a pure-Rust CLI and TUI that does not render its own terminal: it drives tmux or Zellij windows and panes directly, so the terminal itself is exactly as fast as the multiplexer you already use. That speed belongs to tmux, so it earns quick rather than instant; its own dashboard and sidebar are light status and diff views on top. No user reports of slowness or jank turned up in a targeted search; the friction reported is about workflow (merge and conflict edge cases), not performance.

tools.name: Xum
tools.tagline: Xum makes it easy to run parallel coding agents, each with its own isolated workspace, right from your browser or desktop.
tools.valueProp: Xum combines its own model-agnostic agent loop with local worktrees, SSH hosts, Docker, and Coder workspaces in one desktop or browser UI. Unlike Coder Agents, it runs independently of a Coder deployment.

pricing.notes: AGPL app is free; bring model API keys or use optional Xum Gateway evaluation credits. Coder-backed workspaces may incur separate Coder/infrastructure costs.

featureNotes.platforms.windows: Windows installer and support are explicitly labeled alpha on the install page.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: New branches are created on workspace fork; ordinary workspaces can switch or create branches rather than receiving a mandatory branch.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Docs say to ask the agent to open a PR using its Git credentials; no dedicated in-app PR action is documented.
featureNotes.isolation.mergeAssist: Git divergence and potential conflicts appear in the UI, but automated merging is not documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.automations: The CLI supports CI/CD scripts and experimental JavaScript workflows; no built-in scheduler is documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Native notifications fire on response completion or by the agent notify tool; waiting-for-input alerts need a user instruction.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Config/scripts extend Xum behavior, but there is no documented loader for third-party panels or providers. Experimental .xum/tool_pre and tool_post hooks run around built-in tool calls, and trusted JavaScript workflows drive runs; see /hooks/tools and /reference/cli.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: The xum run/workflow CLI drives agent tasks; the local server serves the browser/mobile UI. This is not a documented general-purpose REST API.

github.description: A desktop app for isolated, parallel agentic development

editorial.reachRationale: Product-specific @coder/xum had about 95k npm downloads in 30 days, five recent release assets about 5.5k downloads, 2,038 stars and 23 contributors. The company-wide Coder audience is excluded; the product account and HN query offer little reliable evidence of broad adoption.
editorial.polishRationale: Detailed docs and signed macOS builds, but Windows is alpha and workflows and tool hooks are experimental.
editorial.depthRationale: Managed worktrees, SSH/Docker/Coder runtimes, custom modes and subagents, forked conversations, diff view, notifications and an automation CLI go beyond session switching.
editorial.feelRationale: The docs identify an Electron app, and package.json uses React and Electron. No first-party speed claim or credible product-specific lag report was found, so a typical web-rendered interface supports a neutral feel.

tools.name: Zed
tools.tagline: Multiple Agents, One Editor
tools.valueProp: The one native editor here: a threads sidebar runs many agent threads at once, each on Zed’s own agent or an external one over ACP (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor), with a worktree per thread and OS-level sandboxing of tool calls. Orchestration lives in the editor, not a separate app.

maker.name: Zed Industries, Inc.
maker.funding: Series B: $32M led by Sequoia Capital (announced 2025-08-20), bringing total raised to over $42M.

pricing.notes: Personal $0/forever: 2,000 accepted edit predictions, unlimited use with your own API keys or external agents (Claude Agent, Codex CLI, etc.). Pro $10/mo (14-day free trial, $5 of GPT-5.6 Luna usage, no card required): unlimited edit predictions, $5 of Zed-hosted tokens included, then billed at API list price +10%. Business $30/seat/mo (order forms at 25+ seats, no minimum): org-wide AI model policies, data governance, unified billing, RBAC; no free trial. External Agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) are billed separately by their own providers, Zed does not charge for them.

featureNotes.platforms.cli: The `zed` binary is primarily an editor launcher (e.g. `zed ssh://host/path`), not a headless agent-steering CLI in its own right.
featureNotes.agents.copilotCli: Docs list Copilot among External Agents but qualify it 'where available'; auth is owned by the Copilot integration rather than a documented first-class ACP setup like Claude/Codex/Gemini.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: Docs list Cursor among External Agents but qualify it 'where available' and note Cursor subscriptions do not configure Zed's provider settings; use Cursor's own external-agent/CLI setup.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: 'Custom Agent' entries in Agent Settings let you point Zed at any ACP-compatible command, not literally any CLI, the target process must speak the Agent Client Protocol.
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Threads can be isolated into a Git worktree via the title-bar worktree picker, but creation is a manual per-thread choice, not automatic one-worktree-per-task management.
featureNotes.isolation.containers: OS-level sandboxing (Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap namespaces on Linux, WSL on Windows) restricts the Zed Agent's `terminal` and `fetch` tools by default since v1.14; it is not Docker/microVM-style container isolation and does not describe External Agents, which run their own process.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Worktrees start in detached HEAD; you pick or create a branch yourself via the branch picker rather than Zed auto-creating one per task.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: Remote Development connects to a Zed headless server you install on your own SSH-reachable machine (no vendor relay since v0.157), but there is no separate self-hostable orchestration server for the Threads Sidebar itself.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: The editor, External Agents and your-own-machine Remote Development need no Zed server, but Zed-hosted AI models, Pro/Business billing and multiplayer collaboration depend on Zed's own servers.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Zed has long offered live multiplayer editing (shared cursors, following); whether two people can see/steer the same agent thread specifically was not confirmed within the bounded docs read.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: Partial, not true, specifically for the Threads Sidebar / Agent Panel (the general editor extension ecosystem is irrelevant unless an extension can actually touch that surface): Zed's real, documented, code-loading extension SDK (Rust compiled to WebAssembly, installed via the built-in Extensions panel) provided exactly six capabilities per its own docs, as of September 2026 (docs/extensions/developing-extensions: 'They can provide languages, themes, debuggers, snippets, and MCP servers' plus icon themes) -- none of which can add a new agent, panel, view or command to the Threads Sidebar or Agent Panel. A real 'Agent Server Extensions' capability that *did* let a packaged extension register a new ACP agent into the new-thread menu existed but is explicitly deprecated ('As of Zed v1.5.0, ACP extensions have been deprecated in favor of the ACP Registry', docs/extensions/agent-servers). The two mechanisms that add a new entry to the Threads Sidebar's agent picker are config-level or external-process, not Zed extension code: (1) the ACP Registry (agentclientprotocol.com/registry, a cross-editor spec also used by JetBrains) where any agent developer submits an `agent.json` via pull request and the agent then appears in Zed's New Thread menu as a separate ACP-speaking process Zed spawns and talks to over the wire -- a documented control-protocol integration, not code loaded into Zed itself; (2) manually adding a `agent_servers` entry to `settings.json` (Custom Agent) -- exactly the 'custom agent/provider definitions by config' partial example. Both meet the partial bar; neither is a plugin SDK that loads third-party code into the Threads Sidebar/Agent Panel itself.

github.description: Code at the speed of thought – Zed is a high-performance, multiplayer code editor from the creators of Atom and Tree-sitter.

top.title: Zed editor switching graphics lib from blade to wgpu

editorial.reachRationale: Reach scores the parent editor's real user base, since that is what the parallel-agents feature inherits: 90,893 GitHub stars, a 30,422-member product Discord, an 84,652-follower product X account, weekly releases since 2021, a $32M Sequoia-led Series B (total $42M+), and repeated well-received Show HN/HN front-page stories (e.g. 317-point graphics-engine post) place it as a name most practitioners know, clearly past hobby scale. Not dominant because it is one of several serious editors/agent surfaces (VS Code, Cursor, JetBrains) rather than the default choice for a majority of people running coding agents.
editorial.polishRationale: Docs are thorough, consistently structured and cross-linked, releases ship weekly with detailed per-area changelogs, and the product has shipped continuously since 2021. Judged from documentation rather than direct use.
editorial.depthRationale: Beyond a session switcher, Zed ships per-thread Git worktree isolation with a create_worktree task hook, per-message checkpoints with restore, OS-level sandboxing of agent tool calls with an escalation-request UI, MCP forwarding to external agents, and thread history/import across agent providers, but it lacks a task board/kanban, automated branch-per-task, PR creation, cross-agent messaging or subagent orchestration that some siblings here have.
editorial.feelRationale: Built in Rust on Zed's own GPUI framework (not Electron); the maker markets the editor and its agent UI as running at 'buttery-smooth 120 fps' (zed.dev/blog/120fps, linked directly from the parallel-agents launch post), and the docs describe instant thread switching (ctrl-tab) and a virtualized Threads Sidebar rather than a laggy web view.

tools.name: Zeron
tools.tagline: Access your agents from any device.
tools.valueProp: A native Rust desktop app that boots local-only with no account until you opt into sync. Remote control then runs through Zeron’s own relay, which ships in the repo but is not supported for self-hosting; the iPhone client was TestFlight-only as of September 2026.

maker.name: Wing (wingleeio), zeronsh GitHub org
maker.funding: no disclosed funding; GitHub Sponsors link to the zeronsh org

pricing.notes: No pricing page and no paid tier. The app is free and MIT-licensed; agents run under your own Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Grok, Hermes, Pi, OpenCode and Antigravity CLI logins. The optional multi-device sync (WorkOS sign-in, Cloudflare edge) was free as of September 2026, with no published terms or limits.

featureNotes.platforms.macos: Apple silicon dmg only; no Intel build and no Homebrew cask. The install.sh script refuses macOS and points at the dmg.
featureNotes.platforms.windows: x64 portable zip plus an .exe installer (both on releases since v0.2.66); in-app updates need zeron-update.json beside the portable binary.
featureNotes.platforms.linux: x64 and arm64 tar.gz; install.sh installs a systemd --user service that survives reboots. The sidebar browser additionally needs WebKitGTK 4.1 and JSON-GLib packages, which the installer does not set up.
featureNotes.platforms.ios: A SwiftUI app lives in apps/ios with an internal-only TestFlight workflow; the homepage lists the App Store as 'coming soon'. The phone is a viewport only: no engine runs on it, sessions execute on a desktop or headless host.
featureNotes.platforms.web: Native gpui client only; no browser client.
featureNotes.platforms.cli: The `zeron` binary has headless, daemon install/start/stop, login/logout, status, sync and update subcommands and can open a conversation URL, but it cannot start or prompt an agent from the shell.
featureNotes.execution.remoteOwn: `zeron headless` on a VPS or always-on machine (launchd/systemd service); after `zeron login` every signed-in device drives it through Zeron's Cloudflare Durable Object relay. No SSH or direct-TCP path is documented.
featureNotes.execution.cloudManaged: Zeron provisions no compute; agents only run on devices you install the engine on.
featureNotes.execution.selfHostServer: The edge (Cloudflare Worker + Durable Objects, TypeScript) is in the repo and ZERON_EDGE_URL overrides the endpoint, but ARCHITECTURE.md says a supported self-hosted backend contract is deferred and the overrides are 'development/deployment seams, not a promised compatibility surface'. Auth is WorkOS.
featureNotes.agents.claudeCode: First-class harness with model/effort catalogs and AskUserQuestion bridging. docs/research/acp.md says it moved to the pinned claude-agent-acp adapter in Aug 2026 while docs/PARITY.md still describes the stream-json adapter.
featureNotes.agents.codex: First-class harness; docs disagree on whether it runs through `codex app-server` JSON-RPC or the codex-acp adapter (see claudeCode note). Renders Codex-generated images inline.
featureNotes.agents.opencode: Driven natively over `opencode serve` HTTP/SSE, not ACP.
featureNotes.agents.cursorAgent: `cursor-agent acp`; Cursor's ask_question, create_plan and update_todos extensions are handled. Release notes through v0.2.76 are still fixing abandoned Cursor sessions.
featureNotes.agents.pi: Via the community pi-acp adapter (pinned 0.0.33, managed npm install); requires the pi CLI itself.
featureNotes.agents.anyCli: Harnesses are a fixed enum (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Grok, Hermes, Pi, OpenCode, Antigravity); Settings > Agents only enables or disables detected CLIs. No custom command or generic ACP entry.
featureNotes.agents.builtIn: Homepage: 'Zeron is not a new harness.'
featureNotes.isolation.worktrees: Branch picker has a worktree toggle; Zeron runs `git worktree add` under ~/.zeron/worktrees/<repo>/<name> with an auto-generated name.
featureNotes.isolation.branchPerTask: Only when the worktree toggle is on: each worktree gets a matching auto-named `zeron/<name>` branch.
featureNotes.isolation.diffReview: Changes pane shows the live branch diff (per-file collapse, split/unified) and a commit-history view; line-pinned review comments on diff or file lines are staged on the composer and folded into the next prompt.
featureNotes.isolation.prCreation: Shows an open/merged/closed badge for the branch's existing pull request (polled via the gh CLI) and opens it in the browser; no create-PR, commit or push action was found.
featureNotes.orchestration.parallelSessions: Sessions from every signed-in device appear in one attention-sorted list ('Every machine's sessions, one list').
featureNotes.orchestration.taskBoard: A per-session message queue (reorderable, hold-until-turn-end) exists; there is no task board or queue that feeds agents.
featureNotes.orchestration.subagents: Renders Grok, Devin, Codex and OpenCode native subagents as chips with nested transcripts; Zeron itself cannot spawn or steer agents from an agent.
featureNotes.orchestration.notifications: Desktop banners (macOS notification center, Linux notify-send) plus sounds for task completed, input required, and errors/disconnections, with an 'only when in the background' option. No mobile push documented.
featureNotes.orchestration.voice: Microphone on/off sounds exist only as unused auditions in docs/sound-design; no dictation or speech code.
featureNotes.collaboration.multiUser: WorkOS accounts with organizations ('Create your workspace', memberships), but session and registry rows are private per user and 'never visible to every member of an organization'.
featureNotes.collaboration.sharedSessions: Every device signed into the same account can watch and drive the same session; there is no two-person sharing.
featureNotes.openness.selfHostable: Local-only mode needs no vendor server at all. Multi-device sync depends on Zeron's Cloudflare edge and WorkOS auth, and self-hosting the edge is explicitly unsupported.
featureNotes.openness.byoSubscription: Agent-account switching with rate-limit meters for Claude Code and Codex (credential swap); other agents use their own CLI auth. Zeron resells nothing.
featureNotes.openness.telemetryOptOut: No telemetry code in the desktop app or engine. The landing page loads a PostHog pageview script that honours Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control.
featureNotes.openness.pluginSystem: No plugin or extension SDK for Zeron itself, and it explicitly does not execute third-party code (“Zeron does not fetch or execute VSIX packages at runtime”). The documented mechanism is importing VS Code theme files or theme extension packages, which Zeron compiles into its own theme schema (docs/theme-system.md); that restyles the app and adds nothing to it.
featureNotes.openness.apiOrMcp: Typed JSON RPC over WebSocket on a localhost IPC port that any viewport can attach to, plus a headless engine; described in ARCHITECTURE.md, not documented as a public API. No MCP server.

github.description: A native control plane for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin and other coding agents.

top.title: Show HN: GS2JSON: Turn any Google Sheet to a JSON – No login – open-source

editorial.reachRationale: Created in July 2026, with real development pace (daily releases) but a very small product-specific footprint: a 98-member Discord, no legible HN presence (the query returns only an unrelated namesake), and a founder's personal X account rather than a product one, so this reads as early rather than an established quantity.
editorial.polishRationale: My call from hands-on use: refined, and a good challenger. The gpui UI is what people on X praise, and the README, ARCHITECTURE and PARITY docs are unusually candid. Short of finished: the repo was created in July 2026 and ships several releases a day with fix-heavy notes (Cursor sessions still being stabilised in v0.2.76), macOS is Apple-silicon only, iOS is not public, Linux's browser needs manual packages, and PARITY lists engine hardening and reduced-motion as gaps, as of September 2026.
editorial.depthRationale: Past a session switcher it has managed worktrees with auto-named branches, a live diff pane with line-pinned review comments that feed the next prompt, commit history, a terminal panel, a file tree and editor, a sidebar browser that auto-discovers dev servers, a reorderable message queue, and multi-device remote control; but no PR creation, automations, task board, agent-spawns-agent or API.
editorial.feelRationale: Rust with a gpui (GPU-rendered, Zed's UI framework) frontend built explicitly to replace an earlier Electron/React client, using gpui's virtualized sum-tree list for the transcript; unsolicited X quotes call the UI 'buttery smooth' and a third-party summary notes it is 'Built on GPUI with no Electron or Tauri.' The site owner separately reports it feels exceptionally fast, and no jank complaints turned up.
